userQuestion: This happened years ago — is it too late to sue?
whatsHappening: More than two years seem to have passed since the events. But the day the claim was discovered has not been worked out yet. Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise, you have two years from the day the claim was discovered to start a case. Some proceedings fall outside the Limitations Act, 2002. One example is a proceeding the Real Property Limitations Act applies to. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you first knew four things. First, that the injury, loss or damage happened. Second, that an act or omission caused it or helped cause it. Third, that it was the act or omission of the person you would sue. Fourth, that given the kind of loss, a court case would be a fitting way to try to fix it. The second is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities, in your circumstances, ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless it is proved otherwise. Some claims are about a demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004. For those, the loss happens on the first day the obligation is not performed after a demand is made.
whatToDoNext: The two years do not run while you are a minor and have no litigation guardian for the claim. They also do not run while a physical, mental or psychological condition makes you unable to start a case, and you have no litigation guardian for the claim. You are presumed to have been able to start a case at all times, unless it is proved otherwise. If a pause for such a condition ends with less than six months left, the time is extended to six months after the day it ends. Time also stops while you and the other person have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or help you resolve it. It starts again when the claim is resolved, when that process ends, or when one of you ends or withdraws from the agreement. This pause covers both the two years and the 15 years described below. The other person, or their agent, may have admitted liability in writing and signed it. For some claims, the act or omission is then treated as taking place on the day of that admission. These include a claim for a fixed sum of money or to get back personal property. This counts only if the admission was made before the time ran out. It must also have been made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other person or their agent has the same effect.
yourDeadline:
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel. The two years do not run while the person with the claim is a minor and has no litigation guardian. They also do not run while a physical, mental or psychological condition keeps the person from starting a case, and they have no litigation guardian. A person is presumed able to start a case unless shown otherwise. If that condition ends with less than six months left, the time runs to six months after it ends. The 15 years also do not run while the other side wilfully hides from you that the loss happened, that an act or omission caused it, or that it was theirs. Nor do they run while the other side wilfully misleads you about whether a court case is a proper way to fix it. You must prove this. The two years and the 15 years also stop while the parties have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or help resolve it. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission. For a debt payable on demand, the loss happens on the first day it is not paid after a demand for payment.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: Separately, no case can be started more than 15 years after the day of the act or omission, even if the two years have not run out. For the 15 years, an act or omission that goes on over time counts from the day it stops. A series of acts or omissions about the same obligation counts from the day of the last one. For a demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004, it counts from the first day the obligation is not performed after a demand. Some claims have no time limit at all, such as a claim based on a sexual assault. The 15 years do not run while you are a minor, or unable to start a case because of a physical, mental or psychological condition, and have no litigation guardian. They also do not run while the other person wilfully hides from you that the loss happened, that an act or omission caused it, or that it was theirs. Nor do they run while the other person wilfully misleads you about whether a court case is a fitting way to fix the loss. The burden of proving that one of these 15-year pauses applies is on you. Some time limits in other Acts are listed in the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002. One is section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act. It covers a case for libel in a newspaper or broadcast. That case must be started within three months after the person defamed learned of the libel. First, you must give the defendant written notice of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learned of the libel. The notice must be served the same way as a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. These two time limits apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. The Libel and Slander Act also sets conditions a newspaper or broadcaster must meet to rely on them.

citations.quote: This Act applies to claims pursued in court proceedings other than, (a) proceedings to which the Real Property Limitations Act applies;
Unless this Act provides otherwise, a proceeding shall not be commenced in respect of a claim after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered.

A claim is discovered on the earlier of, (a) the day on which the person with the claim first knew, (i) that the injury, loss or damage had occurred, (ii) that the injury, loss or damage was caused by or contributed to by an act or omission, (iii) that the act or omission was that of the person against whom the claim is made, and (iv) that, having regard to the nature of the injury, loss or damage, a proceeding would be an appropriate means to seek to remedy it; and (b) the day on which a reasonable person with the abilities and in the circumstances of the person with the claim first ought to have known of the matters referred to in clause (a).

For the purposes of subclause (1) (a) (i), the day on which injury, loss or damage occurs in relation to a demand obligation is the first day on which there is a failure to perform the obligation, once a demand for the performance is made.
Subsection (3) applies in respect of every demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004.

For the purposes of this section, the day an act or omission on which a claim is based takes place is, (a) in the case of a continuous act or omission, the day on which the act or omission ceases; (b) in the case of a series of acts or omissions in respect of the same obligation, the day on which the last act or omission in the series occurs; (c) in the case of an act or omission in respect of a demand obligation, the first day on which there is a failure to perform the obligation, once a demand for the performance is made.
Clause (6) (c) applies in respect of every demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004.

A person with a claim shall be presumed to have known of the matters referred to in clause (1) (a) on the day the act or omission on which the claim is based took place, unless the contrary is proved.

The limitation period established by section 4 does not run during any time in which the person with the claim, (a) is a minor; and (b) is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim.

The limitation period established by section 4 does not run during any time in which the person with the claim, (a) is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim because of his or her physical, mental or psychological condition; and (b) is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim.
A person shall be presumed to have been capable of commencing a proceeding in respect of a claim at all times unless the contrary is proved.

If the running of a limitation period is postponed or suspended under this section and the period has less than six months to run when the postponement or suspension ends, the period is extended to include the day that is six months after the day on which the postponement or suspension ends.

If a person with a claim and a person against whom the claim is made have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or assist them in resolving it, the limitation periods established by sections 4 and 15 do not run from the date the agreement is made until, (a) the date the claim is resolved; (b) the date the attempted resolution process is terminated; or (c) the date a party terminates or withdraws from the agreement.

If a person acknowledges liability in respect of a claim for payment of a liquidated sum, the recovery of personal property, the enforcement of a charge on personal property or relief from enforcement of a charge on personal property, the act or omission on which the claim is based shall be deemed to have taken place on the day on which the acknowledgment was made.

This section does not apply unless the acknowledgment is made to the person with the claim, the person's agent or an official receiver or trustee acting under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada) before the expiry of the limitation period applicable to the claim.
Subsections (1), (2), (3), (6) and (7) do not apply unless the acknowledgment is in writing and signed by the person making it or the person's agent.

In the case of a claim for payment of a liquidated sum, part payment of the sum by the person against whom the claim is made or by the person's agent has the same effect as the acknowledgment referred to in subsection (10).

Even if the limitation period established by any other section of this Act in respect of a claim has not expired, no proceeding shall be commenced in respect of the claim after the expiry of a limitation period established by this section.
No proceeding shall be commenced in respect of any claim after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission on which the claim is based took place.

The limitation period established by subsection (2) does not run during any time in which, (a) the person with the claim, (i) is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim because of his or her physical, mental or psychological condition, and (ii) is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim; (b) the person with the claim is a minor and is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim; or (c) the person against whom the claim is made, (i) wilfully conceals from the person with the claim the fact that injury, loss or damage has occurred, that it was caused by or contributed to by an act or omission or that the act or omission was that of the person against whom the claim is made, or (ii) wilfully misleads the person with the claim as to the appropriateness of a proceeding as a means of remedying the injury, loss or damage.
The burden of proving that subsection (4) applies is on the person with the claim.
There is no limitation period in respect of, ... (h) a proceeding based on a sexual assault;
A limitation period set out in or under another Act that applies to a claim to which this Act applies is of no effect unless, (a) the provision establishing it is listed in the Schedule to this Act;
LIBEL AND SLANDER ACT |SECTION 6 |

No action for libel in a newspaper or in a broadcast lies unless the plaintiff has, within six weeks after the alleged libel has come to the plaintiff's knowledge, given to the defendant notice in writing, specifying the matter complained of, which shall be served in the same manner as a statement of claim or by delivering it to a grown-up person at the chief office of the defendant.

userQuestion: My claim was issued — how do I serve the defendant, and by when?
whatsHappening: The registrar has issued your claim. That means it was dated, signed, sealed with the court's seal and given a court file number. The next step is to serve it on each defendant. If you started with a notice of action, you must first file your statement of claim. That is because the notice may not be served separately from the statement of claim. A statement of claim must be served within six months after it is issued. If you started with a notice of action, the notice and the statement of claim must be served together. That must be done within six months after the notice of action was issued.
whatToDoNext: If you used a notice of action, you must file your statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice was issued. After that, you can file it only with the defendant's written consent, or with the court's permission asked for on notice to the defendant. In Ontario, the claim must be served personally, or by one of the alternatives to personal service in the rules. To serve a person personally, leave a copy with that person, unless they are under a disability. To serve a corporation that is not a municipality, leave a copy with an officer, director or agent of it. Or leave it at any of its places of business with a person who appears to control or manage that place. Other kinds of parties are served personally in other ways, such as a municipality, a minor, a partnership or a sole proprietorship. One alternative is to mail a copy, with an acknowledgment of receipt card (Form 16A), to the person's last known address. That service counts only from the date you receive the card back. Another alternative applies if you try to serve personally at the person's home and cannot. You may leave a copy, in a sealed envelope addressed to them, at the home with anyone who appears to be an adult member of the same household. For this method, you must also mail another copy to them at that home on the same day or the next day. Service this way takes effect on the fifth day after the copy is mailed. If the defendant has a lawyer, you may leave a copy with the lawyer or an employee in the lawyer's office. This works only if the lawyer writes on the document, or a copy, that they accept service and the date they accept it. A corporation's head office, registered office or main place of business may not be found at the last address recorded with the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery. If so, you may mail a copy to the corporation at that address. For an extra-provincial corporation, the same applies to its attorney for service in Ontario. If prompt service is impractical for any reason, the court may order substituted service. Where needed in the interest of justice, it may excuse service instead. Service may be proved by an affidavit of the person who served the claim (Form 16B). If the defendant is outside Ontario, other rules apply. In some cases you need the court's permission to serve them there. Some countries are contracting states under the Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents, signed at The Hague in 1965. In one of those countries, the claim must be served in one of two ways. One is through that country's central authority. The other is a way the Convention permits that these rules would also permit in Ontario.
yourDeadline:
Serve the statement of claim on the defendant. You have 6 months after the day the statement of claim was issued. If you started with a notice of action, serve the notice and the statement of claim together within six months after the notice was issued. The time can be extended by filing a consent. The court can also extend it, before or after the time runs out. If you do not serve the claim in time, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay.

If you started with a notice of action, file your statement of claim (Form 14D). You have 30 days after the day the notice of action was issued. This applies only if you started with a notice of action. After the 30 days, you can file the statement of claim only with the defendant's written consent or the court's permission. You must ask for that permission on notice to the defendant.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). userQuestion: The defendant served a statement of defence — what happens now?
whatsHappening: The defendant has answered your claim with a statement of defence. In an action, the pleadings are the statement of claim, the statement of defence and a reply (Form 25A), if there is one. Pleadings close when two things are true. First, you have delivered a reply to every defence, or the time to deliver a reply has run out. Second, every defendant who did not deliver a defence in time has been noted in default.
whatToDoNext: Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a reply if you plan to prove a version of the facts that is different from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. You must also deliver a reply to raise a matter that might take the other side by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in the reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. A reply is due within 10 days after service of the statement of defence. If the defendant also made a counterclaim, you must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after service of the statement of defence and counterclaim. Any reply is due within the same 20 days. If you deliver a reply as well, the reply and defence to counterclaim go in one document. If you deliver a reply, you must admit every fact in the defence that you do not dispute. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. Any party may ask for a jury by delivering a jury notice (Form 47A) at any time before pleadings close. This does not apply if section 108 of the Courts of Justice Act or another statute requires a trial without a jury. An action under the simplified procedure (Rule 76) cannot be tried with a jury. A party may still deliver a jury notice if the action involves a claim arising from slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment. If they do, the action no longer goes under the simplified procedure. The party who delivered the jury notice must also deliver a notice (Form 76A) saying the action goes on as an ordinary action.
yourDeadline:
If a reply is required, deliver it. You have 10 days after the day the statement of defence was served on you. A reply is needed only if you will prove a different version of the facts than the defence pleads, or must raise a matter that could take the other side by surprise. Otherwise you must not deliver one. If the defendant also counterclaimed, you have 20 days instead for a reply and defence to counterclaim. Deliver means serve it on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Your action may be under the simplified procedure, and the defence may object that your claim does not fit it. Then the action stays under that procedure only if your reply gives up the parts of the claim that do not fit. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. That can come 10 days after the defence if no reply is delivered. If a reply is delivered sooner, pleadings close when it is delivered, as long as every defendant has delivered a defence or been noted in default. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If a third party delivered a statement of defence in the main action and you want to reply to it, deliver a reply. You have 10 days after the day the third party's statement of defence was served on you. This applies only where a defendant brought in a third party who has also defended the main action. A reply is needed only if you will prove a different version of the facts than the defence pleads, or must raise a matter that could take the other side by surprise. Otherwise you must not deliver one.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

You must then deliver a notice (Form 76A) saying so, after all the pleadings have been delivered. A claim or part of a claim that you give up cannot be brought in any other proceeding. If any party plans to get evidence through discovery, such as documents or an examination, the parties must agree to a written discovery plan. The plan must be agreed before the earlier of two times: 60 days after pleadings close, or a longer time the parties agree to, and the first try to get the evidence.

citations.quote: In an action commenced by statement of claim or notice of action, pleadings shall consist of the statement of claim (Form 14A, 14B or 14D), statement of defence (Form 18A) and reply (Form 25A), if any.

Pleadings in an action are closed when, (a) the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence in the action or the time for delivery of a reply has expired; and (b) every defendant who is in default in delivering a defence in the action has been noted in default.
"deliver" means serve and file with proof of service, and "delivery" has a corresponding meaning;

A party who intends to prove a version of the facts different from that pleaded in the opposite party's defence shall deliver a reply setting out the different version, unless it has already been pleaded in the claim.

A party who intends to reply in response to a defence on any matter that might, if not specifically pleaded, take the opposite party by surprise or raise an issue that has not been raised by a previous pleading shall deliver a reply setting out that matter, subject to subrule 25.06 (5) (inconsistent claims or new claims).

An allegation that is inconsistent with an allegation made in a party's previous pleading or that raises a new ground of claim shall not be made in a subsequent pleading but by way of amendment to the previous pleading.
A party shall not deliver a reply except where required to do so by subrule (1) or (2).

A reply, if any, shall be delivered within ten days after service of the statement of defence except where the defendant counterclaims, in which case a reply and defence to counterclaim, if any, shall be delivered within twenty days after service of the statement of defence and counterclaim.

The plaintiff and any other defendant to a counterclaim who is already a party to the main action shall deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within twenty days after service of the statement of defence and counterclaim.

Where the plaintiff delivers a reply in the main action, the defence to counterclaim shall be included in the same document as the reply and the document shall be entitled a reply and defence to counterclaim.
A party who delivers a reply shall admit every allegation of fact in the opposite party's defence that the party does not dispute.
A party who does not deliver a reply within the prescribed time shall be deemed to deny the allegations of fact made in the defence of the opposite party.

A party to an action may require that the issues of fact be tried or the damages be assessed, or both, by a jury, by delivering a jury notice (Form 47A) at any time before the close of pleadings, unless section 108 of the Courts of Justice Act or another statute requires that the action be tried without a jury.
An action that is proceeding under this Rule shall not be tried with a jury and, subject to subrule (2), no party to the action may deliver a jury notice under rule 47.01.

A party to an action that is proceeding under this Rule may deliver a jury notice under rule 47.01 if the action involves a claim for relief arising from one of the following: 1. Slander. 2. Libel. 3. Malicious arrest. 4. Malicious prosecution. 5. False imprisonment.

If a jury notice is delivered in accordance with subrule (2), the action may no longer proceed under this Rule and the party delivering the jury notice shall deliver a notice (Form 76A) stating that the action and any related proceedings are continued as an ordinary action.

An action commenced under this Rule continues to proceed under this Rule unless, (a) the defendant objects in the statement of defence to the action proceeding under this Rule because the plaintiff's claim does not comply with subrule (1), and the plaintiff does not abandon in the reply the claims or parts of claims that do not comply;

If an action commenced under this Rule may no longer proceed under this Rule because of an amendment to the pleadings under Rule 26 or as a result of the operation of subrule (5), (a) the action is continued under the ordinary procedure; and (b) the plaintiff shall deliver, after all the pleadings have been delivered or at the time of amending the pleadings, as the case may be, a notice (Form 76A) stating that the action and any related proceedings are continued as an ordinary action.

A party who abandons a claim or part of a claim or amends a pleading so that the claim, counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim complies with subrule (1) may not bring the claim or part in any other proceeding.

Where a party to an action intends to obtain evidence under any of the following Rules, the parties to the action shall agree to a discovery plan in accordance with this rule: 1. Rule 30 (Discovery of Documents). 2. Rule 31 (Examination for Discovery). 3. Rule 32 (Inspection of Property). 4. Rule 33 (Medical Examination). 5. Rule 35 (Examination for Discovery by Written Questions).
The discovery plan shall be in writing
The discovery plan shall be agreed to before the earlier of, (a) 60 days after the close of pleadings or such longer period as the parties may agree to; and (b) attempting to obtain the evidence.

userQuestion: There is a default judgment against me — what can I do?
whatsHappening: You were noted in default. Then a judgment was signed or granted against you. Being noted in default means you are deemed to admit that every fact in the statement of claim is true. You must not deliver a statement of defence or take any other step in the action. To do so, you need the court's leave or the plaintiff's consent. One step needs neither: a motion to set aside the noting of default or any judgment obtained because of it.
whatToDoNext: You may bring a motion to set aside the judgment. Who decides it depends on how the judgment was made. The registrar may have signed it, or the court may have granted it on a motion under rule 19.04. If so, the court may set it aside or change it on terms that are just. Or it may have come from a motion for judgment under rule 19.05, or after a trial. Then a judge may set it aside or change it on terms that are just. If the judgment is set aside, the court or judge may also set aside the noting of default. A document may have been served on you in a way the rules allow. Even so, on that motion you may show that it never came to your notice. Or you may show that you learned of it only after it was served or deemed served.
yourDeadline: If you want the default judgment set aside, bring a motion to set it aside. The rule sets no fixed number of days. The court can set aside a judgment the registrar signed, or one the court granted on a motion under rule 19.04. A judge can set aside one granted on a motion for judgment under rule 19.05, or after a trial. An appeal from a final order of a judge must start within 30 days after the order is made. Appealing a refusal to set aside a default judgment does not by itself stop the judgment from being enforced.
whatHappensAfter: If the court refuses to set aside the judgment, an appeal from that refusal does not by itself put the judgment on hold. Putting it on hold is called a stay. The judgment may be stayed by an order, on terms that are just. The order may come from the court whose decision is being appealed, or from a judge of the court where the appeal or a motion for leave to appeal is brought. A stay from the court whose decision is being appealed ends if no notice of appeal, or notice of motion for leave to appeal, is delivered in time.

userQuestion: What is discovery, and what do I have to hand over?
whatsHappening: Pleadings close when two things are done. First, the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence, or the time for a reply has run out. Second, every defendant who is in default of a defence has been noted in default. If any party wants to get evidence in one of five ways, the parties must agree to a discovery plan. The five are documents, examination for discovery, inspection of property, a medical exam, and examination by written questions. If the court has set a plan for the parties, they do not need to agree on one.
whatToDoNext: You must agree on the plan before the earlier of two times. One is 60 days after pleadings close, or a longer time the parties agree to. The other is when anyone first tries to get the evidence. The plan must be in writing. It must say what the document discovery will cover, given relevance, costs, and how important and complex the issues are. It must give the dates for each party to serve an affidavit of documents (Form 30A or 30B). It must say when and how documents will be produced, and what that will cost. It must name who will be examined orally for discovery, and say when and for how long. It must add anything else that helps finish discovery quickly, in a way that fits how important and complex the case is. You must serve an affidavit of documents on every other party. In it, list every document relevant to any issue in the action that is or was in your possession, control or power. List them as fully as you know or believe. Documents you claim privilege for must be listed too, in a separate schedule, with your grounds. Documents you no longer have go in another schedule. Say when and how you lost them, and where they are now. Do not file the affidavit unless it is relevant to an issue on a pending motion or at trial. Later, you may get a relevant document that is not privileged, or find the affidavit is wrong or incomplete. Then you must serve a supplementary affidavit right away. Another party may serve you with a request to inspect documents (Form 30C). It lets them see the documents your affidavit says you have, except privileged ones. It may also cover documents you have that are named in your originating process, pleadings or a served affidavit. If you get one, you must at once name a date within five days after it was served. You must also name a time between 9:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., and a place. The place is your lawyer's office or some other convenient place. You must then have the documents there at that time. Unless the parties agree otherwise, the documents you listed that are not privileged must be produced at your examination for discovery and at trial. So must any document you have already produced for inspection. No party may spend more than seven hours in all on oral examinations for discovery, however many people are examined. More time needs the consent of the parties or the court's leave. A person examined must answer any proper question about an issue in the action, or about other matters the rules open to discovery. They answer as best they know or believe.
yourDeadline:
If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If you gave an undertaking or took a question under advisement at an examination for discovery, answer it. You have 60 days after the day you gave that response at the examination. If you do not answer in that time, you cannot use that information at trial without the trial judge's permission. You still have to keep an undertaking.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if the plaintiff is under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

userQuestion: Do we have to go to mediation, and what do I need to do for it?
whatsHappening: Mandatory mediation applies to some actions. These include actions started in the City of Ottawa, the City of Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out, such as mortgage actions and actions on the Commercial List in Toronto. The court may also exempt an action from mediation if a party brings a motion asking for that. In mediation, a neutral person helps the parties talk to each other, to help them reach a result they all accept.
whatToDoNext: The parties must choose a mediator. It can be a person on the county's list whom the parties agree on, or a person not on the list if the parties consent. Before the action is set down for trial, one of the parties must file a notice (Form 24.1A) with the mediation co-ordinator. The notice gives the mediator's name and the date of the session. The filing can instead be the mediator's report saying the mediation is over. At least seven days before the session, every party must prepare a statement in Form 24.1C. By then you must also give a copy to every other party and to the mediator. The statement must name the factual and legal issues in dispute, and briefly set out your position and interests. You must attach any documents you think are of central importance in the action. If you are the plaintiff, you must also put a copy of the pleadings with the mediator's copy of your statement. The parties, and their lawyers if they have them, must attend the session unless the court orders otherwise. An insurer may have to pay all or part of a judgment for a party, or pay the party back for it. If so, someone for the insurer must attend, and that party does not have to, unless the court orders otherwise. You may need someone else's okay before you agree to settle. If so, you must arrange before the session to be able to reach that person by phone the whole time.
yourDeadline:
If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

Prepare a statement of issues (Form 24.1C) and give a copy to every other party and to the mediator. Do this at least 7 days before the date of the mediation session. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. The plaintiff must also include a copy of the pleadings with the mediator's copy. A party may fail to do this, so that holding the session is not practical. Then the mediator cancels it and files a certificate of non-compliance. The matter then goes to a judge or associate judge. The judge can dismiss the action of a plaintiff who did not comply. The judge can strike out the defence of a defendant who did not comply, or make other orders.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: A party may fail to attend within the first 30 minutes, so that holding the session is not practical. Then the mediator must cancel it and file a certificate of non-compliance (Form 24.1D). The matter then goes to a judge or associate judge. The judge may hold a case conference. The judge may also set a timetable, strike out any document a party filed, or order a party to pay costs. The judge may dismiss the action if the party who did not comply is a plaintiff, or strike out the defence if that party is a defendant. Or the judge may make any other order that is just. Within 10 days after the mediation ends, the mediator must give the co-ordinator and the parties a report on it. Any agreement that settles some or all of the issues must be signed by the parties or their lawyers.

(c) actions placed on the Commercial List established by practice direction in the Toronto Region; (d) actions under Rule 64 (Mortgage Actions);
The court may make an order on a party's motion exempting the action from this Rule.
In mediation, a neutral third party facilitates communication among the parties to a dispute, to assist them in reaching a mutually acceptable resolution.
The parties shall choose a mediator under subrule 24.1.08 (2).

A mediation under this Rule shall be conducted by, (a) a person chosen by the agreement of the parties from the list for a county; (b) a person assigned by the mediation co-ordinator under subrule 24.1.09 (6) or (6.1) from the list for the county; or (c) a person who is not named on a list, if the parties consent.

Before setting the action down for trial, one of the parties shall file with the mediation co-ordinator, (a) a notice (Form 24.1A) stating the mediator's name and the date of the mediation session; or (b) a mediator's report under subrule 24.1.15 (1) indicating that the mediation has been concluded.
At least seven days before the mediation session, every party shall prepare a statement in Form 24.1C and provide a copy to every other party and to the mediator.
The statement shall identify the factual and legal issues in dispute and briefly set out the position and interests of the party making the statement.
The party making the statement shall attach to it any documents that the party considers of central importance in the action.
The plaintiff shall include a copy of the pleadings with the copy of the statement that is provided to the mediator.
The parties, and their lawyers if the parties are represented, are required to attend the mediation session unless the court orders otherwise.

Unless the court orders otherwise, if an insurer may be liable to satisfy all or part of a judgment in the action or to indemnify or reimburse an insured party for money paid in satisfaction of all or part of a judgment in the action, (a) a representative of the insurer shall attend the mediation session; and (b) despite subrule (1), the insured party is not required to attend the mediation session.

A party who requires another person's approval before agreeing to a settlement shall, before the mediation session, arrange to have ready telephone access to the other person throughout the session, whether it takes place during or after regular business hours.

If it is not practical to conduct a scheduled mediation session because a party fails to attend within the first 30 minutes of the time appointed for the commencement of the session, the mediator shall cancel the session and immediately file with the mediation co-ordinator a certificate of non-compliance (Form 24.1D).
When a certificate of non-compliance is filed, the mediation co-ordinator shall refer the matter to a judge or associate judge.

The judge or associate judge may convene a case conference under rule 50.13, and may, (a) establish a timetable for the action; (b) strike out any document filed by a party; (c) dismiss the action, if the non-complying party is a plaintiff, or strike out the statement of defence, if that party is a defendant; (d) order a party to pay costs; (e) make any other order that is just.
Within 10 days after the mediation is concluded, the mediator shall give the mediation co-ordinator and the parties a report on the mediation.
If there is an agreement resolving some or all of the issues in dispute, it shall be signed by the parties or their lawyers.

userQuestion: My trial is coming up — what do I need to do to be ready?
whatsHappening: Once an action is placed on a trial list, every party is treated as ready for trial. The trial goes ahead when the action is reached on the list, unless a judge orders otherwise. An expert may speak at trial on an issue only if the substance of that evidence is in a report served on time under the rules, unless the trial judge gives leave.
whatToDoNext: If you need a person in Ontario to come to the trial as a witness, you may serve them with a summons to witness (Form 53A). The summons tells them the time and place of the trial. It may also require them to bring documents or other things they have about the case, if the summons lists them. You need the court's leave to serve a summons for an original record or document that can be proved by a certified copy. The summons must be served on the witness personally, not by an alternative to personal service. At the same time, you must pay or offer the witness attendance money set under Tariff A.
yourDeadline:
If your expert will testify on something not in their report, serve a supplementary report on every other party. Do this at least 45 days before the first day of trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. A responding supplementary report must be served at least 15 days before trial. Otherwise the expert cannot testify on that issue without the trial judge's leave. The time can be extended by the judge at a pre-trial conference, by the court on a motion, or by the parties' written consent. But consent cannot move the trial date.

If your action is under the simplified procedure and you set it down for trial, serve a trial record on every party and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure, and only to the party who set it down. It is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Witness affidavits, including any outstanding expert affidavits, must be delivered by the dates the pre-trial judge fixed.

If you want to use business records, such as invoices or account records, under the Evidence Act's business-records rule, give every other party notice that you plan to. Do this at least 7 days before the day you tender the records in evidence. The Act requires at least seven days notice of your plan. It does not name the trial date. The notice must come before the records are offered in evidence. So notice given at least 7 days before the first day of trial covers every day of the trial. Giving notice later, even because of a Sunday or holiday, leaves fewer than 7 days. This notice is set by a statute, the Evidence Act. So it is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, not under the court rules' counting described below. The day the notice is given is not counted, and the day the evidence is offered is. Without the notice, the business-records rule does not apply. Any other party can have the records produced for inspection within five days after giving notice to produce them.

If you want to use a report signed by a doctor or other health practitioner, give every other party notice. Do this at least 10 days before the day you tender the report in evidence. The Act requires at least ten days notice to all other parties before the report is admitted. It does not name the trial date. Notice given at least 10 days before the first day of trial covers every day of the trial. Giving notice later, even because of a Sunday or holiday, leaves fewer than 10 days. This notice is set by a statute, the Evidence Act. So it is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, not under the court rules' counting described below. The day the notice is given is not counted, and the day the report is offered is. The report also needs the court's leave to be admitted. When notice is given, the other parties can get a copy of the report, unless the court orders otherwise. A practitioner who signed a report cannot testify at trial unless the report was given to the other parties this way. The trial judge can allow it anyway.

If you claim special damages and have further amounts or details not in your pleading, deliver notice of them. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. The notice must be delivered right away once the amounts become known, and in any event not less than ten days before trial.

You may want to call the other side as a witness, or its officer, director, employee, sole proprietor or partner. If so, serve them with a summons to witness. Or serve a notice of intention to call them on the other side or its lawyer. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. The 10 days apply to the notice of intention. Attendance money under Tariff A must be paid or offered at the same time. If the person is already at the trial, no summons or attendance money is needed.

If your action is under the simplified procedure and you want to examine or cross-examine someone who gave an affidavit, give notice to the party who filed the affidavit. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The party who filed the affidavit then arranges for that person to attend. It is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If a party is not there when the action is called for trial, the trial judge may go ahead without them. Or the judge may dismiss the absent party's claim or counterclaim and let the party who came prove theirs, or make any other order that is just. A judge may set aside or change, on terms that are just, a judgment made against a party who did not attend the trial.

An expert witness may not testify with respect to an issue, except with leave of the trial judge, unless the substance of his or her testimony with respect to that issue is set out in, (a) a report served under this rule; (b) a supplementary report served on every other party to the action not less than 45 days before the commencement of the trial; or (c) a responding supplementary report served on every other party to the action not less than 15 days before the commencement of the trial.

Where an action is called for trial and a party fails to attend, the trial judge may, (a) proceed with the trial in the absence of the party; (b) where the plaintiff attends and the defendant fails to attend, dismiss the counterclaim, if any, and allow the plaintiff to prove the claim; (c) where the defendant attends and the plaintiff fails to attend, dismiss the action and allow the defendant to prove the counterclaim, if any; or (d) make such other order as is just.
A judge may set aside or vary, on such terms as are just, a judgment obtained against a party who failed to attend at the trial.

verdicts.sentence: If a party is not there when the action is called for trial, the trial judge may go ahead without them.
verdicts.quote: Where an action is called for trial and a party fails to attend, the trial judge may, (a) proceed with the trial in the absence of the party; (b) where the plaintiff attends and the defendant fails to attend, dismiss the counterclaim, if any, and allow the plaintiff to prove the claim; (c) where the defendant attends and the plaintiff fails to attend, dismiss the action and allow the defendant to prove the counterclaim, if any; or (d) make such other order as is just.

verdicts.sentence: Or the judge may dismiss the absent party's claim or counterclaim and let the party who came prove theirs, or make any other order that is just.

userQuestion: My ex has been served — how long do they have to answer?
whatsHappening: Your application has been served on the respondent, and their time to answer has not run out yet. The respondent must serve an answer on every other party and file it within 30 days after being served with the application. If the application was served outside Canada or the United States, that time is 60 days. In an application to dispense with a parent's consent before adoption placement, the time is 20 days, or 40 days if served outside Canada or the United States. To count the days, day one is the day after the respondent was served. If the last day falls on a day when court offices are closed, the time ends on the next day they are open.
whatToDoNext: If your application claims support, property, or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents, the respondent must serve and file a financial statement. They must do it within the same time as the answer, even if they do not serve an answer. If your application makes a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, you must serve the respondent with the papers rule 13 (3.3) lists, unless the court orders otherwise. You must do this no later than 30 days after the day your financial statement had to be served. One of those papers is the statement closest to the valuation date for each account you had then. This covers each bank or other financial account, pension, retirement or other savings plan, and any other savings or investment. For any other property claim, you must serve the information needed to support the claim within the same 30 days, unless the court orders otherwise. With those papers you must serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). You must also file that certificate no later than six days before a case conference. Some cases need the mandatory information program, such as a case with a claim about parenting, support, net family property or the matrimonial home. Some parties are not covered, such as parties in a case going ahead on consent, or where the only claims are for a divorce or costs. Where the program applies, each party must attend no later than 45 days after the case is started. Until your certificate of attendance is filed, you must not take any step in the case, except making an appointment for a case conference. The court may, on a motion, excuse a party from this because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice.
yourDeadline:
The respondent's time to serve an answer on every other party and file it. They have 30 days after the day the respondent was served with the application. If the respondent was served outside Canada and the United States, the time is 60 days. A respondent added by another party’s answer has 14 days. That becomes 30 days if they were served outside Canada and the United States. Other times apply to an application to dispense with a parent’s consent before adoption placement. Service rules decide when the time starts. Papers left at the home with an adult, with a copy mailed, count as served on the fifth day after mailing. Papers left with the respondent after 4 p.m. count as served the next day. If that day is one when court offices are closed, service counts on the next open day. For mail with an acknowledgment card, the rules set no separate start day. The general rule for mail is the fifth day after mailing. That service counts only once the card signed by the respondent is filed. If the application claims support, property or the matrimonial home, the respondent’s financial statement is due in the same time. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. You book your own appointment and the respondent’s. Serve notice of the respondent’s appointment with the application. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take another step in the case. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise on a motion. If you claim support and no property, the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) should have gone with your financial statement. If they did not, serve them now. In any case, serve them before the case conference.

If your application makes a property claim, serve the respondent with the property papers the rule lists. You have 30 days after the day your financial statement was due, which is the day you served the application. For a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, the rule lists the papers. One example is the statement closest to the valuation date for each bank or other account. For any other property claim, serve the information needed to support the claim. If there is also a support claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with the papers. The court can order otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

You must do it within those same 10 days, even if you do not serve a reply. If the respondent does not serve and file an answer, some things follow unless a court orders otherwise. They are not entitled to further notice of steps in the case, except service of an order, and may not take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without them, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial.

citations.quote: A person against whom an application is made shall serve an answer (Form 10, 33B, 33B.1, 33B.2 or 33D.3) on every other party and file it within 30 days after being served with the application.
If an application is served outside Canada or the United States of America, the time for serving and filing an answer is 60 days.

In an application to dispense with a parent’s consent before adoption placement, (Form 8D.1), the time for serving the answer is, (a) 20 days, if the application is served in Canada or the United States of America; (b) 40 days, if the application is served outside Canada or the United States of America.
In these rules or an order, the number of days between two events is counted as follows: 1. The first day is the day after the first event. 2. The last day is the day of the second event.
If the last day of a period of time under these rules or an order falls on a day when court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open.

If an application, answer or motion contains a claim for support, a property claim, or a claim for exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents, (a) the party making the claim shall serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1) with the document that contains the claim; and (b) the party against whom the claim is made shall serve and file a financial statement within the time for serving and filing an answer, reply or affidavit or other document responding to the motion, whether the party is serving an answer, reply or affidavit or other document responding to the motion or not.

A party who is required under subrules (1) to (3) to serve and file a financial statement in relation to a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act shall, no later than 30 days after the day by which the financial statement is required to be served, serve on the other party the following information, unless the court orders otherwise: 1. The statement issued closest to the valuation date for each bank account or other account in a financial institution, pension, registered retirement or other savings plan, and any other savings or investments in which the party had an interest on that date.

A party who is required under subrules (1) to (3) to serve and file a financial statement in relation to a property claim other than a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act shall, no later than 30 days after the day by which the financial statement is required to be served, serve on the other party any information necessary to support the claim, unless the court orders otherwise.

A party who is required to serve documents under subrule (3.1), (3.3), (3.4) or (5.0.1) shall confirm service by, (a) serving a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) together with the documents; and (b) filing the certificate no later than, (i) six days before a case conference, in the case of the applicant or the party making the motion, as the case may be,

This rule applies to cases started after August 31, 2011 that deal with any of the following: 1. A claim respecting decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with respect to a child under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Children’s Law Reform Act. 2. A claim respecting net family property under Part I of the Family Law Act. 3. A claim respecting a matrimonial home under Part II of the Family Law Act. 4. A claim for support under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Family Law Act.

Subrules (4) to (7) do not apply to, (a) a person or agency referred to in subsection 33 (3) of the Family Law Act; (b) the Director of the Family Responsibility Office; (c) parties in cases that are proceeding on consent; (d) parties in cases in which the only claims made are for a divorce, costs or the incorporation of the terms of an agreement or prior court order;
Each party to a case shall attend the program no later than 45 days after the case is started.

A party shall not take any step in the case before his or her certificate of attendance is filed, except that a respondent may serve and file an answer and a party may make an appointment for a case conference.
The court may, on motion, order that any or all of subrules (4) to (7) do not apply to the party because of urgency or hardship or for some other reason in the interest of justice.
A party may, within 10 days after being served with an answer, serve and file a reply (Form 10A) in response to a claim made in the answer.
The consequences set out in paragraphs 1 to 4 of subrule 1 (8.4) apply, with necessary changes, if a respondent does not serve and file an answer.

If an order is made striking out a party’s application, answer, motion to change or response to motion to change in a case, the following consequences apply unless a court orders otherwise: 1. The party is not entitled to any further notice of steps in the case, except as provided by subrule 25 (13) (service of order). 2. The party is not entitled to participate in the case in any way. 3. The court may deal with the case in the party’s absence. 4. A date may be set for an uncontested trial of the case.

userQuestion: The time is up and my ex never answered — what happens now?
whatsHappening: The respondent's time to serve and file an answer has passed, and no answer has been filed. When a respondent does not serve and file an answer, some things follow unless a court orders otherwise. The respondent is not entitled to further notice of steps in the case, except service of an order. They may not take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without them, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. An uncontested trial is a trial where only the party making the claim gives evidence and makes submissions. Court office staff must refuse an answer the respondent asks to file late. Late means after the time the rules set. But a later time may be set by a written consent of the parties, a statute that applies to the case, or a court order. Then late means after that later time.
whatToDoNext: In the Ontario Court of Justice, the clerk acts on or before the first court date. If no answer has been filed, the clerk sends the case to a judge to decide on affidavit evidence. Or, if you ask, the clerk sets a case conference instead. The same applies to a fast track case in the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice. A case there is fast track unless the application claims a divorce, makes a property claim, or makes a family arbitration claim. These steps do not apply to enforcements or to cases under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. Rules 39 (2) and 40 (2) list a few other cases they do not cover. Under the conference rule, when no answer is filed, the clerk must, if you ask, schedule a case conference or set a date for an uncontested trial. In an uncontested divorce case, you can instead ask the clerk to prepare the documents for a judge. A settlement conference or trial management conference is held only if the court orders it. At an uncontested trial, evidence may be given by affidavit in Form 14A or Form 23C. Forms 35.1 and 35.1A may also be used if they apply. But the court may direct that oral evidence must be given. In a divorce case, you must file an affidavit in Form 36, because the respondent filed no answer. It must confirm that the facts in your application are correct, except as the affidavit says. It must also give the other facts rule 36 (5) lists. With the affidavit you must file three copies of a draft divorce order (Form 25A) and a stamped envelope addressed to each party. Will the divorce order have a support order in it? Then also file an extra copy of the draft divorce order and two copies of a draft support deduction order. Where the mandatory information program applies, you must not take any step until your certificate of attendance is filed, except making an appointment for a case conference.
yourDeadline:
Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot ask for an uncontested trial or take another step. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If your application claims a divorce, two papers must be filed before the divorce is granted. One is a marriage certificate or marriage registration certificate. The other is a report on earlier divorce cases started by either spouse. The certificate is not needed if your application says it is impractical to get one and explains why. In that case, your Form 36 affidavit must give enough facts to prove the marriage. Once those papers and the affidavit papers are filed, the clerk prepares a certificate (Form 36A) and presents the documents to a judge. The judge may grant the divorce as set out in the draft order, or have the clerk return the documents to you to make needed corrections. The judge may also change the draft order or refuse the divorce. Before doing either, the judge must first let you file another affidavit, or come to court to explain why the order should be made without change.
