citations.quote: An originating process shall be served personally as provided in rule 16.02 or by an alternative to personal service as provided in rule 16.03.
Where an action is commenced by a statement of claim, the statement of claim shall be served within six months after it is issued.
Where an action is commenced by a notice of action, the notice of action and the statement of claim shall be served together within six months after the notice of action is issued.

Where an attempt is made to effect personal service at a person's place of residence and for any reason personal service cannot be effected, the document may be served by, (a) leaving a copy, in a sealed envelope addressed to the person, at the place of residence with anyone who appears to be an adult member of the same household; and (b) on the same day or the following day mailing another copy of the document to the person at the place of residence, and service in this manner is effective on the fifth day after the document is mailed.

Service of a document may be made by sending a copy of the document together with an acknowledgment of receipt card (Form 16A) by mail to the last known address of the person to be served, but service by mail under this subrule is only effective as of the date the sender receives the card.

Where the head office, registered office or principal place of business of a corporation or, in the case of an extra-provincial corporation, the attorney for service in Ontario cannot be found at the last address recorded with the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery, service may be made on the corporation by mailing a copy of the document to the corporation or to the attorney for service in Ontario, as the case may be, at that address.

Where it appears to the court that it is impractical for any reason to effect prompt service of an originating process or any other document required to be served personally or by an alternative to personal service under these rules, the court may make an order for substituted service or, where necessary in the interest of justice, may dispense with service.
In an order for substituted service, the court shall specify when service in accordance with the order is effective.
Where an order is made dispensing with service of a document, the document shall be deemed to have been served on the date of the order for the purpose of the computation of time under these rules.

Where a document has been served in a manner other than one authorized by these rules or an order, the court may make an order validating the service where the court is satisfied that, (a) the document came to the notice of the person to be served; or (b) the document was served in such a manner that it would have come to the notice of the person to be served, except for the person's own attempts to evade service.
Subject to subrule (3), the court may by order extend or abridge any time prescribed by these rules or an order, on such terms as are just.
A motion for an order extending time may be made before or after the expiration of the time prescribed.
Service of a document may be proved by an affidavit of the person who served it (Form 16B).

A party who has not been served with the originating process but delivers a defence, notice of intent to defend or notice of appearance shall be deemed to have been served with the originating process as of the date of delivery.
"deliver" means serve and file with proof of service, and "delivery" has a corresponding meaning;

a statement of defence (Form 18A) shall be delivered, (a) within twenty days after service of the statement of claim, where the defendant is served in Ontario; (b) within forty days after service of the statement of claim, where the defendant is served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States of America; or (c) within sixty days after service of the statement of claim, where the defendant is served anywhere else.

A defendant who delivers a notice of intent to defend within the prescribed time is entitled to ten days, in addition to the time prescribed by rule 18.01, within which to deliver a statement of defence.

userQuestion: The defendant was noted in default — how do I get judgment?
whatsHappening: The registrar has noted the defendant in default, and no judgment has been signed or granted yet. A defendant noted in default is deemed to admit the truth of all the facts stated in your statement of claim. They may not deliver a defence or take any other step in the action unless the court gives leave or you consent. The one step they may take without that is a motion to set aside the noting of default, or any judgment obtained because of the default. A defendant noted in default is not entitled to notice of any step in the action, and need not be served with documents in it. There are exceptions. They include when the court orders otherwise, or when a party requires the defendant to attend personally. They also include some documents the rules list, such as an amended pleading or a counterclaim.
whatToDoNext: For some kinds of claims, you may require the registrar to sign judgment against the defendant. One kind is a claim for a debt or liquidated demand in money (Form 19A). This includes interest, if you claimed it in the statement of claim. Another is a claim to recover possession of land (Form 19B). Another is a claim to recover possession of personal property (Form 19C). The last is a claim for foreclosure, sale or redemption of a mortgage (Forms 64B to 64D, 64G to 64K and 64M). Before the registrar signs, you must file a requisition for default judgment (Form 19D) with the registrar. It must state that the claim is one of the kinds for which default judgment may properly be signed. It must state whether any part of the claim has been paid, and give the date and amount of any partial payment. If you claimed prejudgment interest in the statement of claim, it must set out how the interest is calculated. If you claimed postjudgment interest at a rate other than the one in section 129 of the Courts of Justice Act, it must set out that rate. It must also state whether you want the registrar to fix your costs or want them assessed. If part of the claim has been paid, the default judgment is limited to the rest of the claim. The registrar may decline to sign if unsure whether the claim is one of those kinds. The registrar may also decline if unsure of the amount or rate of interest that can properly be recovered. If the registrar declines, you may move before a judge for judgment under rule 19.05. If the registrar declines and your claim is one of the kinds listed above, you may instead make a motion to the court for default judgment. For any claim with no signed default judgment, you may move before a judge for judgment against the defendant on the statement of claim. If the claim is for unliquidated damages, the motion must be supported by evidence given by affidavit. On a motion for judgment, the facts in your claim being deemed admitted does not by itself entitle you to judgment, unless those facts entitle you to it.
yourDeadline:
Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: When the registrar signs default judgment, the registrar must fix your costs under Tariff A and include them in the judgment. This does not apply if the judgment directs a reference. It also does not apply if you said in the requisition that you want costs assessed. In those cases, the judgment includes costs to be decided on the reference or assessment. On a motion for judgment, the judge may grant judgment, dismiss the action, or order that the action go to trial with oral evidence. If the action goes to trial, a motion for judgment on the statement of claim against the defendant noted in default may be made at the trial. The court may set aside the noting of default on terms that are just. A judgment against a defendant noted in default does not stop you from going after the same defendant for any other relief.

citations.quote: Where a defendant has been noted in default, the plaintiff may require the registrar to sign judgment against the defendant in respect of a claim for, (a) a debt or liquidated demand in money, including interest if claimed in the statement of claim (Form 19A); (b) the recovery of possession of land (Form 19B); (c) the recovery of possession of personal property (Form 19C); or (d) foreclosure, sale or redemption of a mortgage (Forms 64B to 64D, 64G to 64K and 64M).

A defendant who has been noted in default, (a) is deemed to admit the truth of all allegations of fact made in the statement of claim; and (b) shall not deliver a statement of defence or take any other step in the action, other than a motion to set aside the noting of default or any judgment obtained by reason of the default, except with leave of the court or the consent of the plaintiff.

Despite any other rule, a defendant who has been noted in default is not entitled to notice of any step in the action and need not be served with any document in the action, except where the court orders otherwise or where a party requires the personal attendance of the defendant, and except as provided in, (a) subrule 26.04 (3) (amended pleading); (b) subrule 27.04 (3) (counterclaim);

Before the signing of default judgment, the plaintiff shall file with the registrar a requisition for default judgment (Form 19D), (a) stating that the claim comes within the class of cases for which default judgment may properly be signed; (b) stating whether there has been any partial payment of the claim and setting out the date and amount of any partial payment; (c) where the plaintiff has claimed prejudgment interest in the statement of claim, setting out how the interest is calculated; (d) where the plaintiff has claimed postjudgment interest in the statement of claim at a rate other than as provided in section 129 of the Courts of Justice Act, setting out the rate; and (e) stating whether the plaintiff wishes costs to be fixed by the registrar or assessed.
Where the claim has been partially satisfied, the default judgment shall be confined to the remainder of the claim.

The registrar may decline to sign default judgment if uncertain, (a) whether the claim comes within the class of cases for which default judgment may properly be signed; or (b) of the amount or rate that is properly recoverable for prejudgment or postjudgment interest.

If the registrar declines to sign default judgment, the plaintiff may, (a) move before a judge for judgment under rule 19.05; or (b) in the case of a claim referred to in subrule (1), make a motion to the court for default judgment.

Where a defendant has been noted in default, the plaintiff may move before a judge for judgment against the defendant on the statement of claim in respect of any claim for which default judgment has not been signed.
A motion for judgment under subrule (1) shall be supported by evidence given by affidavit if the claim is for unliquidated damages.

A plaintiff is not entitled to judgment on a motion for judgment or at trial merely because the facts alleged in the statement of claim are deemed to be admitted, unless the facts entitle the plaintiff to judgment.

On signing a default judgment, the registrar shall fix the costs under Tariff A to which the plaintiff is entitled against the defendant in default and shall include the costs in the judgment unless, (a) the judgment directs a reference; or (b) the plaintiff states in the requisition that he or she wishes to have the costs assessed, in which case the judgment shall include costs to be determined on the reference or on assessment.
On a motion for judgment under subrule (1), the judge may grant judgment, dismiss the action or order that the action proceed to trial and that oral evidence be presented.
Where an action proceeds to trial, a motion for judgment on the statement of claim against a defendant noted in default may be made at the trial.
The noting of default may be set aside by the court on such terms as are just.
A judgment obtained against a defendant who has been noted in default does not prevent the plaintiff from proceeding against the same defendant for any other relief.

userQuestion: The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?
whatsHappening: The defendant has made a claim against you in the same case. This is called a counterclaim. A defendant may use it to make any claim against the plaintiff in the main action. The counterclaim goes in the same document as the defence, called a statement of defence and counterclaim.
whatToDoNext: Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. A reply to the defence is required in two cases, and allowed only then. One is if you plan to prove a version of the facts that differs from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. The other is to raise a matter that might take the defendant by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in a reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. If you do deliver a reply, it must go in one document with your defence to counterclaim, called a reply and defence to counterclaim. That one document is due within the same 20 days. In your defence to counterclaim, you must admit every fact in the counterclaim that you do not dispute. Any fact you do not deny is taken as admitted, unless you say you have no knowledge of it. If the counterclaim is for damages, the amount stays in dispute unless you specifically admit it. If you plan to prove a different version of the facts, denying theirs is not enough. You must set out your own version. You must also set out any point you will rely on to defeat the counterclaim, if it might take the defendant by surprise or raise a new issue. If the 20 days pass, you may still deliver your defence to counterclaim at any time before you are noted in default.
yourDeadline:
Deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C). You have 20 days after the day the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. If you also deliver a reply, put both in one document called a reply and defence to counterclaim. If you do not deliver a defence to counterclaim in time, the defendant can have you noted in default on the counterclaim. You would then be treated as admitting the facts it alleges. Judgment could then be given against you on it. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. With a counterclaim, that is not before the defendant replies to your defence to counterclaim, or the 10 days for that reply run out. Delivering the jury notice with your defence to counterclaim avoids any doubt. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If the defendant delivers a reply to your defence to counterclaim (Form 27D), it is due within 10 days after your defence to counterclaim is served. A counterclaim is tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise. But if the counterclaim may unduly complicate or delay that trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party, the court may order separate trials. It may instead order the counterclaim to go ahead as a separate action.

citations.quote: A defendant may assert, by way of counterclaim in the main action, any right or claim against the plaintiff including a claim for contribution or indemnity under the Negligence Act in respect of another party's claim against the defendant.
A counterclaim (Form 27A or 27B) shall be included in the same document as the statement of defence and the document shall be entitled a statement of defence and counterclaim.
"deliver" means serve and file with proof of service, and "delivery" has a corresponding meaning;

The plaintiff and any other defendant to a counterclaim who is already a party to the main action shall deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within twenty days after service of the statement of defence and counterclaim.

A party who intends to prove a version of the facts different from that pleaded in the opposite party's defence shall deliver a reply setting out the different version, unless it has already been pleaded in the claim.

A party who intends to reply in response to a defence on any matter that might, if not specifically pleaded, take the opposite party by surprise or raise an issue that has not been raised by a previous pleading shall deliver a reply setting out that matter, subject to subrule 25.06 (5) (inconsistent claims or new claims).
A party shall not deliver a reply except where required to do so by subrule (1) or (2).

An allegation that is inconsistent with an allegation made in a party's previous pleading or that raises a new ground of claim shall not be made in a subsequent pleading but by way of amendment to the previous pleading.
(4) A party who does not deliver a reply within the prescribed time shall be deemed to deny the allegations of fact made in the defence of the opposite party.

Where the plaintiff delivers a reply in the main action, the defence to counterclaim shall be included in the same document as the reply and the document shall be entitled a reply and defence to counterclaim.

A reply, if any, shall be delivered within ten days after service of the statement of defence except where the defendant counterclaims, in which case a reply and defence to counterclaim, if any, shall be delivered within twenty days after service of the statement of defence and counterclaim.
In a defence, a party shall admit every allegation of fact in the opposite party's pleading that the party does not dispute.
Subject to subrule (6), all allegations of fact that are not denied in a party's defence shall be deemed to be admitted unless the party pleads having no knowledge in respect of the fact.
In an action for damages, the amount of damages shall be deemed to be in issue unless specifically admitted.

Where a party intends to prove a version of the facts different from that pleaded by the opposite party, a denial of the version so pleaded is not sufficient, but the party shall plead the party's own version of the facts in the defence.

In a defence, a party shall plead any matter on which the party intends to rely to defeat the claim of the opposite party and which, if not specifically pleaded, might take the opposite party by surprise or raise an issue that has not been raised in the opposite party's pleading.
A defendant may deliver a statement of defence at any time before being noted in default under this rule.

Rules 19.01 to 19.08 apply, with necessary modifications, to counterclaims, crossclaims and third party claims, subject to rules 28.07 (default of defence to crossclaim) and 29.07 (default of defence to third party claim).
A reply to defence to counterclaim (Form 27D), if any, shall be delivered within ten days after service of the defence to counterclaim.
A counterclaim shall be tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise.

Where it appears that a counterclaim may unduly complicate or delay the trial of the main action, or cause undue prejudice to a party, the court may order separate trials or order that the counterclaim proceed as a separate action.

userQuestion: How do I get my action set down for trial, and is there a deadline?
whatsHappening: After pleadings close, a party who is ready for trial may set the action down for trial. That party must not be in default under the rules or a court order. Any counterclaim or crossclaim in the action is set down with it. Once it is set down, the registrar at the place of trial must put the action on the right trial list.
whatToDoNext: If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must file a paper with the mediation co-ordinator before it is set down. It is either a notice (Form 24.1A) naming the mediator and the date of the session, or a mediator's report saying the mediation has ended. In a defended action, you set it down by serving a trial record on every party to the action or to a counterclaim or crossclaim. You also serve it on any third or later party. Then you file the trial record with proof of service right away. If the court orders the trial of an undefended action, you set it down by just filing a trial record. The trial record must hold these items, in this order. First comes a table of contents that describes each document by what it is and its date. Next come a copy of any jury notice, and a copy of the pleadings, including those for any counterclaim or crossclaim. Next comes a copy of any demand or order for particulars of a pleading, and the particulars given in answer. Next comes a copy of any notice of amounts and particulars of special damages that was delivered. Next comes a copy of any order about the trial, including an order made under Rule 6.1. Last comes a signed certificate. If you have no lawyer and act for yourself, you sign it. It states that the record holds the required documents and that the time to deliver pleadings has run out. Where it applies, it also states that a defendant who did not deliver a defence has been noted in default. Where it applies, it also states that judgment was obtained against a defendant, or that the action was discontinued or dismissed against one. Before the trial, you must also add to the record a copy of some later papers. These are any notice of special damages, or any order about the trial, made after you filed the record. They also include any order under rule 50.07 and the pre-trial conference report under rule 50.08. In an undefended action, they include any affidavit to be used as evidence. The way of setting down is different for an action under the simplified procedure (Rule 76). There, you must set it down within 180 days after the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend is filed. This is done by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party to the action and to any counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim. You then file it with proof of service right away.
yourDeadline:
Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: Once you set the action down, you must not start or continue any motion or discovery without the court's leave. Setting down does not end your duty to keep the undertakings you gave on an examination for discovery. Duties under some other rules also still apply. One is the discovery plan (rule 29.1.03). Others are telling of documents or errors found later (rule 30.07), and giving up a claim of privilege (rule 30.09). Others are the rule on failing to answer on discovery (rule 31.07), and telling of facts learned later (rule 31.09). The last are answering a request to admit (rule 51.03), and serving expert reports (rule 53.03). You may also still serve a request to admit facts or documents under rule 51.02. Some motions do not need leave. One is a motion to make a party meet a duty under rule 29.1.03, 30.07, 30.09, 31.07, 31.09, 51.03 or 53.03. Another is a motion for a separate hearing on some issues under rule 6.1.01. When the action is on a trial list, all parties are taken to be ready for trial, and the trial goes ahead when the action is reached, unless a judge orders otherwise. Unless the court orders otherwise, the parties must book a pre-trial conference with the registrar within 180 days after the action is set down. The date and time must suit all parties. Unless a court order or practice direction says otherwise, the date must be 30 to 120 days before the later of two days. One is the first day fixed for the trial, and the other is the first day of the sitting when the trial is expected. If they do not, the registrar sets a date and time and tells the parties, subject to any earlier order. Within 60 days after the action is set down, the parties must also agree on dates for serving experts' reports, unless the court orders otherwise.

Where an action is defended, a party who wishes to set it down for trial may do so by serving a trial record prepared in accordance with rule 48.03 on every party to the action or to a counterclaim or crossclaim in the action and on any third or subsequent party and forthwith filing the trial record with proof of service.

Subject to subrule (3), a party who has set an action down for trial shall not initiate or continue any motion or form of discovery without leave of the court.
(2) Subrule (1) does not, (a) relieve a party from complying with undertakings given by the party on an examination for discovery;

(c) preclude a party from resorting to rule 51.02 (request to admit facts or documents).

(3) Leave of the court is not required for, (a) a motion to compel compliance with any obligation imposed by a rule listed in clause (2) (b); or (b) a motion under rule 6.1.01 for a separate hearing on one or more issues in a proceeding, including separate hearings on the issues of liability and damages.
Where an action is placed on a trial list, (a) all parties shall be deemed to be ready for trial; and
(c) the trial shall proceed when the action is reached on the trial list unless a judge orders otherwise.

Unless the court orders otherwise, within 180 days after an action is set down for trial, the parties shall schedule with the registrar a date and time acceptable to all parties and consistent with the requirements of subrule (2.1) to appear before a judge or associate judge for a pre-trial conference.

(2.1) Unless otherwise provided by a court order or applicable practice direction, a pre-trial conference shall be scheduled for a date that is not more than 120 days and not less than 30 days before the later of the following dates: 1. The first day fixed for the trial. 2. The first day of the sitting during which the trial is expected to be held.

If the parties do not schedule a pre-trial conference within 180 days after the action is set down for trial, the registrar shall, subject to any previous order, (a) schedule a date and time consistent with the requirements of subrule (2.1) for the parties to appear before a judge or associate judge for a pre-trial conference; and (b) give notice to the parties to appear at the scheduled date and time.

userQuestion: I have a judgment but they will not pay — how do I collect?
whatsHappening: You have a judgment for money, by default or after a hearing, and it has not been paid. The rules call a person who is entitled to enforce an order for money the creditor. The person it can be enforced against is called the debtor. Besides any other method the law provides, an order for money may be enforced in four ways. They are a writ of seizure and sale (Form 60A), garnishment, a writ of sequestration (Form 60B), and the appointment of a receiver.
whatToDoNext: To get a writ of seizure and sale, file a requisition with the registrar where the case was started. The requisition says how much is owing and the rate of postjudgment interest. It also lists the date and amount of any payment made since the order. Include a copy of the order as entered. Also include any other proof needed to show the amount awarded and your right to it. A lawyer or a person licensed by the Law Society may instead ask for the writ through the Teranet software. You need the court's leave first in two cases. One is if six years or more have passed since the date of the order. The other is if enforcing the order is subject to a condition. If the order is for payment at or after a set future time, the writ cannot be issued until that time has passed. You may file the writ with a sheriff. You may then file a direction to enforce (Form 60F) with the sheriff, with a copy of the order as entered. The direction tells the sheriff to enforce the writ. Garnishment lets you collect debts that other people owe to the debtor. To use it, file a requisition for garnishment (Form 60G) with the registrar where the case was started. Include a copy of the order as entered, and an affidavit. Also include any other proof needed to show the amount awarded and your right to it. The affidavit must state several things the rule lists, such as the amount owing with postjudgment interest. It must also name each person the notice is to go to, and say why you believe they owe or will owe the debtor money. The same two cases need the court's leave before a notice of garnishment is issued. The registrar then issues a notice of garnishment (Form 60H) for each person named, who is called a garnishee. You must serve the notice on the debtor with a copy of your affidavit. You must also serve it on the garnishee with a blank garnishee's statement (Form 60I). It must be served by ordinary mail, by personal service, or by an alternative to personal service. If the garnishee is a financial institution, serve it at the branch where the debt is payable. You may also examine the debtor. You can ask about things such as why they have not paid, their income and property, and the debts owed to and by them. If the debtor is a corporation, an officer or director may be examined for it. For a partnership or sole proprietorship, a partner or sole proprietor whom the order can be enforced against may be examined. Only one such examination of a debtor may be held in a 12-month period in the same case, unless the court orders otherwise. The debtor must be served with a notice of examination personally or by an alternative to personal service. A person examined on the debtor's behalf must be served with a notice of examination in one of two ways. It may be served on the debtor's lawyer of record. Or it may be served on that person personally, and not by an alternative to personal service.
yourDeadline:
If you have a writ of seizure and sale, renew it before it expires. You have 6 years after the day the writ was issued. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 6 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. A writ filed with a sheriff is renewed by filing a request to renew (Form 60E) with the sheriff. A writ not filed with a sheriff is renewed with the registrar who issued it. A renewal can be filed only in the six years before the expiry it relates to. A notice of garnishment also lasts six years and can be renewed before it expires.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: A garnishee who admits owing the debtor money must pay it to the sheriff as the notice sets out, subject to section 7 of the Wages Act. Some garnishees dispute the garnishment, or pay less than the notice says. Within 10 days after being served, such a garnishee must serve you and the debtor with a garnishee's statement (Form 60I), and file it. Under a writ, you may not take any step to sell land until four months after the writ was filed with the sheriff. No sale of land may be held until six months after it was filed. If the writ was withdrawn, these times run from when it was filed again. If a notice of appeal is delivered, the parts of the order for paying money are put on hold. The hold lasts until the appeal is decided. It does not cover parts that award support or enforce a support order. A judge of the appeal court may order that the hold does not apply. While an order is on hold, no steps may be taken under it or to enforce it, except as a judge of the appeal court orders or as the rules allow. A writ of execution can still be issued and filed in a sheriff's office or land registry office. But no instruction or direction to enforce the writ may be given to a sheriff until the hold ends. An appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment does not put that judgment on hold, but a court order may do so. You are entitled to the costs of your enforcement steps, unless the court orders otherwise on a motion. These costs are on a partial indemnity scale.

verdicts.sentence: While an order is on hold, no steps may be taken under it or to enforce it, except as a judge of the appeal court orders or as the rules allow.
verdicts.quote: Where an order is stayed, no steps may be taken under the order or for its enforcement, except, (a) by order of a judge of the court to which a motion for leave to appeal has been made or an appeal has been taken; or (b) as provided in subrules (2) and (3).

verdicts.sentence: A writ of execution can still be issued and filed in a sheriff's office or land registry office.
verdicts.quote: A stay does not prevent the issue of a writ of execution or the filing of the writ in a sheriff's office or land registry office, but no instruction or direction to enforce the writ shall be given to a sheriff while the stay remains in effect.

verdicts.sentence: But no instruction or direction to enforce the writ may be given to a sheriff until the hold ends.
verdicts.quote: A stay does not prevent the issue of a writ of execution or the filing of the writ in a sheriff's office or land registry office, but no instruction or direction to enforce the writ shall be given to a sheriff while the stay remains in effect.

verdicts.sentence: An appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment does not put that judgment on hold, but a court order may do so.
verdicts.quote: The delivery of a notice of appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment does not stay the default judgment, but it may be stayed by order and rule 63.02 applies as if the appeal were from the default judgment.

verdicts.sentence: You are entitled to the costs of your enforcement steps, unless the court orders otherwise on a motion.

An examination in aid of execution. 2. The issuing, service, filing, enforcement and renewal of a writ of execution and notice of garnishment. 3. Any other procedure authorized by these rules for enforcing the order.

userQuestion: I delivered my statement of defence — what happens next?
whatsHappening: You have served and filed your statement of defence. Discovery has not started. In these rules, to deliver a document means to serve it and file it with proof of service. Pleadings close when two things are true. First, the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence, or the time for a reply has run out. Second, every defendant whose time to deliver a defence has run out without delivering one has been noted in default.
whatToDoNext: You may start a third party claim (Form 29A) against a person who is not a party to the action, in any of three cases. First, that person is or may be liable to you for all or part of the plaintiff's claim. Second, that person is or may be liable to you for a separate claim for damages or other relief. That claim must arise out of the events in the action, or related events. Third, that person should be bound by the decision on an issue between the plaintiff and you. If you bring a third party claim, it must be issued within 10 days after you deliver your defence, or at any time before you are noted in default. It may also be issued within 10 days after the plaintiff delivers a reply to your defence. It may be issued at any time with the plaintiff's consent or the court's leave. The court must give leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. You must serve it on the third party within 30 days after it is issued. Serve the third party personally or by an alternative to personal service. Include all the pleadings delivered so far in the action. This includes those in any counterclaim, crossclaim or other third party claim. You must also serve it on every other party in the same time, but personal service is not needed for them. You may crossclaim against another defendant in the same three cases. If you claim contribution from another defendant under the Negligence Act, you must do it by crossclaim. A crossclaim (Form 28A) must be in the same document as your defence, called a statement of defence and crossclaim. A statement of defence and crossclaim must be delivered within the time for delivering your defence, or at any time before you are noted in default. After that, it may be delivered with the court's leave. The court must give leave unless the plaintiff would be prejudiced. If your defence has no crossclaim and you want to add one, you may amend your defence. You may amend without leave before pleadings close, if the change does not add, remove or replace a party. Otherwise you need the consent of all parties, or the court's leave. If the change adds or replaces a party, that person must also consent, unless the court gives leave. You may ask for a jury to decide the facts, the damages, or both. To do so, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) at any time before pleadings close. You cannot do this if section 108 of the Courts of Justice Act or another statute requires a trial without a jury. An action under the simplified procedure cannot be tried with a jury. In such an action, no party may deliver a jury notice, with one exception. A party may deliver one if the action involves a claim arising from slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment. If a party does that, the action can no longer go on under the simplified procedure. That party must also deliver a notice (Form 76A) saying the action and any related proceedings go on as an ordinary action. The parties must agree to a discovery plan if any party intends to get evidence under the discovery rules. These rules cover discovery of documents, examination for discovery, and inspection of property. They also cover medical examination, and examination for discovery by written questions. The plan must be agreed within 60 days after pleadings close, or a longer time the parties agree to. But it must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first.
yourDeadline:
You can bring in someone who is not yet a party if they are or may be liable to you for all or part of the plaintiff's claim. You can also do it for a related claim, or if they should be bound by the result. To do this, issue a third party claim (Form 29A). You have 10 days after the day you delivered your statement of defence. You can also issue it at any time before you are noted in default. Or you can issue it within 10 days after the plaintiff delivers a reply to your defence. After that, you can issue it at any time with the plaintiff's consent or the court's leave. The court must give leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. You must serve it within 30 days after it is issued. The two-year limitation period still applies to your claim against the third party. For a claim for contribution and indemnity, the Limitations Act, 2002 treats the day you were served with the plaintiff's claim as the day of the act or omission.

If you issued a third party claim, serve it on the third party with all the pleadings delivered so far, and on every other party. You have 30 days after the day the third party claim was issued. The third party must be served personally or by an alternative to personal service. The other parties to the main action must be served in the same time, but not personally. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. That can come 10 days after the defence if no reply is delivered. If a reply is delivered sooner, pleadings close when it is delivered, as long as every defendant has delivered a defence or been noted in default. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If you counterclaimed and want to reply to the defence to counterclaim, deliver a reply to defence to counterclaim (Form 27D). You have 10 days after the day the defence to counterclaim was served on you. This applies only if you counterclaimed. A reply is needed only if you will prove a different version of the facts than the defence pleads, or must raise a matter that could take the other side by surprise. Otherwise you must not deliver one. If you crossclaimed, you have the same 10 days to reply to a defence to crossclaim (Form 28C). If you brought a third party claim, you also have 10 days to reply to the third party defence (Form 29C). Each runs from service of that defence.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If the action is under the simplified procedure, the plaintiff sets it down for trial by serving and filing a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C). They have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. If the plaintiff does not do it, any other party may.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: The plaintiff may deliver a reply within 10 days after your defence was served. If you counterclaimed, the time for a reply and defence to counterclaim is 20 days after your defence and counterclaim was served. If the plaintiff does not deliver a reply in time, the plaintiff is treated as denying the facts in your defence.

citations.quote: "deliver" means serve and file with proof of service, and "delivery" has a corresponding meaning;

A reply, if any, shall be delivered within ten days after service of the statement of defence except where the defendant counterclaims, in which case a reply and defence to counterclaim, if any, shall be delivered within twenty days after service of the statement of defence and counterclaim.

Pleadings in an action are closed when, (a) the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence in the action or the time for delivery of a reply has expired; and (b) every defendant who is in default in delivering a defence in the action has been noted in default.
A party who does not deliver a reply within the prescribed time shall be deemed to deny the allegations of fact made in the defence of the opposite party.

A party may amend the party's pleading, (a) without leave, before the close of pleadings, if the amendment does not include or necessitate the addition, deletion or substitution of a party to the action; (b) on filing the consent of all parties and, where a person is to be added or substituted as a party, the person's consent; or (c) with leave of the court.

A defendant may crossclaim against a co-defendant who, (a) is or may be liable to the defendant for all or part of the plaintiff's claim; (b) is or may be liable to the defendant for an independent claim for damages or other relief arising out of, (i) a transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences involved in the main action, or (ii) a related transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences; or (c) should be bound by the determination of an issue arising between the plaintiff and the defendant.
A defendant who claims contribution from a co-defendant under the Negligence Act shall do so by way of crossclaim.
A crossclaim (Form 28A) shall be included in the same document as the statement of defence and the document shall be entitled a statement of defence and crossclaim.

A defendant who has delivered a statement of defence that does not contain a crossclaim and who wishes to crossclaim may amend the statement of defence in accordance with rules 26.02 and 26.03 in order to add the crossclaim

A statement of defence and crossclaim shall be delivered, (a) within the time prescribed by rule 18.01 for delivery of the statement of defence in the main action or at any time before the defendant is noted in default; or (b) subsequently with leave, which the court shall grant unless the plaintiff would be prejudiced thereby.

A defendant may commence a third party claim against any person who is not a party to the action and who, (a) is or may be liable to the defendant for all or part of the plaintiff's claim; (b) is or may be liable to the defendant for an independent claim for damages or other relief arising out of, (i) a transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences involved in the main action, or (ii) a related transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences; or (c) should be bound by the determination of an issue arising between the plaintiff and the defendant.
A third party claim (Form 29A) shall be issued within 10 days after the defendant delivers a statement of defence, or at any time before the defendant is noted in default.
A third party claim may be issued within 10 days after the plaintiff delivers a reply in the main action to the defendant's statement of defence.
A third party claim may be issued at any time with the plaintiff's consent or with leave, which the court shall grant unless the plaintiff would be prejudiced thereby.

A third party claim shall be served on the third party personally or by an alternative to personal service under rule 16.03, together with all the pleadings previously delivered in the main action or in any counterclaim, crossclaim or third or subsequent party claim in the main action, within thirty days after the third party claim is issued.
A third party claim shall also be served on every other party to the main action within the time for service on the third party, but personal service is not required.

Where a party to an action intends to obtain evidence under any of the following Rules, the parties to the action shall agree to a discovery plan in accordance with this rule: 1. Rule 30 (Discovery of Documents). 2. Rule 31 (Examination for Discovery). 3. Rule 32 (Inspection of Property). 4. Rule 33 (Medical Examination). 5. Rule 35 (Examination for Discovery by Written Questions).
The discovery plan shall be agreed to before the earlier of, (a) 60 days after the close of pleadings or such longer period as the parties may agree to; and (b) attempting to obtain the evidence.

A party to an action may require that the issues of fact be tried or the damages be assessed, or both, by a jury, by delivering a jury notice (Form 47A) at any time before the close of pleadings, unless section 108 of the Courts of Justice Act or another statute requires that the action be tried without a jury.
An action that is proceeding under this Rule shall not be tried with a jury and, subject to subrule (2), no party to the action may deliver a jury notice under rule 47.01.

A party to an action that is proceeding under this Rule may deliver a jury notice under rule 47.01 if the action involves a claim for relief arising from one of the following: 1. Slander. 2. Libel. 3. Malicious arrest. 4. Malicious prosecution. 5. False imprisonment.

If a jury notice is delivered in accordance with subrule (2), the action may no longer proceed under this Rule and the party delivering the jury notice shall deliver a notice (Form 76A) stating that the action and any related proceedings are continued as an ordinary action.

userQuestion: I missed the time to file my defence — is it too late?
whatsHappening: The time to deliver your statement of defence has run out. But you have not been noted in default yet. Since your time has run out, the plaintiff may ask the registrar to note you in default. To do that, the plaintiff files proof that the statement of claim was served on you, or was deemed served. If the plaintiff has not done so, another defendant who has delivered a statement of defence may move to have the court order you noted in default. That motion must be on notice to the plaintiff. If you are under a disability, such as being a minor, you may be noted in default only with a judge's leave.
whatToDoNext: If you want to defend, you may still deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A) at any time before you are noted in default. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. The time to deliver it may be extended by filing a consent in writing. The court may also extend the time by order, on terms that are just. A motion to extend time may be made before or after the time has run out. A motion is made by a notice of motion (Form 37A). The exception is where the kind of motion or the facts make one unneeded, or the rules say otherwise.
yourDeadline: If you want to defend, deliver your statement of defence. The rules set no further fixed number of days. But you can deliver it only until you are noted in default. The plaintiff can have that done at any time by filing proof of service. After that, you get no notice of further steps. The time can also be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.
whatHappensAfter: If you are noted in default first, you are deemed to admit that every fact in the statement of claim is true. You then must not deliver a defence or take any other step, except a motion to set aside the noting of default or a judgment obtained because of it, unless the court gives leave or the plaintiff consents. You also get no notice of further steps, with some exceptions, such as when the court orders otherwise or a party requires you to attend personally.

userQuestion: There is a judgment against me and they are trying to collect — what can they do?
whatsHappening: A judgment to pay money has been made against you. In the rules, you are the debtor, and the person entitled to enforce it is the creditor. The rules list four ways to enforce an order to pay money. They are a writ of seizure and sale (Form 60A), garnishment, a writ of sequestration (Form 60B), and appointing a receiver. A writ of sequestration may be issued only with the court's leave, obtained on a motion. The court may grant leave only if it is satisfied that other ways of enforcing the order are not working, or are not expected to work. Any other method the law provides may also be used.
whatToDoNext: Garnishment means the creditor collects debts that other people owe you. The creditor must serve the notice of garnishment on you, with a copy of the creditor's affidavit. Each notice names one garnishee, a person the creditor believes owes or will owe you money. A garnishee who admits owing you money must pay it to the sheriff, as the notice says. This is subject to section 7 of the Wages Act. You may bring a motion for a garnishment hearing. At the hearing, the court may, for example, change or pause periodic payments. A copy of your notice of motion must be served on the sheriff by ordinary mail, by personal service, or by an alternative to personal service. Once the sheriff gets it, the sheriff must pause payments to the creditor under the notice until the motion is decided or abandoned. The creditor may also examine you about things such as why the order is not paid, your income and property, and the debts you owe and that others owe you. The notice of examination must be served on you personally or by an alternative to personal service. Only one such examination may be held in a 12 month period in the same case, unless the court orders otherwise. If six years or more have passed since the order, or its enforcement depends on a condition, the creditor needs the court's leave first. That applies before a writ of seizure and sale or a notice of garnishment is issued.
yourDeadline:
If you want to appeal a final order, serve a notice of appeal with a certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C). You have 30 days after the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. Which court hears the appeal depends on the order. Some final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Divisional Court. These include an order to pay one sum of $50,000 or less, or payments of $50,000 or less in the first 12 months, not counting costs. They also include an order dismissing a claim for $50,000 or less. So does an order dismissing a larger claim where the judge or jury says the award would have been $50,000 or less. Other final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Court of Appeal. A final order of an associate judge goes to the Divisional Court. An appeal only about costs, or from an order made with everyone's consent, needs leave first. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court. Delivering a notice of appeal pauses the parts of the order that say to pay money, until the appeal is decided. This does not apply to support.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If you deliver a notice of appeal from the order, any part of it that says to pay money is put on hold until the appeal is decided. This does not apply to support. It also does not apply to an appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment. But in that case, the default judgment may be put on hold by an order. A judge of the appeal court may also order that the hold does not apply. If the judgment was made after you were noted in default, it may be set aside or changed on terms that are just. The court or a judge decides that, depending on how the judgment was made. When the amount owing is paid, a creditor using garnishment must right away serve a notice of termination of garnishment (Form 60J) on the garnishee and the sheriff.

userQuestion: The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?
whatsHappening: A motion for summary judgment asks the court to decide all or part of the claim on affidavits or other evidence. When a plaintiff brings it, it asks for judgment on all or part of the claim. When a defendant brings it, it asks that all or part of the claim be dismissed. The court must grant summary judgment if it is satisfied there is no genuine issue that needs a trial on a claim or defence. It must also grant it if the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way, and the court is satisfied that is appropriate.
whatToDoNext: If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.
yourDeadline:
If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. You must also give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 2 p.m. five days before the hearing. If you do not, the motion is not heard.

If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. You cannot rely only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, showing there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is how your evidence of specific facts reaches the court. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If the moving party did not email you a copy of their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 10 a.m. four days before the hearing.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: To decide if there is a genuine issue that needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties gave. A judge may weigh the evidence and judge how believable a person who swore an affidavit is. The judge may also draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. But a judge does not use these powers if the interest of justice means they should be used only at a trial. For this, a judge may also order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may set out the facts not in dispute and the issues to be tried. It may also order the case to go to trial quickly. The court may order a party to pay the costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity basis in two cases. One is if the party acted unreasonably in making or responding to the motion. The other is if the party acted in bad faith to cause delay.

citations.quote: A plaintiff may, after the defendant has delivered a statement of defence or served a notice of motion, move with supporting affidavit material or other evidence for summary judgment on all or part of the claim in the statement of claim.
A defendant may, after delivering a statement of defence, move with supporting affidavit material or other evidence for summary judgment dismissing all or part of the claim in the statement of claim.
The court shall grant summary judgment if, (a) the court is satisfied that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial with respect to a claim or defence; or
(b) the parties agree to have all or part of the claim determined by a summary judgment and the court is satisfied that it is appropriate to grant summary judgment.

In response to affidavit material or other evidence supporting a motion for summary judgment, a responding party may not rest solely on the allegations or denials in the party's pleadings, but must set out, in affidavit material or other evidence, specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue requiring a trial.

An affidavit for use on a motion for summary judgment may be made on information and belief as provided in subrule 39.01 (4), but, on the hearing of the motion, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference from the failure of a party to provide the evidence of any person having personal knowledge of contested facts.
An affidavit for use on a motion may contain statements of the deponent's information and belief, if the source of the information and the fact of the belief are specified in the affidavit.
On a motion for summary judgment, each party shall serve on every other party to the motion a factum that meets the requirements of rule 4.06.1.
The responding party's factum shall be served and filed with proof of service in the court office where the motion is to be heard at least four days before the hearing.
The moving party's factum shall be served and filed with proof of service in the court office where the motion is to be heard at least seven days before the hearing.

Where a motion is made on notice, the moving party shall, unless the court orders otherwise before or at the hearing of the motion, serve a motion record on every other party to the motion and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion is to be heard, at least seven days before the hearing
(c) a copy of all affidavits and other material served by any party for use on the motion;
at least seven days before the hearing, and the court file shall not be placed before the judge or associate judge hearing the motion unless he or she requests it or a party requisitions it.

Where a motion record is served a responding party who is of the opinion that it is incomplete may serve on every other party, and file, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion is to be heard, at least four days before the hearing, a responding party's motion record containing, in consecutively numbered pages arranged in the following order, (a) a table of contents describing each document, including each exhibit, by its nature and date and, in the case of an exhibit, by exhibit number or letter; and (b) a copy of any material to be used by the responding party on the motion and not included in the motion record.

In determining under clause (2) (a) whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial, the court shall consider the evidence submitted by the parties and, if the determination is being made by a judge, the judge may exercise any of the following powers for the purpose, unless it is in the interest of justice for such powers to be exercised only at a trial: 1. Weighing the evidence. 2. Evaluating the credibility of a deponent. 3. Drawing any reasonable inference from the evidence.
A judge may, for the purposes of exercising any of the powers set out in subrule (2.1), order that oral evidence be presented by one or more parties, with or without time limits on its presentation.

Where summary judgment is refused or is granted only in part, the court may make an order specifying what material facts are not in dispute and defining the issues to be tried, and order that the action proceed to trial expeditiously.

The court may fix and order payment of the costs of a motion for summary judgment by a party on a substantial indemnity basis if, (a) the party acted unreasonably by making or responding to the motion; or (b) the party acted in bad faith for the purpose of delay.
