userQuestion: How do offers to settle work, and does the timing matter?
whatsHappening: A party may serve an offer to settle one or more of the claims in the case on any other party, on the terms the offer sets out (Form 49A). Rule 49 applies to actions and applications, and with needed changes to motions, counterclaims, crossclaims and third or later party claims. In this rule, a plaintiff includes an applicant, and a defendant includes a respondent. An offer to settle is treated as an offer of compromise made without prejudice. No pleading may say that an offer was made. If an offer is not accepted, nothing about it may be told to the court at the hearing until liability and the relief, other than costs, have been decided. An offer must not be filed until then either.
whatToDoNext: You may make an offer at any time, but if it is made less than seven days before the hearing starts, the costs results in rule 49.10 will not apply. You may withdraw your offer at any time before it is accepted, by serving written notice of withdrawal on the party you made it to. That notice may be in Form 49B. If an offer sets a time to accept it and it is not accepted or withdrawn in that time, it is treated as withdrawn when the time ends. You may accept an offer by serving an acceptance of offer (Form 49C) on the party who made it, before it is withdrawn or the court decides the claim. If you rejected an offer, or made a counter-offer that was not accepted, you may still accept the first offer. This is so unless it was withdrawn or the court has decided the claim. A plaintiff's offer to settle for money may say the defendant must pay the money into court or to a trustee. If it does, the defendant may accept only by paying the money as the offer says and telling the plaintiff about the payment. A party under disability, such as a minor, may make, withdraw and accept an offer. But if they accept an offer, or their own offer is accepted, it is not binding on them without a judge's approval under rule 7.08, except as that rule provides.
yourDeadline:
For the costs rules in rule 49.10 to apply to an offer to settle, serve the offer (Form 49A). Do this at least 7 days before the first day of trial. An offer can be made at any time. But if it is made less than seven days before the hearing, the rule 49.10 costs rules do not apply. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. The offer must also stay open, not withdrawn or expired, until the hearing starts. Rule 49 also applies, with needed changes, to motions, counterclaims, crossclaims and third party claims. For an offer on a motion, the hearing is the hearing of that motion. Several defendants may be said to be jointly, or jointly and severally, liable. They may also have rights of contribution or indemnity between them. If both are true, the rule 49.10 costs rules apply only if the offer meets the terms of rule 49.11. An offer can be withdrawn by written notice at any time before it is accepted. It ends when any time it gives for acceptance runs out. It cannot be accepted after the court decides the claim.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: The costs results in rule 49.10 can apply to an offer made at least seven days before the hearing starts. For them to apply, the offer must not be withdrawn or expire before the hearing starts, and it must not be accepted. Say the plaintiff made such an offer, and the judgment is as good for the plaintiff as the offer, or better. Then the plaintiff is entitled to partial indemnity costs up to the date the offer was served, and substantial indemnity costs from that date, unless the court orders otherwise. Say the defendant made such an offer, and the judgment is as good for the plaintiff as the offer, or worse. Then the plaintiff is entitled to partial indemnity costs up to the date the offer was served, and the defendant to partial indemnity costs from that date, unless the court orders otherwise. The party who wants one of these results has to prove how the judgment compares to the offer. Rule 49.11 adds terms where two or more defendants are said to be jointly, or jointly and severally, liable. It does so if they may also have rights of contribution or indemnity between them. In that case, these results apply only if the offer meets the terms below. An offer made by the plaintiff must be made to all the defendants and settle the claim against all of them. An offer made to the plaintiff must settle the claim against all the defendants. It must also do one of two things. One is to pay the costs of any defendant who does not join in making the offer. The other is to be made by all the defendants. Its terms must then make them jointly and severally liable to the plaintiff for the whole amount. Despite rules 49.03, 49.10 and 49.11, the court may take into account any written offer, its date and its terms when it decides costs. Say an accepted offer does not deal with costs. If the defendant made the offer, the plaintiff is entitled to costs assessed up to the date the plaintiff was served with the offer. If the plaintiff made the offer, the plaintiff is entitled to costs assessed up to the date the notice of acceptance was served. If a party does not comply with an accepted offer, the other party has two choices. They may make a motion to a judge for judgment on the offer's terms. Or they may carry on with the case as if no offer had been accepted.

citations.quote: A party to a proceeding may serve on any other party an offer to settle any one or more of the claims in the proceeding on the terms specified in the offer to settle (Form 49A).
This Rule applies to actions, applications and, with necessary modifications, motions, counterclaims, crossclaims and third or subsequent party claims.
"plaintiff" includes an applicant.
"defendant" includes a respondent
An offer to settle shall be deemed to be an offer of compromise made without prejudice.
No statement of the fact that an offer to settle has been made shall be contained in any pleading.

Where an offer to settle is not accepted, no communication respecting the offer shall be made to the court at the hearing of the proceeding until all questions of liability and the relief to be granted, other than costs, have been determined.
An offer to settle shall not be filed until all questions of liability and the relief to be granted in the proceeding, other than costs, have been determined.

An offer to settle may be made at any time, but where the offer to settle is made less than seven days before the hearing of the proceeding commences, the costs consequences referred to in rule 49.10 do not apply.
An offer to settle may be withdrawn at any time before it is accepted by serving written notice of withdrawal of the offer on the party to whom the offer was made.
The notice of withdrawal of the offer may be in Form 49B.
Where an offer to settle specifies a time within which it may be accepted and it is not accepted or withdrawn within that time, it shall be deemed to have been withdrawn when the time expires.

An offer to settle may be accepted by serving an acceptance of offer (Form 49C) on the party who made the offer, at any time before it is withdrawn or the court disposes of the claim in respect of which it is made.

Where a party to whom an offer to settle is made rejects the offer or responds with a counter-offer that is not accepted, the party may thereafter accept the original offer to settle, unless it has been withdrawn or the court has disposed of the claim in respect of which it was made.

An offer by a plaintiff to settle a claim in return for the payment of money by a defendant may include a term that the defendant pay the money into court or to a trustee and the defendant may accept the offer only by paying the money in accordance with the offer and notifying the plaintiff of the payment.

A party under disability may make, withdraw and accept an offer to settle, but the acceptance of an offer made by a party under disability, or the acceptance by a party under disability of an offer made by another party, is not binding on the party under disability without the approval of a judge under rule 7.08, except as otherwise provided by that rule.
"disability", where used in respect of a person, means that the person is, (a) a minor,

Where an offer to settle, (a) is made by a plaintiff at least seven days before the commencement of the hearing of the proceeding; (b) is not withdrawn and does not expire before the commencement of the hearing of the proceeding; and (c) is not accepted by the defendant, and the plaintiff obtains a judgment as favourable as or more favourable than the terms of the offer to settle, the plaintiff is entitled to partial indemnity costs to the date the offer to settle was served and substantial indemnity costs from that date, unless the court orders otherwise.

Where an offer to settle, (a) is made by a defendant at least seven days before the commencement of the hearing of the proceeding; (b) is not withdrawn and does not expire before the commencement of the hearing of the proceeding; and (c) is not accepted by the plaintiff, and the plaintiff obtains a judgment as favourable as or less favourable than the terms of the offer to settle, the plaintiff is entitled to partial indemnity costs to the date the offer was served and the defendant is entitled to partial indemnity costs from that date, unless the court orders otherwise.

The burden of proving that the judgment is as favourable as the terms of the offer to settle, or more or less favourable, as the case may be, is on the party who claims the benefit of subrule (1) or (2).

Where there are two or more defendants, the plaintiff may offer to settle with any defendant and any defendant may offer to settle with the plaintiff, but where the defendants are alleged to be jointly or jointly and severally liable to the plaintiff in respect of a claim and rights of contribution or indemnity may exist between the defendants, the costs consequences prescribed by rule 49.10 do not apply to an offer to settle unless,
(a) in the case of an offer made by the plaintiff, the offer is made to all the defendants, and is an offer to settle the claim against all the defendants; or

(b) in the case of an offer made to the plaintiff, (i) the offer is an offer to settle the plaintiff's claim against all the defendants and to pay the costs of any defendant who does not join in making the offer, or (ii) the offer is made by all the defendants and is an offer to settle the claim against all the defendants, and, by the terms of the offer, they are made jointly and severally liable to the plaintiff for the whole amount of the offer.

Despite rules 49.03, 49.10 and 49.11, the court, in exercising its discretion with respect to costs, may take into account any offer to settle made in writing, the date the offer was made and the terms of the offer.

Where an accepted offer to settle does not provide for the disposition of costs, the plaintiff is entitled, (a) where the offer was made by the defendant, to the plaintiff's costs assessed to the date the plaintiff was served with the offer; or (b) where the offer was made by the plaintiff, to the plaintiff's costs assessed to the date that the notice of acceptance was served.

Where a party to an accepted offer to settle fails to comply with the terms of the offer, the other party may, (a) make a motion to a judge for judgment in the terms of the accepted offer, and the judge may grant judgment accordingly; or (b) continue the proceeding as if there had been no accepted offer to settle.

userQuestion: Is there a time limit to ask for my share of our property after our marriage ended?
whatsHappening: You are asking whether a claim to equalize net family property can still be started. The Family Law Act gives this right when a divorce is granted or a marriage is declared a nullity. It also gives it when the spouses have separated and there is no reasonable prospect that they will live together again. In those cases, the spouse whose net family property is smaller is entitled to half the difference between the two. When a spouse dies, the surviving spouse is entitled to half the difference if the deceased spouse's net family property was larger. Here, a spouse is one of two people who are married to each other. It also includes one of two people who entered a void or voidable marriage, if the person relying on it acted in good faith.
whatToDoNext: A spouse or a former spouse may apply to the court to decide this. The personal representative of a spouse who has died may also apply. But this right is personal between the spouses, with two exceptions about a spouse's estate. A claim under section 5 (1) or (3) that was started before a spouse's death may be continued by or against the estate. A claim under section 5 (2), which is the claim on a spouse's death, may be made by or against the estate. For this claim, the court is the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice, not the Ontario Court of Justice. A claim based on a divorce, nullity, separation or death must not be brought after the earliest of three dates. One is two years after the day a divorce or a judgment of nullity ends the marriage. One is six years after the day the spouses separate with no reasonable prospect of living together again. One is six months after the first spouse's death. A divorce generally takes effect on the 31st day after the day the judgment is given. Other parts of that section of the Divorce Act can change that day, such as when the court orders an earlier date or there is an appeal. Once a divorce granted under the Divorce Act takes effect, it ends the marriage. The court may, on a motion, extend a time set by the Family Law Act. It must be satisfied of three things. There are apparent grounds for relief. Relief is not available because of a delay that was in good faith. No one will suffer substantial prejudice because of the delay. When a spouse dies, the surviving spouse must choose, or elect, what to receive. The choice is between the entitlement under section 5 and what comes under the will, under Part II of the Succession Law Reform Act, or both, depending on the case. The election must be in the form set by the regulations. It must be filed in the office of the Estate Registrar for Ontario within six months after the first spouse's death. If it is not filed in time, the surviving spouse is treated as having chosen the will or the Succession Law Reform Act, or both, as the case may be. That does not apply if the court, on an application, orders otherwise.
yourDeadline:
Apply to equalize net family property, if a divorce or nullity judgment ended the marriage. You have 2 years after the day the divorce or judgment of nullity ended the marriage. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. The time ends on the earliest of three dates. One is 2 years after a divorce or a nullity judgment ends the marriage. One is 6 years after the spouses separate with no reasonable prospect of living together again. One is 6 months after the first spouse dies. The court can extend the time on a motion. It must find three things. There are apparent grounds for relief. The delay was in good faith. No one will suffer substantial prejudice from it. This claim is only for married spouses. That includes a void or voidable marriage entered into in good faith. A divorce usually takes effect on the 31st day after the judgment. The 2 years count from the day it takes effect.

Apply to equalize net family property, if the spouses have separated. You have 6 years after the day the spouses separated with no reasonable prospect of living together again. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 6 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This is one of the three dates above. The time ends on whichever comes first. The court can extend it, as set out above.

Apply to equalize net family property, if the first spouse has died. You have 6 months after the first spouse’s death. This is one of the three dates above. The time ends on whichever comes first. The court can extend it, as set out above. A period of months ends on the day with the same number as the start day. If that month has no such day, it ends on the last day of the month (Legislation Act, 2006, s. 89 (6)).

If your spouse has died and you want your equalization entitlement, file your choice (election) with the Estate Registrar for Ontario. You have 6 months after the first spouse’s death. If you do not file it in time, you are treated as choosing what the will or the Succession Law Reform Act gives you, or both. The court can order otherwise on an application. The court can also extend a time set by the Family Law Act on a motion. It must find apparent grounds for relief, a delay in good faith, and no substantial prejudice to anyone. A period of months ends on the day with the same number as the start day. If that month has no such day, it ends on the last day of the month (Legislation Act, 2006, s. 89 (6)).

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: Once an application is made, each party must serve on the other, and file with the court, a statement sworn or declared to be true. It gives details of things such as the party's property, debts and other liabilities at the date of the marriage and at the valuation date. The court's powers include ordering one spouse to pay the other the amount the court finds that spouse is entitled to.

userQuestion: I cannot find my ex or they keep avoiding the papers — what now?
whatsHappening: Your application has been filed, and you have tried to serve it on the respondent without success. If it was not served on or before the court date, the clerk must set a new court date for that respondent when you ask. You must then make the needed change to the application and serve it on that respondent right away.
whatToDoNext: You may ask the court, by a motion, to order substituted service. This means serving the document by a method the court chooses. The court may make this order if you do two things. First, give detailed evidence of the steps taken to find the respondent. If they were found, also show the steps taken to serve them. Second, show that the method could reasonably be expected to bring the document to their attention. You may bring this motion without notice, unless the person to be served is a government agency. If the court orders service by advertisement, Form 6A must be used. The court may also, on a motion without notice, order that service is not required. It may do so only if both of these are true. First, reasonable efforts to find the respondent have not worked or would not work. Second, no method of substituted service could reasonably be expected to bring it to their attention. Say the document was served in a way other than the ways the rules or an order allow. The court may then approve that service if the document came to the respondent's attention. It may also approve it if the document would have come to their attention had they not been evading service. A motion, with or without notice, needs a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A). If the motion is limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters, you may use a motion form (Form 14B) instead. For a motion without notice, you must file the documents on or before the motion date, unless the court orders otherwise. The mandatory information program applies to some cases. Where it applies, you must not take any step in the case until your certificate of attendance is filed. The one exception for you is making an appointment for a case conference. The court may, on a motion, excuse a party from this because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice.
yourDeadline:
Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take another step in the case. That includes a motion for substituted service. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise on a motion.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: An order made on a motion without notice (Form 14D) must require the matter to come back to the court. That must be within 14 days or on a date the court chooses, and to the same judge if possible. Unless the court orders otherwise, you must serve the order right away on all parties it affects. You must serve it together with all the documents used on the motion. Once the application is served, service may be proved in ways the rules list, such as an affidavit of service (Form 6B).

userQuestion: My ex filed an answer and is claiming things against me — what happens next?
whatsHappening: The respondent has served and filed an answer, so your case is defended. In the answer, the respondent may make a claim against you. They may also make a claim against another person, who then also becomes a respondent in the case. In each case where an answer is filed, a judge must hold at least one conference. This does not apply in an international child abduction case. In a child protection case, a case conference may be held if a party asks for one or the court considers it appropriate.
whatToDoNext: If the answer makes a claim, you may serve and file a reply (Form 10A) to respond to it, within 10 days after you were served with the answer. The answer may make a claim against you for support, a property claim, or a claim for exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents. If it does, you must serve and file a financial statement within the time for serving and filing a reply. You must do this whether or not you serve a reply. The financial statement is in Form 13 if there is a support claim but no property or matrimonial home claim. It is in Form 13.1 if there is a property or matrimonial home claim, with or without a support claim. In the Ontario Court of Justice, the clerk acts on or before the first court date. If an answer has been filed, the clerk confirms that the case is ready for a hearing, case conference or settlement conference, and schedules it. The same applies to a fast track case in the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice. A case there is fast track unless the application claims a divorce, makes a property claim, or makes a family arbitration claim. In a standard track case there, the clerk must schedule a case conference when any party asks. The same is true in other Superior Court of Justice family cases started on or after July 1, 2004. These scheduling steps do not apply to enforcements. Rules 39 (2), 40 (2) and 41 (2) list other cases they leave out. If you ask for a case conference, you must serve and file a case conference notice (Form 17). Where the mandatory information program applies, you may not take any step in the case until your certificate of attendance is filed. The one exception is making an appointment for a case conference. On a motion, the court may order that this does not apply to you because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Before a conference, you must confer, or make best efforts to confer, with every other party, by talking or in writing. userQuestion: I was served with an automatic order — what is it, and where does it come from?
whatsHappening: An automatic order (Form 8.0.1) is an order that the court clerk issues when certain family claims are made. The clerk gives it to the party who made the claim. The rule covers claims made on or after February 1, 2022. They are claims about four things. One is decision-making responsibility or parenting time for a child. That claim is under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Children’s Law Reform Act. Another is net family property, under Part I of the Family Law Act. Another is a matrimonial home, under Part II of the Family Law Act. The last is support, under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Family Law Act. A claim is made when an application that contains it is issued. It is also made when a document that contains it is filed. That document can be an answer, a motion to change a final order or agreement, or a response to a motion to change. No automatic order is issued if the case is going ahead with the consent of the parties. The clerk also does not issue one if the only such claims are about making the terms of an agreement or an earlier order part of an order. It is the same if the only such claims are about a family arbitration, or an arbitration agreement or award. Nor is one issued in an application by a person or agency named in subsection 33 (3) of the Family Law Act.
whatToDoNext: The party who got the order from the clerk must serve it on every other party. If that party made the claim in an application, they must serve the order together with the application. If they made it in a later document, they must serve the order promptly after they get it from the clerk. In that case, they must serve it no later than seven days after it was issued. They do not have to serve it on a person or agency named in subsection 33 (3) of the Family Law Act.
whatHappensAfter: Only one automatic order is issued in a case. If another such claim is made later in the case, the clerk does not issue a new one.

citations.quote: This rule applies to a case in which any of the following claims is made, if the claim is made on or after February 1, 2022: 1. A claim respecting decision-making responsibility or parenting time with respect to a child under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Children’s Law Reform Act. 2. A claim respecting net family property under Part I of the Family Law Act. 3. A claim respecting a matrimonial home under Part II of the Family Law Act. 4. A claim for support under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Family Law Act.

For the purposes of this rule, a claim is made when any of the following occurs: 1. An application that contains the claim is issued. 2. An answer, motion to change a final order or agreement under rule 15 or response to motion to change that contains the claim is filed.
On the making of a claim to which this rule applies, the clerk shall issue an automatic order (Form 8.0.1) and provide it to the party making the claim.

Subrule (3) does not apply, (a) if an automatic order has already been issued in the case; (b) if the case is proceeding on consent of the parties; (c) if the only claims to which this rule applies relate to, (i) the incorporation of the terms of an agreement or prior court order, or (ii) a family arbitration, family arbitration agreement or family arbitration award; or (d) in an application brought by a person or agency referred to in subsection 33 (3) of the Family Law Act.

The party to whom the automatic order is provided shall serve the automatic order on every other party in the case in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the claim is made in an application, the automatic order shall be served together with the application. 2. If the claim is made in an answer, motion to change a final order or agreement under rule 15 or response to motion to change, the automatic order shall be served promptly after the party receives it from the clerk, but in any event not later than seven days after the automatic order is issued.
Despite subrule (5), the automatic order is not required to be served on a person or agency referred to in subsection 33 (3) of the Family Law Act.

userQuestion: We have a trial management conference — what do I have to file for it?
whatsHappening: A trial management conference helps plan the trial. Its purposes include deciding how the trial will go and estimating the time it needs. It can also set the trial date, if this has not already been done. The papers you must serve and file depend on which court the case is in.
whatToDoNext: If you asked for the conference, you must serve and file your papers no later than six days before it. If no party asked for it, the six days apply to the applicant or the party who made the motion. The other party must serve and file no later than four days before the conference. In the Ontario Court of Justice, the paper is a trial management conference brief (Form 17E). In the Superior Court of Justice or its Family Court, you need three things. The first is the trial scheduling endorsement form. It must be filled in by the parties and endorsed by the court, unless it was already filed. The second is an offer to settle all outstanding claims in the case. The third is an outline of your opening statement. Some Superior Court cases use a trial management conference brief (Form 17E) instead. These are child protection cases, cases set for an uncontested trial, enforcements, and requests to enforce a family arbitration award. This does not apply if a court order requires the trial scheduling endorsement form in that case. Before the conference, you must talk or write to every other party, or make your best effort to. Discuss requests for financial disclosure, settling the issues for now, and settling them for good. You do not have to if a court order forbids that contact. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party with no licensed representative. Each party must fill in a confirmation of conference (Form 17F). First give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other method. This copy step does not apply in a child protection case. Then give the clerk Form 17F no later than 2 in the afternoon, three days before the conference. You can take it to the court office or email it there. You can also send it through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not go ahead if the clerk does not get it on time. You must come to the conference, unless the court orders otherwise. If you have a licensed representative, they must come too. They must have full knowledge of and authority in the case.
yourDeadline:
If you asked for the trial management conference, serve and file your conference papers. In the Ontario Court of Justice, that is a trial management conference brief (Form 17E). In the Superior Court, it is the endorsed trial scheduling form if it is not already filed, an offer to settle all outstanding claims, and an outline of your opening statement. A case the rules exempt from that form uses a trial management conference brief instead. If no one asked for the conference, this time is for the applicant or the party who made the motion. Do this at least 6 days before the date of the trial management conference. If you have served corrected, updated or extra financial disclosure, serve and file an updated certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) by the same day. Before the conference, talk or write to every other party, or make your best effort to. Discuss requests for financial disclosure and settling the issues for now, and settling them for good. You do not have to if a court order forbids it. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party with no licensed representative. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the other party, serve and file your conference papers, as listed above. Do this at least 4 days before the date of the trial management conference. The extra steps listed above apply to you too. Where they say "by the same day", your day is this 4-day one. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation of conference (Form 17F) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the trial management conference. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not go ahead without it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: At the conference, the judge may set times for events in the case or give directions for the next steps, if it is fitting. Trial management conference briefs become part of the continuing record. An agreement made at a conference does not take effect until the parties sign it and it is witnessed. userQuestion: The judge made a final order — can I appeal it or get it changed?
whatsHappening: Rule 38 of the Family Law Rules covers appeals from the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice. It applies to appeals under the laws it lists, such as section 48 of the Family Law Act and section 73 of the Children's Law Reform Act. A final order of a Superior Court judge is appealed to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal. The Courts of Justice Act decides which one, based on the kind of order. For example, a final order of a Family Court judge made only under an Ontario law goes to the Divisional Court. For appeals to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal, rules 61, 62 and 63 of the Rules of Civil Procedure apply, with necessary changes.
whatToDoNext: To appeal a final order of the Ontario Court of Justice, you must serve a notice of appeal (Form 38) within 30 days after the date of the order. Serve it on every other party affected by the appeal or entitled to appeal, and on the clerk of the court where the order was made. Some appeals are under section 121 of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. For those, also serve every other person entitled to notice under subsection 79 (3) of that Act who appeared at the hearing. Then you must file the notice within 10 days after serving it. If you serve it but do not file it in those 10 days, the appeal is treated as withdrawn, unless the court orders otherwise. To appeal to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal, you must serve a notice of appeal within 30 days after the order was made, unless a statute or the rules say otherwise. Use Form 61A.3 for the Divisional Court or Form 61A.2 for the Court of Appeal. Serve it on every party whose interest may be affected by the appeal, subject to the exceptions in rule 61.04 (1.1), and on anyone a statute entitles to be heard on the appeal. With it, you must serve and file an appellant's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C), with proof of service. The certificate sets out only the parts of the evidence that you think the appeal needs. You must file the notice of appeal, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within ten days after service. Some appeals need leave of the court the appeal goes to. This includes an appeal from an order made with the consent of the parties. It also includes an appeal only about costs that were in the discretion of the court that made the costs order. Some appeals to the Court of Appeal need that court's leave. To ask for it, use a notice of motion for leave to appeal (Form 61A.1). For a Superior Court judge's final costs order, leave to appeal to the Divisional Court must come from a panel of that court. For that, the notice of motion for leave is in Form 61A. You must serve a notice of motion for leave within 15 days after the order is made, unless a statute provides otherwise. You must then file it, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within five days after service. If leave is granted, you must deliver the notice of appeal within seven days after leave is granted. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. For the Divisional Court, deliver the appellant's certificate respecting evidence with it in that time. Sometimes you appeal costs together with an appeal that does not need leave. Then you ask for leave to appeal the costs in the notice of appeal, or in a supplementary notice of appeal, as part of the relief sought. The panel hearing the other appeal decides on leave, and if leave is granted, it may then hear the costs appeal. In that case, the separate leave motion steps above are not used. An order made under the Divorce Act cannot be appealed more than thirty days after the day it was made. On special grounds, the appeal court or one of its judges may extend that time, before or after it runs out. A judgment granting a divorce cannot be appealed on or after the day the divorce takes effect. Subject to the rest of section 12 of the Divorce Act, a divorce takes effect on the thirty-first day after the day the judgment is given. Apart from an appeal, the court may, on motion, change an order that was obtained by fraud or that contains a mistake. It may also change an order that needs to deal with a matter that was before the court but that it did not decide. The same applies to an order made without notice. It also applies to an order made with notice, if an affected party was not there when it was made. That is when the notice was inadequate, or the party could not be there for a reason the court accepts. Rule 14, the rule on motions, applies to that kind of motion, with necessary changes. This is different from a motion to change a final order under rule 15. Under rule 15, a party who wants a final order changed must serve and file a motion to change (Form 15). It must have all required attachments. If the parties and any assignee agree to the change, the parties file a consent motion to change (Form 15C) instead. They file it with the other papers the rule lists. If the agreed change is only to child support, they file Form 15D instead. That is a consent motion to change child support, filed with the other papers the rule lists. For orders under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, rule 15 covers only a final order made under section 102 of that Act.
yourDeadline:
If you want to appeal a final order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice, serve a notice of appeal (Form 38). Serve every other party affected and the clerk where the order was made. You have 30 days after the date of the order or decision being appealed. File the notice within 10 days after serving it. If you do not, the appeal is treated as withdrawn unless the court orders otherwise. A final order of the Superior Court of Justice or its Family Court is different. The appeal goes to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal, depending on the order. Serve the notice of appeal within 30 days after the order. Serve the appellant's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C) with it. File the notice within 10 days after serving it. Some appeals need leave of the court the appeal goes to. That includes an appeal from an order made on consent, and an appeal only about costs. For a Superior Court order going to the Divisional Court, serve a notice of motion for leave within 15 days after the order. File it within 5 days after serving it. An order under the Divorce Act cannot be appealed more than 30 days after it was made. The appeal court can extend that time on special grounds. A divorce itself cannot be appealed once it takes effect. That is usually the 31st day after the judgment. On an appeal to the Superior Court of Justice, serving the notice does not stop a support order from being enforced. The court can give more time.

If another party serves you a draft of the order for approval, serve your approval or a notice disputing approval (Form 25E). You have 10 days after the day the draft order was served on you for approval. If you serve neither in that time, the order can be signed without your approval. If you dispute it, serve Form 25E with a copy of the order redrafted as you propose. Also serve notice of the time the clerk sets to settle it by telephone. Serve these on the party who served the draft, and on every other party it was served on. The party the order favours prepares the draft and serves it for approval. Another party may prepare it if that party has no licensed representative. Another party may also prepare it if that party does not do so within 10 days. Where no party has a licensed representative, the clerk prepares the order.

If the court asks for written submissions on costs, serve and file yours. You have 15 days after the day the court required the written submissions. Any reply submission is due within 30 days after the court asked. A submission can be no longer than three pages. For the costs of a trial, the limit is five pages. These times and limits apply unless the court orders otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: On an appeal to the Superior Court of Justice, serving a notice of appeal does not stay a support order or an order that enforces a support order. It does stay any other payment order made under the order, until the appeal is decided. On an appeal to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal, delivering a notice of appeal stays any part of the order for the payment of money until the appeal is decided. That does not apply to a part that awards support or enforces a support order.

userQuestion: I disagree with a temporary order — can I appeal it, and how fast?
whatsHappening: A temporary order of the Ontario Court of Justice is appealed to the Superior Court of Justice. The steps are the same as for a final order. But the time to serve the notice of appeal is shorter. An appeal from an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge goes to the Divisional Court, but only with leave.
whatToDoNext: To appeal a temporary order of the Ontario Court of Justice, you must serve a notice of appeal (Form 38) within seven days after the date of the order. Serve it on every other party affected by the appeal or entitled to appeal, and on the clerk of the court where the order was made. Some appeals are under section 121 of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. For those, also serve every other person entitled to notice under subsection 79 (3) of that Act who appeared at the hearing. In a case under that Act, you have 30 days after the date of the temporary order to serve it instead. Then you must file the notice within 10 days after serving it. If you serve it but do not file it in those 10 days, the appeal is treated as withdrawn, unless the court orders otherwise. For an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge, you must get leave from a panel of the Divisional Court. Rules 61, 62 and 63 of the Rules of Civil Procedure apply to this, with necessary changes. You ask for leave with a notice of motion for leave to appeal (Form 61A). You must serve it within 15 days after the order is made, unless a statute provides otherwise. You must then file it, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within five days after service. A case may be under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. If so, the motion for leave is combined with the notice of appeal.
yourDeadline:
If you want to appeal a temporary order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice, serve a notice of appeal (Form 38). Serve every other party affected and the clerk of the court where the order was made. You have 7 days after the date of the temporary order. File it within 10 days after serving it. If you do not, the appeal is treated as withdrawn unless the court orders otherwise. In a child protection case, the time to serve is 30 days. A temporary order made by a judge of the Superior Court of Justice is different. An appeal to the Divisional Court then needs leave. Under the civil rules, serve a notice of motion for leave to appeal (Form 61A) within 15 days after the order. File it with proof of service within 5 days after serving it. The court can give more time.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, the motion for leave is heard together with the appeal. In any other case, the motion for leave to appeal is heard in writing, without the parties or lawyers attending. But if the court decides from the written papers that an oral hearing is warranted, it must order one. On an appeal to the Superior Court of Justice, serving a notice of appeal does not stay a support order or an order that enforces a support order. It does stay any other payment order made under the temporary order, until the appeal is decided.

userQuestion: We both want the divorce, or my spouse is not contesting it — how does a divorce go through on paper?
whatsHappening: Either spouse may start a divorce case. The application can name the other spouse as the respondent. Or it can be a joint application with no respondent. In a joint application, the divorce and any other order need the consent of both spouses. In a joint application, the divorce is dealt with on affidavit evidence. It is also dealt with that way if the respondent files no answer, or files one and then withdraws it. An Ontario court can hear a divorce if either spouse has habitually lived in Ontario for at least one year right before the case started. A divorce can be based on separation. If so, the spouses must have lived separate and apart for at least one year before the divorce is decided. They must also have been living apart when the case started. Living together again for up to 90 days in total, mainly to try to reconcile, does not by itself break that year. A divorce can also be based on what the spouse the case is brought against has done since the marriage. This means adultery by that spouse since the marriage. Or it means physical or mental cruelty by that spouse since the marriage, if it makes living together intolerable. If the application claims adultery with another person, that person does not need to be named. If named, that person must be served with the application and has all the rights of a respondent.
whatToDoNext: Before the court can grant the divorce, a marriage certificate must be filed. A marriage registration certificate can be filed instead. This is not needed if the application says it is impractical to get one and explains why. A report on earlier divorce cases started by either spouse must also be filed. It is issued under the Central Registry of Divorce Proceedings Regulations (Canada). You must also file an affidavit for divorce in Form 36. You file it as the applicant if the respondent files no answer, or files one and later withdraws it. In a joint application, the applicants file it. The affidavit must confirm that all the information in the application is correct, except as it says. If neither kind of marriage certificate has been filed, it must give enough facts to prove the marriage. If the marriage did not take place in Canada, it must give proof of any earlier divorce, or of the death of a party's earlier spouse. It must describe the support arrangements for any children of the marriage, as the Divorce Act requires. The income and financial facts that section 21 of the child support guidelines requires must be attached. They go in as exhibits. It must also give any other facts the court needs to grant the divorce. With the affidavit, you must file three copies of a draft divorce order (Form 25A). You must also file a stamped envelope addressed to each party. If the divorce order is to include a support order, you must file one more copy of the draft divorce order. The clerk files that copy with the Director of the Family Responsibility Office. You must also file two copies of a draft support deduction order. If no answer is filed, the clerk must, on request, prepare the documents for a judge in an uncontested divorce.
whatHappensAfter: Once all of this is filed, the clerk prepares a certificate (Form 36A). The clerk then gives the documents to a judge. The judge may grant the divorce as set out in the draft order. Or the judge may have the clerk send the papers back to you to make any needed corrections. The judge may also grant the divorce with changes to the draft order, or refuse it. But first, the judge must let you file another affidavit or come to court. This lets you explain why the order should be made without change. The court must be satisfied that reasonable arrangements have been made to support any children of the marriage. It looks at the applicable guidelines to decide this. If those arrangements have not been made, it holds back the divorce until they are. The court must also satisfy itself that there has been no collusion in the divorce application. If it finds collusion in presenting the application, it must dismiss it. Under the Act, collusion is an agreement or plot to subvert the administration of justice. An applicant may be part of it directly or indirectly. It includes any agreement to make up or hide evidence, or to deceive the court. An agreement is not collusion as far as it deals with separation or financial support. The same goes for division of property, parenting time or decision-making responsibility. Some divorces are based on adultery or cruelty. In those cases, the court must make sure there was no condonation or connivance by the spouse bringing the case. If that spouse condoned or connived at the act or conduct complained of, the court must dismiss the application. The exception is where the court finds the public interest would be better served by granting the divorce. Living together again for up to 90 days in total, mainly to try to reconcile, is not treated as condonation. With some exceptions, such as an appeal, a divorce takes effect on the 31st day after the judgment granting it. When the divorce takes effect, either party may ask the clerk for a divorce certificate (Form 36B). The clerk first checks the court record to see that no appeal is still open. The clerk also checks that no order has extended the time to appeal, unless that extra time ran out with no appeal. If satisfied, the clerk issues the certificate. Unless the court orders otherwise, the clerk mails it to the parties if stamped envelopes were filed, or emails it to them.

If no answer is filed, (a) the clerk shall, on request, schedule a case conference or set a date for an uncontested trial or, in an uncontested divorce case, prepare the documents for a judge; and

Once the requirements of subrules (4) to (6) have been met, the clerk shall prepare a certificate (Form 36A) and present the documents to a judge, who may, (a) grant the divorce as set out in the draft order; (b) have the clerk return the documents to the applicant to make any needed corrections; or (c) grant the divorce but make changes to the draft order, or refuse to grant the divorce, after giving the applicant a chance to file an additional affidavit or come to court to explain why the order should be made without change.

When a divorce takes effect, the clerk shall, on either party’s request, (a) check the continuing record or, if there is no continuing record, the court file, to verify that, (i) no appeal has been taken from the divorce order, or any appeal from it has been disposed of, and (ii) no order has been made extending the time for an appeal, or any extended time has expired without an appeal; and (b) if satisfied of those matters, issue a divorce certificate (Form 36B) and, unless the court orders otherwise, (i) mail it to the parties if stamped envelopes have been filed, or (ii) email it to the parties.

A court in a province has jurisdiction to hear and determine a divorce proceeding if either spouse has been habitually resident in the province for at least one year immediately preceding the commencement of the proceeding.

Breakdown of a marriage is established only if (a) the spouses have lived separate and apart for at least one year immediately preceding the determination of the divorce proceeding and were living separate and apart at the commencement of the proceeding; or (b) the spouse against whom the divorce proceeding is brought has, since celebration of the marriage, (i) committed adultery, or (ii) treated the other spouse with physical or mental cruelty of such a kind as to render intolerable the continued cohabitation of the spouses.
(ii) by reason only that the spouses have resumed cohabitation during a period of, or periods totalling, not more than ninety days with reconciliation as its primary purpose.
(a) to satisfy itself that there has been no collusion in relation to the application for a divorce and to dismiss the application if it finds that there was collusion in presenting it;

(b) to satisfy itself that reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of any children of the marriage, having regard to the applicable guidelines, and, if such arrangements have not been made, to stay the granting of the divorce until such arrangements are made;

(c) where a divorce is sought in circumstances described in paragraph 8(2)(b), to satisfy itself that there has been no condonation or connivance on the part of the spouse bringing the proceeding, and to dismiss the application for a divorce if that spouse has condoned or connived at the act or conduct complained of unless, in the opinion of the court, the public interest would be better served by granting the divorce.

For the purposes of this section, a continuation or resumption of cohabitation during a period of, or periods totalling, not more than ninety days with reconciliation as its primary purpose shall not be considered to constitute condonation.

In this section, collusion means an agreement or conspiracy to which an applicant for a divorce is either directly or indirectly a party for the purpose of subverting the administration of justice, and includes any agreement, understanding or arrangement to fabricate or suppress evidence or to deceive the court, but does not include an agreement to the extent that it provides for separation between the parties, financial support, division of property or the exercise of parenting time or decision-making responsibility.
Subject to this section, a divorce takes effect on the thirty-first day after the day on which the judgment granting the divorce is rendered.

A divorce in respect of which an appeal is pending at the end of the period referred to in subsection (1), unless voided on appeal, takes effect on the expiration of the time fixed by law for instituting an appeal from the decision on that appeal or any subsequent appeal, if no appeal has been instituted within that time.

userQuestion: The other side wants a final order without a trial — how do I respond to a summary judgment motion?
whatsHappening: A party may move for summary judgment after the respondent serves an answer, or after the time to serve one ends. Summary judgment is a final order made without a trial. It can cover all or part of a claim or defence in the case. This motion can be made in any case that does not include a divorce claim, including a child protection case. In a case that includes a divorce claim, the divorce claim may be split from the rest of the case. Or the rule 36 steps for an uncontested divorce may be used for it. The party making the motion must serve an affidavit or other evidence. It must set out specific facts showing there is no genuine issue that needs a trial. In general, no motion may be heard before a conference on the main issues has been completed. That limit does not apply to a motion for summary judgment.
whatToDoNext: In response, you may not rely only on allegations or denials. You must set out specific facts in an affidavit or other evidence. These facts must show there is a genuine issue for trial. If the motion was made with a notice of motion (Form 14), you must serve and file your response no later than four days before the motion date. The court may draw conclusions against you if your evidence is not from someone with personal knowledge of the facts in dispute.
yourDeadline:
Serve and file your response. Include an affidavit or other evidence with specific facts showing there is a genuine issue for trial. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. You cannot rely only on allegations or denials. If your evidence does not come from someone who knows the facts personally, the court may draw conclusions against you. If there is no genuine issue that needs a trial, the court makes a final order. Your last financial statement may be more than 30 days old when the motion is heard. If so, update it by this same day with an affidavit or a new statement. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: To decide if a genuine issue needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties submitted. It may also weigh the evidence, decide how believable a person who swore an affidavit is, and draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. It does not use these powers if the interest of justice calls for them to be used only at a trial. To use them, it may order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If no genuine issue needs a trial of a claim or defence, the court must make a final order on it. If the only genuine issue is how much a party is entitled to, the court must order a trial to decide the amount. If the only genuine issue is a question of law, the court must decide it and make a final order. If the court does not make a final order, or orders a trial of an issue, it may give directions. For example, it may say which facts are not in dispute and how and when the case will go to trial.

The party making the motion shall serve an affidavit or other evidence that sets out specific facts showing that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial.

In response to the affidavit or other evidence served by the party making the motion, the party responding to the motion may not rest on mere allegations or denials but shall set out, in an affidavit or other evidence, specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.
If a party’s evidence is not from a person who has personal knowledge of the facts in dispute, the court may draw conclusions unfavourable to the party.
If there is no genuine issue requiring a trial of a claim or defence, the court shall make a final order accordingly.
A motion for summary judgment under subrule (1) may be made in any case (including a child protection case) that does not include a divorce claim.

In a case that includes a divorce claim, the procedure provided in rule 36 (divorce) for an uncontested divorce may be used, or the divorce claim may be split from the rest of the case under subrule 12 (6).

In determining whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial, the court shall consider the evidence submitted by the parties, and the court may exercise any of the following powers for the purpose, unless it is in the interest of justice for such powers to be exercised only at a trial: 1. userQuestion: My action was struck off the trial list — how do I get it back on?
whatsHappening: One way an action is struck off is that it is called for trial and all the parties fail to attend, and the trial judge strikes it off the list. Once an action is struck off a trial list, it cannot be put back on any trial list without leave, which is the court's permission. If a judge struck it off, the leave must come from a judge. In any other case, the leave comes from the court.
whatToDoNext: To get the action back on a trial list, you bring a motion for leave to restore it. You make a motion with a notice of motion, in Form 37A. In some cases a notice is not needed, or the rules say to do it another way. If you do not bring this motion within 30 days after the action was struck off, a defendant may ask to have it dismissed for delay. Only a defendant who is not in default can do this. The registrar must also dismiss the action for delay, unless the court orders otherwise. This happens if, two years after it was struck off, it is not back on a trial list and has not ended in some other way. There are exceptions, including these. One is a timetable signed by all the parties. A party must file it, with a draft order, at least 30 days before the two years end. The timetable must list the steps left before the action is restored and the dates for them. It must also give a date, no more than two years after the two years end, by which the action must be restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party may bring a motion for a status hearing. That motion must be brought before the two years end. At a status hearing, you must show cause why the action should not be dismissed for delay. The court may dismiss the action for delay. If it is satisfied the action should go on, it may instead make other orders, such as setting deadlines for the steps left. Last, the registrar does not dismiss the action if you are under a disability at the time it would do so.
yourDeadline:
Bring a motion for leave to restore the action to the trial list. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 30 days after the day the action was struck off the trial list. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. If a judge struck the action off, the leave must come from a judge.

Have the action restored to a trial list, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 2 years after the day the action was struck off the trial list. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If the registrar does dismiss the action, the registrar must serve the order on the parties. That dismissal may be set aside under rule 37.14.

userQuestion: The registrar dismissed my action for delay — can I undo that?
whatsHappening: The registrar has made an order dismissing your action for delay. Unless the court orders otherwise, the registrar must do this in two cases, with some exceptions. One is when the action was not set down for trial or ended by the fifth anniversary of the day it started. The other is when it was struck off a trial list, and two years later it was not back on a list or ended some other way. The order is in Form 48D, and the registrar must serve it on the parties.
whatToDoNext: A dismissal by the registrar may be set aside under rule 37.14. Under that rule, if a registrar's order affects you, you may move to set it aside or change it. If you do, you must serve your notice of motion forthwith after the order comes to your attention. The notice of motion must name the first open hearing date that is at least three days after you serve it. The notice of motion is in Form 37A. The motion may be made to a judge or associate judge, at a place set under rule 37.03. On the motion, the court may set aside or change the order on such terms as are just. The rules also let any party make a motion about costs within 30 days after an action is dismissed for delay.
yourDeadline:
If you want the dismissal set aside, serve a notice of motion to set it aside. The rule sets no fixed number of days. Serve the notice of motion forthwith (right away) after the order comes to your attention. It must name the first available hearing date at least three days after you serve it.

If the action was dismissed for delay, you can ask the court to deal with the costs of the action. Do this by making a motion about the costs. You have 30 days after the day the action was dismissed. Any party to the action can make this motion. The rule's own words cover any action "dismissed for delay". The registrar's five-year order is a dismissal for delay. The only doubt comes from rule 48.14 (9). That rule applies the dismissal rules to a registrar's order, but it names only rules 24.03 to 24.05. So the rules' text does not settle whether this rule, 24.05.1, reaches that order. Bringing the motion within the 30 days avoids the doubt. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: The dismissal cannot be used as a defence to a later action, unless the order says so. A defendant who counterclaimed may choose to go on with the counterclaim. userQuestion: I want to drop my lawsuit — how do I stop it?
whatsHappening: You are the plaintiff, and you want to stop all or part of your action against one or more defendants. The rules call this discontinuing the action. How you do it depends on whether pleadings have closed. Pleadings close when two things are true. First, you have delivered a reply to every defence, or the time to deliver a reply has run out. Second, every defendant who is late with a defence has been noted in default. To deliver means to serve and file with proof of service.
whatToDoNext: Before pleadings close, you may discontinue by serving a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A) on every party who was served with the statement of claim. You then file the notice with proof of service. After pleadings close, you may discontinue with leave of the court. At any time, you may instead discontinue by filing the consent of all parties. If any party is under a disability, the action can be discontinued by or against that party only with a judge's leave. That leave is asked for by a motion under rule 7.07.1.
yourDeadline:
To discontinue without the court's leave or everyone's consent, act before pleadings close. Serve a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A) on all parties served with the statement of claim. File it with proof of service. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. After that, you need the court's leave. You can also discontinue at any time by filing the consent of all parties. If any party is under a disability, discontinuing by or against that party needs a judge's leave. A defendant who counterclaimed then has 30 days to choose to go on with the counterclaim. The discontinuance itself is not a defence to a later action on the same claim, unless the leave order or a filed consent says otherwise. But a later action can be put on hold until the costs of the discontinued one are paid.

If you want the court to deal with the costs of the discontinued action, make a motion about the costs. You have 30 days after the day the action was discontinued. Any party to the action can make this motion. It applies whether all or part of the action was discontinued. If a crossclaim or third party claim is treated as dismissed, a costs motion about it can be made within 30 days after that deemed dismissal. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: A defendant who counterclaimed may deliver a notice of election to go on with the counterclaim (Form 23B) within 30 days after the discontinuance. If that defendant does not, the counterclaim is deemed discontinued without costs. If a defendant you discontinue against made a crossclaim or third party claim, that claim is deemed dismissed 30 days after the discontinuance, unless the court orders otherwise in those 30 days. Any party to the action may make a motion about the costs of the action within 30 days after it is discontinued. The discontinuance itself is not a defence to a later action, unless the order giving leave or a consent filed by the parties says otherwise. userQuestion: A defendant in someone else's lawsuit has brought me into it — what do I do?
whatsHappening: A defendant in the main action has brought a third party claim against you. A defendant may do this against a person who is not a party to the action, in three cases. One is a person who is or may be liable to the defendant for all or part of the plaintiff's claim. whatsHappening: Another defendant in the action has made a crossclaim against you. It is part of that defendant's statement of defence, in one document called a statement of defence and crossclaim. First, the crossclaim asks only for contribution or indemnity under the Negligence Act. Second, you have delivered a statement of defence in the main action. Third, you rely on the facts in that statement of defence. You do not rely on a different version of the facts, or on anything that might take the co-defendant by surprise. In that case, you are deemed to deny the facts in the crossclaim and to rely on the facts in your statement of defence. Otherwise, if you are noted in default on the crossclaim, you are deemed to admit all the facts it alleges. userQuestion: The plaintiff dropped the case against me — what happens to my counterclaim?
whatsHappening: The plaintiff has discontinued, or dropped, the action against you. You had made a counterclaim. A plaintiff may discontinue all or part of an action in one of three ways. Before the close of pleadings, the plaintiff serves a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A) on all parties served with the claim. The plaintiff then files it with proof of service. After the close of pleadings, the plaintiff needs the leave, or permission, of the court. At any time, the plaintiff can file the consent of all parties. But if a party to the action is under disability, the action may be discontinued by or against that party only with a judge's leave, asked for by motion.
whatToDoNext: To go on with your counterclaim, you may deliver a notice of election to proceed with the counterclaim (Form 23B) within 30 days after the discontinuance. To deliver means to serve and file with proof of service. If you do not deliver it in time, your counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. You may also have made a crossclaim or a third party claim. If so, it is treated as dismissed 30 days after the discontinuance, unless the court orders otherwise in those 30 days. Any party to the action may make a motion about the costs of the action within 30 days after it is discontinued.
yourDeadline:
If you want to go on with your counterclaim, deliver a notice of election to proceed with the counterclaim (Form 23B). You have 30 days after the day the action was discontinued. If you do not, the counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. You may also have made a crossclaim or third party claim. If so, it is treated as dismissed 30 days after the discontinuance, unless the court orders otherwise within those 30 days. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want the court to deal with the costs of the discontinued action, make a motion about the costs. You have 30 days after the day the action was discontinued. Any party to the action can make this motion. It applies whether all or part of the action was discontinued. If a crossclaim or third party claim is treated as dismissed, a costs motion about it can be made within 30 days after that deemed dismissal. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
