userQuestion: The plaintiff is not moving the case forward — can I get it dismissed?
whatsHappening: The plaintiff has let a time in the rules pass. You are thinking about asking the court to dismiss the action for delay. In two cases, the court must dismiss an action for delay, unless the plaintiff shows that this would be unjust. One is where the action was not set down for trial or ended by the fifth anniversary of its start. The other is where it was struck off a trial list. Then, by the second anniversary of that, it was not put back on a list or ended. A special rule applies if the plaintiff is under disability, set out below.
whatToDoNext: If you are not in default under the rules or a court order, you may make a motion to have the action dismissed for delay. You may do this where the plaintiff has failed to do one of four things. The first is to serve the claim on all the defendants within the time set by the rules. The second is to have a defendant who did not deliver a defence noted in default within 30 days after that default. The third is to set the action down for trial within six months after the close of pleadings. The fourth is to move for leave to put the action back on a trial list within 30 days after it was struck off. If the plaintiff is under disability, you must serve your notice of motion on the plaintiff's litigation guardian. If that guardian is not the Children's Lawyer or the Public Guardian and Trustee, you must also serve one of them. Serve the Children's Lawyer if the plaintiff is a minor, and the Public Guardian and Trustee in any other case. If one of them was served but is not the guardian, the action may be dismissed only if they confirm to the court that they were served and take no position. That applies unless a judge orders otherwise.
whatHappensAfter: If your motion succeeds, you must serve a copy of the order dismissing the action on every defendant who has crossclaimed against you. Their crossclaim against you is then treated as dismissed 30 days after the order is served on them. That applies unless the court orders otherwise in those 30 days. If you made a counterclaim, you may deliver a notice of election to proceed with it (Form 23B) within 30 days after the dismissal. If you do not, the counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. If you made a crossclaim or a third party claim, it is treated as dismissed, unless the court orders otherwise. Any party to the action may make a motion about the costs of the action within 30 days after the dismissal. The dismissal is not a defence to a later action, unless the order dismissing the action says otherwise.

userQuestion: The plaintiff's case was dismissed for delay — what happens to my counterclaim?
whatsHappening: The action against you was dismissed for delay, and you had made a counterclaim in it. Your counterclaim can go on, but only if you choose to go on with it and give notice in time. This also applies when the registrar, not a judge, dismissed the action for delay.
whatToDoNext: If you want to go on with your counterclaim, you may deliver a notice of election to proceed with the counterclaim (Form 23B) within 30 days after the dismissal. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. If you do not deliver it in time, your counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. Separately, rule 24.05.1 says that if an action is dismissed for delay, any party to the action may make a motion about the costs of the action within 30 days after the dismissal.
yourDeadline:
If you want to go on with your counterclaim, deliver a notice of election to proceed with the counterclaim (Form 23B). You have 30 days after the day the action was dismissed. If you do not, the counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. This applies to a dismissal by the registrar as well as by the court. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If the action was dismissed for delay, you can ask the court to deal with the costs of the action. Do this by making a motion about the costs. You have 30 days after the day the action was dismissed. Any party to the action can make this motion. The rule's own words cover any action "dismissed for delay". The registrar's five-year order is a dismissal for delay. The only doubt comes from rule 48.14 (9). That rule applies the dismissal rules to a registrar's order, but it names only rules 24.03 to 24.05. So the rules' text does not settle whether this rule, 24.05.1, reaches that order. Bringing the motion within the 30 days avoids the doubt. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If your counterclaim goes on, the rules on dismissal for delay also apply to it, with needed changes. The dismissal of the action for delay is not a defence to a later action, unless the order dismissing it says otherwise.

userQuestion: My lawyer got off the record — what do I have to do now?
whatsHappening: The court has made an order removing your lawyer from the record. The order must include your contact details and the text of the rules that apply to you. Your lawyer must serve the order on you. They may do this in person or by an alternative to personal service. Or they may mail it to your last known address. They also mail it to any other address where they believe it will come to your notice. Your lawyer stays your lawyer of record until one of two things happens. You deliver a notice changing that, or the order is entered and your lawyer has met the rules for serving and filing it.
whatToDoNext: If you are not a corporation, not under disability and not acting in a representative role, you must do one of two things within 30 days after being served with the order. You must either appoint a new lawyer by serving a notice in Form 15B, or serve a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C). To appoint a lawyer, serve a notice of appointment of lawyer (Form 15B) on every other party, and file it with proof of service. A notice of intention to act in person sets out your address for service and phone number. You serve it on your former lawyer and every other party, and file it with proof of service. If you do neither in time, the court may dismiss your case or strike out your defence. In an appeal, a judge of the appeal court may, on motion, dismiss your appeal, or the court hearing the appeal may refuse to hear you. A corporation must have a lawyer unless the court gives leave. Within 30 days after being served with the order, a corporation must do one of two things. It must appoint a new lawyer (Form 15B), or get and serve on every other party an order letting someone who is not a lawyer act for it. If it does not, the court may dismiss its case or strike out its defence, and in an appeal the same results as above can follow. If you act in a representative role, or are the litigation guardian of a party under disability, you must appoint a new lawyer (Form 15B) within 30 days after being served with the order. If that is not done, another party must ask the court for directions or ask for a case conference. Until that motion has been heard or that case conference has been held, no party may take a further step in the case, unless the court orders otherwise. A claim started for a minor under section 61 of the Family Law Act is different. There, the rule above for other clients who miss the 30 days applies, with needed changes.
yourDeadline:
If you are an individual, do one of two things. Appoint a new lawyer by serving a notice (Form 15B). Or serve a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C). You have 30 days after the day you were served with the order removing your lawyer. If you do not, the court may dismiss your case or strike out your defence. In an appeal, a judge of the appeal court may dismiss the appeal, or the court hearing it may refuse to hear you. A corporation has 30 days to do one of two things instead. It can appoint a new lawyer. Or it can get and serve an order letting someone who is not a lawyer represent it. The same results follow if it does not. A party acting in a representative role, or the litigation guardian of a party under disability, has 30 days to appoint a new lawyer. The time can be extended by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: When you act in person, anything the rules require or permit a lawyer to do must be done by you, with two listed exceptions. If you act in person, you may later appoint a lawyer by serving and filing a notice of appointment of lawyer (Form 15B).

citations.quote: If an order is made removing from the record a lawyer for a client to whom subrules (12) and (14) do not apply, the client shall, within 30 days after being served with the order, (a) appoint a new lawyer of record by serving a notice in Form 15B under subrule 15.03 (2); or (b) serve a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C) under subrule 15.03 (3).

An order removing a lawyer from the record shall include, (a) the client's last known address, or the address for service if different; (b) another address, if any, where the lawyer believes a copy of the order is likely to come to the client's attention; (c) the telephone number and any email address of the client; (e) if the client is a party under disability or a party who acts in a representative capacity, the text of subrules (14), (15) and, if applicable, (17); and (f) if the client is not a corporation, a party under disability or a party who acts in a representative capacity, the text of subrules (16) and (17).
The lawyer shall serve an order made on motion under subrule (1) by a method of service specified in subrule (6) on the client

(a) personally or by an alternative to personal service under rule 16.03; or (b) by mailing a copy to the client at, (i) the client's last known address, and (ii) another address, if any, where the lawyer believes the copy is likely to come to the client's attention.

A lawyer of record shall act as and remains the lawyer of record for his or her client until, (a) the client delivers a notice under rule 15.03; or (b) an order removing the lawyer from the record has been entered and the lawyer has satisfied the service and filing requirements of subrules 15.04 (6), (7) (if applicable), (8), (10) and (11).

A party acting in person may appoint a lawyer of record by serving on every other party and filing, with proof of service, a notice of appointment of lawyer (Form 15B) giving the name, address and telephone number of the lawyer of record.

Subject to subrule 15.01 (1) or (2), a party who has a lawyer of record may elect to act in person by serving on the lawyer and every other party and filing, with proof of service, a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C) that sets out the party's address for service and telephone number.

If a client to whom subrule (16) applies fails to comply with that subrule, (a) the court may dismiss the client's proceeding or strike out the client's defence; and (b) in an appeal, (i) a judge of the appellate court may, on motion, dismiss the client's appeal, or (ii) the court hearing the appeal may deny the client the right to be heard.
A party to a proceeding that is a corporation shall be represented by a lawyer, except with leave of the court.

If an order is made removing from the record a lawyer acting for a corporation, the corporation shall, within 30 days after being served with the order, (a) appoint a new lawyer of record by serving a notice in Form 15B under subrule 15.03 (2); or (b) obtain and serve on every other party an order under subrule 15.01 (2) granting it leave to be represented by a person other than a lawyer.

If the corporation fails to comply with subrule (12), (a) the court may dismiss its proceeding or strike out its defence; and (b) in an appeal, (i) a judge of the appellate court may, on motion, dismiss the corporation's appeal, or (ii) the court hearing the appeal may deny it the right to be heard.

If an order is made removing from the record a lawyer acting for a party who acts in a representative capacity or who is under disability, the party acting in a representative capacity or the litigation guardian of the party under disability shall, within 30 days after being served with the order, appoint a new lawyer of record by serving a notice in Form 15B under subrule 15.03 (2).

Where a party to a proceeding is not represented by a lawyer but acts in person, anything these rules require or permit a lawyer to do shall be done by the party.

userQuestion: The other side served an amended claim or defence — do I have to respond again?
whatsHappening: Another party has changed one of its pleadings and served the amended version on you. Unless the court orders otherwise, it must be served right away on every party. That includes parties to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim in the action. A party may amend without the court's permission before pleadings close, if the change does not add, remove or replace a party. Otherwise, it needs the filed consent of all parties, or the court's permission. If a person is being added or replaced as a party, that person's consent must be filed too. The changes must be underlined, so you can tell the new wording from the original. If a pleading has been amended more than once, each later change has one more underline.
whatToDoNext: Unless the court orders otherwise, your time to respond to the amended pleading is the longer of two times. One is the time that was left to respond to the original pleading. The other is 10 days after the amended pleading was served on you. If you responded to the original and do not respond to the amended pleading in time, you are treated as relying on your original pleading. It then stands as your answer to the amended one. An originating process is a document that starts a proceeding, such as a statement of claim. Is the amended pleading an originating process? Then the way it is served depends on whether you responded to the original. If you were served with the original and responded to it, it does not have to be served on you personally. If you did not respond to the original, it must be served on you personally or by an alternative to personal service. This applies even if you were noted in default.
yourDeadline:
Respond to the amended pleading. You have 10 days after the day the amended pleading was served on you. You have the longer of two times: these 10 days, or the time that was left to respond to the original pleading. The court can order otherwise. If you had already responded to the original, you may choose not to respond again. You are then treated as relying on your original pleading.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: Proof that the amended pleading was served must be filed right away. This does not apply to an amended originating process.

citations.quote: "originating process" means a document that commences a proceeding under these rules, and includes, (a) a statement of claim,

A party may amend the party's pleading, (a) without leave, before the close of pleadings, if the amendment does not include or necessitate the addition, deletion or substitution of a party to the action; (b) on filing the consent of all parties and, where a person is to be added or substituted as a party, the person's consent; or (c) with leave of the court.
An amendment to a pleading shall be underlined so as to distinguish the amended wording from the original
Where a pleading has been amended more than once each subsequent amendment shall be underlined with an additional line for each occasion.

An amended pleading shall be served forthwith on every person who is, at the time of service, a party to the main action or to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim in the main action, unless the court orders otherwise.
Proof of service of an amended pleading other than an originating process shall be filed forthwith after it is served.

Where an amended pleading is an originating process, (a) it need not be served personally on a party who was served with the original pleading and responded to it; and (b) it shall be served personally or by an alternative to personal service under rule 16.03 on an opposite party who has not responded to the original pleading, whether or not the party has been noted in default.

A party shall respond to an amended pleading within the time remaining for responding to the original pleading, or within ten days after service of the amended pleading, whichever is the longer period, unless the court orders otherwise.

A party who has responded to a pleading that is subsequently amended and does not respond to the amended pleading within the prescribed time shall be deemed to rely on the party's original pleading in answer to the amended pleading.

userQuestion: My case is under the simplified procedure — what are the steps after the defence?
whatsHappening: Your action is going ahead under the simplified procedure in Rule 76, and a defence or notice of intent to defend has been filed. The usual rules for an action still apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise. Pleadings close when the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence, or the time for a reply has run out. Also, every defendant who is in default in delivering a defence must have been noted in default.
whatToDoNext: Within 10 days after pleadings close, you must serve an affidavit of documents (Form 30A or 30B) on every other party. You pay the cost. It must disclose every relevant document you have or once had in your possession, control or power. Disclose them as fully as you know and believe. Within the same 10 days, you must also serve copies of the documents listed in its Schedule A. Unless the court orders otherwise, the affidavit must list people who might reasonably be expected to know about the issues. Give their names and addresses. Unless the court orders otherwise, a party may not call a witness at trial who is not named in that party's affidavit of documents. Being named in a supplementary one also counts. Within 60 days after the first defence or notice of intent to defend is filed, the parties must meet or talk by phone. They must consider whether all relevant documents have been disclosed, and whether any or all issues can be settled. Some steps are not allowed. One is examination for discovery by written questions and answers under Rule 35. Another is cross-examining someone on an affidavit under rule 39.02. A third is examining a witness on a motion under rule 39.03. Oral examinations for discovery are limited. No party may examine for more than three hours in total, no matter how many people are examined. If you bring a motion, you must serve a motion form (Form 76B) under rule 37.07, and submit it to the court before the motion is brought and heard. If you plan to call expert evidence at trial, you must comply with rule 53.03. An expert's report served under rule 53.03 must be attached to the expert's affidavit. In that affidavit, the expert adopts the report as evidence in the action. If you are the plaintiff, you must set the action down for trial within 180 days after the first defence or notice of intent to defend is filed. You do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C). Serve it on every party to the action and to any counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim. You must then file the notice right away, with proof of service. If the plaintiff has not set the action down, any other party may do it. Whoever sets the action down must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion.
yourDeadline:
If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. If you are not the plaintiff, this is not your duty. If the plaintiff does not do it, any other party may. The party who sets it down must certify that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If you gave an undertaking or took a question under advisement at an examination for discovery, answer it. You have 60 days after the day you gave that response at the examination. If you do not answer in that time, you cannot use that information at trial without the trial judge's permission. You still have to keep an undertaking.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if the plaintiff is under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: A pre-trial conference is then scheduled under rule 50.02. At least 30 days before it, the parties must agree to a proposed trial management plan. The plan lists every witness, including experts, that a party plans to call at trial. It also divides the trial time between the parties, and the total may not be more than five days. It sets each party's time for an opening statement and for evidence in chief, given by affidavit and under rule 31.11. It also sets time to cross-examine, to re-examine, and for oral argument.

citations.quote: Pleadings in an action are closed when, (a) the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence in the action or the time for delivery of a reply has expired; and (b) every defendant who is in default in delivering a defence in the action has been noted in default.
The rules that apply to an action apply to an action that is proceeding under this Rule, unless this Rule provides otherwise.

A party to an action under this Rule shall, within 10 days after the close of pleadings and at the party's own expense, serve on every other party, (a) an affidavit of documents (Form 30A or 30B) disclosing to the full extent of the party's knowledge, information and belief all documents relevant to any matter in issue in the action that are or have been in the party's possession, control or power; and (b) copies of the documents referred to in Schedule A of the affidavit of documents.

The affidavit of documents shall include a list of the names and addresses of persons who might reasonably be expected to have knowledge of matters in issue in the action, unless the court orders otherwise.

At the trial of the action, a party may not call as a witness a person whose name has not been disclosed in the party's affidavit of documents or any supplementary affidavit of documents, unless the court orders otherwise.

The following are not permitted in an action under this Rule: 1. Examination for discovery by written questions and answers under Rule 35. 2. Cross-examination of a deponent on an affidavit under rule 39.02. 3. Examination of a witness on a motion under rule 39.03.

Despite rule 31.05.1 (time limit on discovery), no party shall, in conducting oral examinations for discovery in relation to an action proceeding under this Rule, exceed a total of three hours of examination, regardless of the number of parties or other persons to be examined.
The moving party shall serve a motion form (Form 76B) in accordance with rule 37.07 and shall submit it to the court before the motion is brought and heard.

Within 60 days after the filing of the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend, the parties shall, in a meeting or telephone call, consider whether, (a) all documents relevant to any matter in issue have been disclosed; and (b) settlement of any or all issues is possible.
A party who intends to call expert evidence at the trial of the action shall comply with rule 53.03.
An expert's report served under rule 53.03 shall be appended to an affidavit of the expert in which the expert adopts the report for the purpose of giving it as evidence in the action.

Despite rule 48.02 (how action set down for trial), the plaintiff shall, within 180 days after the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend is filed, set the action down for trial by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party to the action and any counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim and forthwith filing the notice with proof of service.
If the plaintiff does not act under subrule (1), any other party may do so.
The party who sets the action down for trial shall certify in the notice of readiness for pre-trial conference that there was a settlement discussion.
A pre-trial conference shall be scheduled in accordance with rule 50.02.

At least 30 days before the pre-trial conference, the parties shall agree to a proposed trial management plan that contains the following: 1. A list of every witness, including every expert witness, whose evidence a party intends to adduce at trial. 2. A division of time between the parties, the total of which shall not exceed five days, that sets out the allotted times for each party for, i. opening statement, ii. the presentation of evidence in chief by affidavit and under rule 31.11, iii. cross-examination of deponents, iv. re-examination of any deponents who are cross-examined, and v. oral argument.

userQuestion: I got a request to admit — what happens if I do not answer?
whatsHappening: Another party has served you with a request to admit (Form 51A). It asks you to admit that a fact is true, or that a document is authentic. For example, authentic includes that a document said to be a copy is a true copy of the original. Any admission counts for this case only.
whatToDoNext: Within 20 days after the request is served on you, you must serve a response to request to admit (Form 51B) on the party who sent it. If you do not serve a response in time, you are treated as admitting the facts or documents in the request, for this case only. In your response, you may specifically deny that a fact is true or that a document is authentic. Or you may refuse to admit it, but your response must then set out your reason for refusing. Anything in the request that your response does not deny, or refuse with a reason, is treated as admitted for this case.
yourDeadline:
Serve a response to request to admit (Form 51B) on the party who sent the request. You have 20 days after the day the request to admit was served on you. If you do not respond in time, you are treated as admitting the facts or documents in the request, for this case only. You are also treated as admitting anything your response does not specifically deny, or refuse to admit with a reason. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: Say you deny or refuse to admit something, and it is later proved at the hearing. The court may take your denial or refusal into account when it decides costs. An admission in your response, or one you are treated as making, may be withdrawn on consent or with leave of the court. Any party may bring a motion to a judge in this case for the order they say the admission entitles them to, and the judge may make the order that is just.

userQuestion: A judge decided a motion against me — can I appeal it, and by when?
whatsHappening: Where your appeal goes depends on who made the order. An appeal from an interlocutory order of an associate judge goes to the Superior Court of Justice. An appeal from an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge goes to the Divisional Court, but only with leave as the rules provide. Those Divisional Court appeal rights do not apply to an order made under section 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act. Instead, an appeal from an order made under section 137.1 goes to the Court of Appeal.
whatToDoNext: To appeal an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge, you must first get leave from a panel of the Divisional Court. To ask for it, serve a notice of motion for leave to appeal (Form 61A). You must serve it within 15 days after the order was made, unless a statute provides otherwise. Then file it, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within five days after you serve it. You must also serve a motion record, a factum, and any transcripts of evidence. Within 30 days after filing the notice, you must file the motion record, factum, and any transcripts and book of authorities, with proof of service. Your factum must be limited to facts, issues, law and authorities that relate to a ground on which leave may be granted. The motion for leave is heard in writing, without the parties or lawyers attending. Leave from an interlocutory order is not granted unless one of two things is shown to the panel. One is a conflicting decision by another judge or court on the same matter, where the panel thinks leave is desirable. The other is good reason to doubt the order is correct. For that one, the appeal must also involve matters so important that, in the panel's view, leave should be granted. For an interlocutory order of an associate judge, the appeal goes to a judge. You start it by serving a notice of appeal (Form 62A). Serve it on all parties whose interests may be affected, within seven days after the order was made. The notice must state what you are asking for and your grounds of appeal. At the hearing, you may not rely on other grounds unless the judge hearing the appeal gives leave. The notice must name the first available hearing date that is not less than seven days after you serve it. File it, with proof of service, in the court office where the appeal will be heard, no later than seven days before the hearing date. You must also serve an appeal record and a factum on every other party. Serve them, and file them there with proof of service, no later than seven days before the hearing. A judge may excuse you from that step, in whole or in part, before or at the hearing.
yourDeadline:
If you want to appeal an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge, serve a notice of motion for leave to appeal to the Divisional Court (Form 61A). You have 15 days after the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within five days after you serve it. A panel of the Divisional Court hears the leave motion in writing. The same leave process applies to a final order of a Superior Court judge that is only about costs. Within 30 days after filing the notice of motion, file your motion record, factum, any transcripts and any book of authorities, with proof of service. If leave is granted, deliver the notice of appeal, with your certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C), within seven days after leave is granted.

If you want to appeal an interlocutory order of an associate judge, serve a notice of appeal (Form 62A) on all parties whose interests may be affected. You have 7 days after the day the order was made. This appeal goes to a judge, not to the Divisional Court. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. The notice must name the first available hearing date at least seven days after you serve it. File it with proof of service no later than seven days before that hearing date.

If you are appealing an associate judge's order, serve your appeal record and factum on every other party and file them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the appeal will be heard. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted.

If you are responding to an appeal from an associate judge's order, serve your factum, and any more material needed, on every other party. File it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the appeal will be heard. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted.

If the other side asks the Divisional Court for leave to appeal and you oppose it, file your factum, any motion record and any book of authorities. File them with proof of service. You have 25 days after the day you were served with the moving party's motion record. This applies to a motion for leave to appeal an interlocutory order or a costs order of a Superior Court judge.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If the Divisional Court grants leave, you must deliver the notice of appeal and your certificate respecting evidence within seven days after leave is granted. From then on, Rule 61 applies to the appeal. Delivering a notice of appeal stays any part of the order for paying money. The stay lasts until the appeal is decided. It does not cover a part that awards support or enforces a support order. A judge of the appeal court may order, on terms that are just, that this stay does not apply. If the order refused to set aside a default judgment, a notice of appeal does not stay that judgment, but it may be stayed by order.

userQuestion: My action has been set down for trial — what has to happen before the pre-trial conference?
whatsHappening: Your action has been set down for trial. The pre-trial conference has not happened yet. At this conference, the parties go before a judge or associate judge. It is a way to settle some or all of the issues without a hearing. For issues that do not settle, the court can give orders or directions to help the case end fairly, quickly and at the least cost. If your action was set down before March 31, 2022, rule 50.02 as it read on March 30, 2022 still applies.
whatToDoNext: Unless the court orders otherwise, the parties must book the conference with the registrar within 180 days after the action was set down. The time must suit all the parties. The date must be 30 to 120 days before the first trial day, unless an order or practice direction says otherwise. If the trial sittings start later, count back from the first day of the sittings. Subject to any earlier order, if the parties do not book it in time, the registrar books it and tells them when to come. Unless the court orders otherwise, the parties must agree on dates for serving expert reports within 60 days after the action was set down. If you will call an expert at trial, you must serve the expert's signed report on every other party at least 90 days before the conference. It must include set details, such as the expert's opinion and reasons, and a signed form on the expert's duty (Form 53). If your expert will answer another party's expert, you must serve that report on every other party at least 60 days before the conference. Without the trial judge's leave, an expert may not testify on an issue unless it is in a report served under this rule. A supplementary report also counts if it is served on every other party at least 45 days before trial. So does a responding supplementary report served on every other party at least 15 days before trial. At least 30 days before the conference, you must deliver a certificate of readiness (Form 50A). Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. It says if you will call expert evidence at trial. If so, it says for each expert if the report was served in time, and if not, why. At least five days before the conference, you must file a pre-trial conference brief with proof of service. It gives short statements of set matters, without argument. They are what the case is about, the issues and your position, and the witnesses you expect to call and how long each will take. They also include the steps still needed before the action is ready for trial, and how long those steps will take. If any party plans to ask for separate hearings under rule 6.1.01, the brief also gives your position on that. Some of this is different if your action is under the simplified procedure. Then the parties must agree on a proposed trial management plan at least 30 days before the conference. An appellate court means the Court of Appeal or the Divisional Court, as the case requires. userQuestion: The judge decided my case and I disagree — can I appeal, and by when?
whatsHappening: A final order of an associate judge is appealed to the Divisional Court. Some final orders of a Superior Court judge also go to the Divisional Court. One kind is an order to pay one sum of $50,000 or less, not counting costs. Another is an order for payments that add up to $50,000 or less in the first 12 months, not counting costs. A third is an order that dismisses a claim for $50,000 or less. The last is an order that dismisses a larger claim, where the judge or jury says the award would have been $50,000 or less. Other final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Court of Appeal. The exception is when another Act sends the appeal to the Divisional Court. An order made under section 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act also goes to the Court of Appeal.
whatToDoNext: If you want to appeal, serve a notice of appeal within 30 days after the order was made. This applies unless a statute or the rules say otherwise. Use Form 61A.2 for the Court of Appeal, or Form 61A.3 for the Divisional Court. Serve it on every party whose interest may be affected by the appeal, and on anyone a statute allows to be heard on the appeal. You do not have to serve a defendant who was noted in default. You also do not have to serve a respondent who did not deliver a notice of appearance. This does not apply if that respondent was heard at the hearing with leave. With the notice, you must serve and file an appellant's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C), with proof of service. It lists only the parts of the evidence that you think are needed for the appeal. The notice of appeal must state what you are asking for, your grounds of appeal, and why the appeal court can hear it. That last part includes whether leave to appeal is needed and, if so, whether it was granted. File the notice of appeal, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within 10 days after you serve it. If you serve it but do not file it in that time, you are treated as having given up the appeal, unless the court orders otherwise. An appeal only about costs that the judge had the choice to award needs leave of the appeal court first. So does an appeal from an order made with the consent of the parties. To ask for leave, serve a notice of motion for leave to appeal within 15 days after the order was made, unless a statute says otherwise. Use Form 61A.1 for the Court of Appeal, or Form 61A for the Divisional Court. File it with proof of service in the Registrar's office within five days after you serve it. If leave is granted, deliver the notice of appeal within seven days after leave is granted. If the Divisional Court granted leave under rule 62.02, also deliver the appellant's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C) with it within those seven days. You may want to add a costs-only appeal to an appeal that needs no leave. If so, ask for leave in the notice of appeal, or in a supplementary notice of appeal. The panel that hears the main appeal decides whether to grant leave. Maybe the other side appealed, and you want the order set aside or changed. If so, serve a notice of cross-appeal (Form 61E) within 15 days after you were served with their notice of appeal. The same applies if you will ask for a different result should their appeal succeed. File it, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. If your cross-appeal is under a statute that needs leave to appeal, you must get leave. An order extending a time limit for an appeal can be made only by a judge of the appeal court.

If you want to appeal a final order, serve a notice of appeal with a certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C). You have 30 days after the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. Which court hears the appeal depends on the order. Some final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Divisional Court. These include an order to pay one sum of $50,000 or less, or payments of $50,000 or less in the first 12 months, not counting costs. They also include an order dismissing a claim for $50,000 or less. So does an order dismissing a larger claim where the judge or jury says the award would have been $50,000 or less. Other final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Court of Appeal. A final order of an associate judge goes to the Divisional Court. An appeal only about costs, or from an order made with everyone's consent, needs leave first. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court. For a costs-only appeal, the motion for leave must be served within 15 days after the order, in either appeal court.

If the other side appealed and you want the order changed too, serve a notice of cross-appeal (Form 61E). You have 15 days after the day you were served with the notice of appeal. This applies if you want the order set aside or changed. It also applies if you want a different result if the appeal succeeds. Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

userQuestion: An appeal has been started — what has to be done next, and by when?
whatsHappening: An appeal starts when a notice of appeal is served. Before it can be heard, the appellant must perfect it. That means serving and filing the appeal documents. Delivering the notice of appeal puts part of the order on hold until the appeal is decided. The hold covers any part for paying money. It does not cover a part that awards or enforces support. This hold does not apply to an appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment. But that default judgment may still be stayed by an order. A judge of the appeal court may order that the hold does not apply, on terms that are just.
whatToDoNext: If you are the appellant, file the notice of appeal, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within 10 days after you served it. If you do not, you are treated as having given up the appeal, unless the court orders otherwise. Within 30 days after filing it, file proof that you ordered a transcript of all oral evidence the parties have not agreed to leave out. If it is needed in the interest of justice, a judge of the appeal court may give special directions about the transcript. Perfect the appeal within 30 days after filing the notice of appeal if no transcript is needed. If a transcript is needed, you have 60 days after you get notice that the evidence has been transcribed. To perfect it, serve the appeal book and compendium, the exhibit book, any transcript and your factum. Serve them on every other party and anyone else entitled to be heard. File them with the Registrar, with proof of service. Then serve and file a certificate of perfection, with proof of service. If you are the respondent, serve a respondent's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61D) on the appellant. Do this within 15 days after you were served with the appellant's certificate. File it with proof of service. It confirms the appellant's certificate, or lists things to add or remove. If you do not serve and file it in time, you are treated as confirming the appellant's certificate. Instead of these certificates, the parties may make an agreement about the documents and transcript within 30 days after the notice of appeal was served. As respondent, deliver your factum and compendium within 60 days. The time starts when you are served with the appeal book and compendium, exhibit book, any transcript and the appellant's factum. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. If you are the respondent and want the order set aside or changed, serve a notice of cross-appeal (Form 61E). Do this within 15 days after you were served with the notice of appeal. The same applies if you will ask for a different result should the appeal succeed. File it, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. If your cross-appeal is under a statute that needs leave to appeal, you must get leave. If you do not deliver a notice of cross-appeal, no cross-appeal can be heard without leave of the court hearing the appeal. If you cross-appeal, you also deliver a factum as appellant in the cross-appeal, with your factum or as part of it. The appellant then delivers a factum as respondent to the cross-appeal within 10 days after your factum is served. Your cross-appeal factum is late if it is not delivered within 60 days after the appeal book, transcript and appellant's factum were served. Then the appellant may ask the Registrar, on five days notice, to dismiss the cross-appeal for delay.
yourDeadline:
If you are the appellant, file the notice of appeal, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office. You have 10 days after the day you served the notice of appeal. The 30 days to file proof that you ordered a transcript, and the 30 days to perfect an appeal that needs no transcript, are both counted from the day you file it. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court.

If you are the respondent, serve a respondent's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61D) on the appellant. File it with proof of service. You have 15 days after the day you were served with the appellant's certificate, which comes with the notice of appeal. It confirms the appellant's certificate, or sets out additions or deletions. If you do not serve and file it in time, you are treated as confirming the appellant's certificate. A notice of cross-appeal has the same 15 days. It must be filed with proof of service within 10 days after it is served.

If you are the appellant, file proof that you have ordered a transcript of all oral evidence the parties have not agreed to leave out. You have 30 days after the day you filed the notice of appeal. If you do not, the respondent can ask the Registrar, on ten days notice, to dismiss the appeal for delay. If the problem is not fixed before that motion is heard, the Registrar dismisses the appeal. Costs are then fixed at $750. A judge of the appeal court can allow more time.

If you are the appellant and no transcript is needed, perfect the appeal by serving and filing the appeal documents. You have 30 days after the day you filed the notice of appeal. If you do not, the respondent can move to have the appeal dismissed for delay. Or the Registrar can give notice that it will be dismissed unless it is perfected within 10 days. If the problem is not fixed in time, the Registrar dismisses the appeal, with costs fixed at $750. A judge of the appeal court can allow more time after a Registrar's notice. If there is a cross-appeal, deliver your factum as respondent to it within 10 days after the respondent's factum is served.

If you are the appellant and a transcript is needed, perfect the appeal by serving and filing the appeal documents. You have 60 days after the day you received notice that the evidence has been transcribed. If you do not, the respondent can move to have the appeal dismissed for delay. The Registrar can also give notice that the appeal will be dismissed unless it is perfected within 10 days. The Registrar can do this if the transcript is not filed within 60 days after the Registrar was told it was ready. The Registrar can also do it if the appeal is not perfected within one year after the notice of appeal was filed. If the problem is not fixed in time, the Registrar dismisses the appeal, with costs fixed at $750. If there is a cross-appeal, deliver your factum as respondent to it within 10 days after the respondent's factum is served.

If you are the respondent, deliver your factum and compendium. You have 60 days after the day you were served with the appeal book and compendium, exhibit book, any transcript and the appellant's factum. Deliver means serve it on the other parties and file it with proof of service. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

userQuestion: I missed my conference, or forgot to confirm it — what happens now?
whatsHappening: Each party must confirm a conference with the clerk by 2 p.m. three days before the conference date. Unless the court orders otherwise, a conference is not held if that confirmation was not given on time. The parties must come to each conference, unless the court orders otherwise. A party who has a licensed representative must also have that representative there, with full knowledge of the case and authority in it.
whatToDoNext: For any conference that is set, each party must give the clerk a confirmation of conference (Form 17F). It is due no later than 2 p.m. three days before the conference date. You can deliver it to the court office, email it to the court office, or submit it online through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Before you give it to the clerk, you must give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other method, except in a child protection case. Costs are not awarded at a conference unless a party was not prepared or did not serve the required documents, or one of the other cases below applies. The other cases are a party who did not make required disclosure, made the conference unproductive in some other way, or did not follow the rules. In that case, the judge must order that party to pay the costs of the conference right away, decide the amount, and give any directions needed.
yourDeadline:
If the clerk serves a notice of approaching dismissal, take one of the five steps below, or the case is dismissed without further notice. You have 60 days after the day the notice of approaching dismissal was served. Step one: get an order giving more time. Step two: file an agreement signed by all parties and their licensed representatives, if any, for a final order on all issues. File it with a notice of motion for an order carrying it out. Step three: serve and file a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) of all outstanding claims. Step four: schedule or adjourn the case for trial. Step five: arrange a case conference or settlement conference for the first available date. After a missed conference, the clerk serves that notice if three things are true. It was a case or settlement conference. It was set for 365 days or more after the case started. And a judge did not adjourn it. The clerk also serves one if the case was not settled, withdrawn, or scheduled or adjourned for trial before day 365. If a conference arranged as step five also does not go ahead, and a judge did not adjourn it, the case is dismissed without further notice. A judge can set aside the clerk's dismissal order on a motion. These rules do not apply to an enforcement. They do not apply to cases under rules 37, 37.1 and 37.2. Those cover support across borders, provisional orders and child abduction across borders. In the Superior Court and the Family Court, they do not apply to a request to enforce a family arbitration award (rule 32.1). In the Ontario Court of Justice and the Family Court, they do not apply to a child protection case.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If costs are not awarded at the conference, the court can still award costs for it later in the case. When a person does not follow the rules, the court may make orders such as an order for costs, a fine, dismissing a claim, or striking out a document. It may also postpone the trial or another step in the case.

whatsHappening: A party may bring a motion without notice only in certain cases. One is when notice is not needed or not reasonably possible. The other three are about serious harm from giving notice, or from the delay that serving it takes, such as when a child may soon be taken out of Ontario. An order is in effect from the day it is made, unless it says otherwise.
whatToDoNext: An order made without notice must send the matter back to court, to the same judge if possible, within 14 days or on a date the court chooses. Unless the court orders otherwise, the order must be served right away on every party affected, along with all the documents used on the motion. You may bring a motion asking the court to change the order, because the court may change an order that was made without notice. Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

userQuestion: I got a notice that my family case will be dismissed — how do I stop that?
whatsHappening: The clerk has served a notice of approaching dismissal (Form 39) in your family case. The clerk sends this notice by mail or email if the case was not settled, withdrawn, or scheduled or adjourned for trial before the 365th day after it started, and no order gave more time. The clerk also sends it if a case conference or settlement conference was set for the 365th day or later, but it did not take place that day and a judge did not adjourn it. Once the notice is served, the case will be dismissed without further notice unless one of the parties takes a step within 60 days.
whatToDoNext: To stop the dismissal, one of the parties must take one of five steps within 60 days after the notice is served. One step is to get an order that gives more time. The parties cannot give more time just by agreeing to it, as only an order can. A second step is to file an agreement for a final order that deals with all issues in the case. All parties and their licensed representatives, if any, must sign it. File it with a notice of motion for an order that carries out the agreement. A third step is to serve on all parties, and file, a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) that drops all claims still left in the case. A fourth step is to schedule or adjourn the case for trial. A fifth step is to arrange a case conference or settlement conference for the first available date. If you take the fifth step, the conference must go ahead on that date or be adjourned by a judge, or the case will be dismissed without further notice.
yourDeadline:
Take one of the five steps below, or the case is dismissed without further notice. You have 60 days after the day the notice of approaching dismissal was served. Step one: get an order giving more time. Step two: file an agreement signed by all parties and their licensed representatives, if any, for a final order on all issues. File it with a notice of motion for an order carrying it out. Step three: serve and file a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) of all outstanding claims. Step four: schedule or adjourn the case for trial. Step five: arrange a case conference or settlement conference for the first available date. Only one party needs to take a step. The parties cannot extend this time by agreement. Only a court order can. If a conference arranged as step five does not go ahead, and a judge did not adjourn it, the case is dismissed without further notice. If the clerk dismisses the case, a judge can set aside the dismissal order on a motion. These rules do not apply to an enforcement. They do not apply to cases under rules 37, 37.1 and 37.2. Those cover support across borders, provisional orders and child abduction across borders. In the Superior Court and the Family Court, they do not apply to a request to enforce a family arbitration award (rule 32.1). In the Ontario Court of Justice and the Family Court, they do not apply to a child protection case. If the notice came by mail, it counts as served on the fifth day after mailing. If it came by email, it counts as served on the date in the email, or the next day if sent after 4 p.m. To be safe, count from the day it was mailed or emailed.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If no step is taken in time, the clerk dismisses the case by preparing and signing an order, with no costs payable by any party. The clerk serves that order on each party by mail or email. If the clerk dismissed the case because no step was taken within the 60 days, a judge may, on motion, set aside that order.

userQuestion: A notice of default hearing has been issued about unpaid support — what do I have to do?
whatsHappening: At a default hearing, the payor must come to court. The payor must explain why support was not paid as the order requires. The payor is the person who must pay under the order. The clerk issues the notice (Form 30) when the party enforcing the order files a statement of money owed. If the recipient is enforcing, the recipient also files a request (Form 30A). The Director of the Family Responsibility Office may be enforcing instead. If so, the rules on enforcement by the recipient apply to the Director. The notice must be served on the payor by special service, and filed. When the payor could face jail, the notice may be served only by leaving a copy with the payor, unless the court orders otherwise. Someone other than the party who must serve it has to do the serving. That does not apply if the court orders otherwise, or if the party serving is the Director of the Family Responsibility Office.
whatToDoNext: If you are the payor, you have 10 days after you were served with the notice. In that time, you must serve two forms on the party enforcing the order and file them. That party is the recipient, or the Director if the Director is enforcing. The two forms are a financial statement and a default dispute (Form 30B). If the recipient is enforcing, the Act says the financial statement must be in the form the court rules set. Under the rules, that is Form 13. If the Director is enforcing, its notice may ask you to give the Director a financial statement and proof of income. In that case, the Act says the financial statement must be in the form set by the regulations. You are presumed to admit that the statement of money owed is correct. That changes only if you file a default dispute that says it is wrong and gives detailed reasons. You must also appear in court to explain the default. If you do not file the financial statement or do not appear, the court may issue a warrant for your arrest to bring you to court. If you are the recipient enforcing the order, you must serve and file a new statement of money owed. Do this not more than seven days before the hearing. If the Director is enforcing, it must do this only in two cases. One is if it asks the court to enforce more than the notice shows. The other is if the court directs it.
yourDeadline:
If you are the payor, serve a financial statement and a default dispute (Form 30B) on the party enforcing the order, and file them. You have 10 days after the day you were served with the notice of default hearing. The party enforcing is the recipient, or the Director of the Family Responsibility Office. Use Form 13 for the financial statement. If the Director is enforcing, use the form the regulations require, as the notice will say. Also give the Director the proof of income the notice asks for. You are presumed to agree that the statement of money owed is correct. That changes only if you file a default dispute saying it is wrong and giving detailed reasons. You must also come to court to explain the default. If you do not file the financial statement or do not come, the court can issue a warrant for your arrest. At the hearing, you are presumed able to pay unless you show otherwise. Unless the court finds you cannot pay for valid reasons, it can order payments, security, or jail for up to 180 days. The court can decide and enforce the amount owing up to the hearing date.

If you are the recipient enforcing the order, serve and file a new statement of money owed no more than 7 days before the default hearing. That means within the last 7 days before it, not earlier. If the Director of the Family Responsibility Office is enforcing, the Director must do this only in two cases. One is if it asks the court to enforce more than the notice shows. The other is if the court directs it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: At the hearing, the court may decide and enforce the amount owing as of the hearing date. Unless shown otherwise, the payor is presumed able to pay the arrears and later payments. A statement of arrears the Director prepared and served is also presumed correct for arrears that built up while the order was filed with it. The court may make orders unless it is satisfied the payor cannot pay for valid reasons. These orders include paying all or part of the arrears, and giving security. They also include jail for up to 180 days, or until the arrears are paid, if sooner. The court may suspend a jail order on conditions. These orders do not stop arrears from building up. They also do not limit other ways to enforce the order.

userQuestion: I was served with a contempt motion for not following an order — what could happen?
whatsHappening: A contempt motion enforces an order that is not a payment order, in the same case the order was made in. Unless the court orders otherwise, the notice of contempt motion (Form 31) must be served together with a supporting affidavit, by special service. To bring you before the court, the court may issue a warrant for your arrest, but only if two things are true. Your attendance must be needed in the interest of justice. And it must be that you are not expected to come on your own.
whatToDoNext: Unless the court orders otherwise, you, as the party responding, must serve all your evidence in response. After that, the party making the motion may serve evidence that replies to any new matters raised by your evidence. Unless the court orders otherwise, no other evidence may be used. Most motions must wait until a conference on the main issues in the case is completed. That wait does not apply to a motion for a contempt order. Any affidavit on this motion, including yours, must as much as possible hold only what the signer knows first-hand. It may include things the signer learned from someone else only if three things are true. The source must be named, and the signer must say they believe it is true. For a contempt motion, the information must also not be expected to be disputed.
yourDeadline: Rule 31 sets no separate time to respond to a notice of contempt motion (Form 31). The general rule for responding to a motion sets 4 days before the motion date. But that rule is worded for a notice of motion in Form 14, not Form 31. Under the motion rules, the party responding serves all their evidence in response. The safe course is to serve and file your evidence at least 4 days before the motion date.
whatHappensAfter: If the court finds you in contempt, it may order you to go to jail for a period and on terms that are just. It may also order you to pay a fine, pay a penalty to a party, or pay costs. Or it may order you to do anything else it decides, not do what it forbids, or obey any other order. The court may also give permission to issue a writ of temporary seizure (Form 28C) against your property. Some contempt orders are made under one of three provisions. For those, the jail time and the fine cannot be more than the relevant Act allows. The first provision is s. 38 of the Children’s Law Reform Act. The second is s. 49 of the Family Law Act. The third is s. 53 of the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996. An order for jail or a fine may be put on hold on conditions. A party may later say, in a Form 32C affidavit on a motion with special service, that you broke such a condition. The court may then issue a warrant of committal against you. The court may, on motion, change a contempt order.

citations.quote: An order, other than a payment order, may be enforced by a contempt motion made in the case in which the order was made, even if another penalty is available.
The notice of contempt motion (Form 31) shall be served together with a supporting affidavit, by special service in accordance with subrule 6 (4), unless the court orders otherwise.
An affidavit for use on a motion shall, as much as possible, contain only information within the personal knowledge of the person signing the affidavit.

The affidavit may also contain information that the person learned from someone else, but only if, (a) the source of the information is identified by name and the affidavit states that the person signing it believes the information is true; and (b) in addition, if the motion is a contempt motion under rule 31, the information is not likely to be disputed.
The following restrictions apply to evidence for use on a motion, unless the court orders otherwise: | 2. The party responding to the motion shall then serve all the evidence in response.
No notice of motion or supporting evidence may be served and no motion may be heard before a conference dealing with the substantive issues in the case has been completed.
Subrule (4) does not apply to a motion, | (b) for a contempt order under rule 31

To bring before the court a person against whom a contempt motion is made, the court may issue a warrant for the person’s arrest if, (a) the person’s attendance is necessary in the interest of justice; and (b) the person is not likely to attend voluntarily.

If the court finds a person in contempt of the court, it may order that the person, (a) be imprisoned for any period and on any conditions that are just; (b) pay a fine in any amount that is appropriate; (c) pay an amount to a party as a penalty; (d) do anything else that the court decides is appropriate; (e) not do what the court forbids; (f) pay costs in an amount decided by the court; and (g) obey any other order.
The court may also give permission to issue a writ of temporary seizure (Form 28C) against the person’s property.

In a contempt order under one of the following provisions, the period of imprisonment and the amount of a fine may not be greater than the relevant Act allows: 1. Section 38 of the Children’s Law Reform Act. 2. Section 49 of the Family Law Act. 3. Section 53 of the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996.
A contempt order for imprisonment or for the payment of a fine may be suspended on appropriate conditions.

If a party, on a motion with special service (subrule 6 (3)) on the person in contempt, states by an affidavit in Form 32C (or by oral evidence, with the court’s permission) that the person has not obeyed a condition imposed under subrule (8), the court may issue a warrant of committal against the person.
The court may, on motion, change an order under this rule, give directions and make any other order that is just.
