userQuestion: The other side asked me for a list of my documents — what do I have to give them, and by when?
whatsHappening: Another party has asked you for an affidavit listing your documents. It lists every document that is relevant to any issue in the case. That means each one you control, or can get on request.
whatToDoNext: Within 10 days after the request, you must give the other party that affidavit. Papers that must be served under rule 13 (financial disclosure) are left out of this 10-day duty. The duty is also not on the Office of the Children’s Lawyer or on children’s aid societies. If you claim a document is protected by legal privilege, the court may, on motion, look at it and decide. You may use a document you claim is privileged at trial only in one of two ways. One is if the other party was allowed to see it and given a free copy at least 30 days before the settlement conference. The other is on the terms the trial judge thinks fit. Later, you may find a document that should have been listed, or find the list is wrong or not complete. If so, you must right away serve a new affidavit with the correct list. If you do not follow this rule or an order under it, the court may order you to give the affidavit, let the other party examine a document, or give them a free copy. It may also order that a document that helps your case cannot be used without its permission. Or it may order that you cannot get disclosure until you comply. Those orders are in addition to the court’s general powers when the rules or an order are not followed. They include an order for costs, a penalty or fine, dismissing a claim, or striking out a document a party filed.
yourDeadline:
Give the other party an affidavit listing every document that is relevant to any issue in the case. List those in your control, or that you can get on request. You have 10 days after the day of the other party's request. This does not cover the financial papers rule 13 requires. Those have their own rules. The other party can then ask to see a listed document, unless it is protected by legal privilege. They can get a copy at their own cost. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: On request, the other party is entitled to examine any document in your list, unless it is protected by legal privilege. They are also entitled to a copy of it, at their own cost at the legal aid rate. For a document listed in a corrected affidavit, they are entitled to examine it and get a copy free of charge, unless it is privileged.

citations.quote: Subject to subrule (1.1), every party shall, within 10 days after another party’s request, give the other party an affidavit listing every document that is, (a) relevant to any issue in the case; and (b) in the party’s control, or available to the party on request.
Subrule (1) does not apply, (a) to the Office of the Children’s Lawyer or to children’s aid societies; and (b) in respect of documents required to be served under rule 13 (financial disclosure).

The other party is entitled, on request, (a) to examine any document listed in the affidavit, unless it is protected by a legal privilege; and (b) to receive, at the party’s own expense at the legal aid rate, a copy of any document that the party is entitled to examine under clause (a).
If a party claims that a document is protected by a legal privilege, the court may, on motion, examine it and decide the issue.

A party who claims that a document is protected by a legal privilege may use it at trial only, (a) if the other party has been allowed to examine the document and been supplied with a copy, free of charge, at least 30 days before the settlement conference; or (b) on the conditions the trial judge considers appropriate, including an adjournment if necessary.

A party who, after serving an affidavit required under subrule (1), (6) or (6.1), finds a document that should have been listed in it, or finds that the list is not correct or not complete, shall immediately serve on the other party a new affidavit listing the correct information.

The other party is entitled, on request, (a) to examine any document listed in an affidavit served under subrule (8), unless it is protected by a legal privilege; and (b) to receive, free of charge, a copy of any document that the party is entitled to examine under clause (a).

If a party does not follow this rule or obey an order made under this rule, the court may, in addition to any power to make an order under subrule 1 (8) or (8.1), (a) order the party to give another party an affidavit, let the other party examine a document or supply the other party with a copy free of charge; (b) order that a document favourable to the party’s case may not be used except with the court’s permission; or (c) order that the party is not entitled to obtain disclosure under these rules until the party follows the rule or obeys the order.

If a person fails to obey an order in a case or a related case, the court may deal with the failure by making any order that it considers necessary for a just determination of the matter, including, (a) an order for costs; (a.1) an order to pay an amount to a party or into court as a penalty or fine; (b) an order dismissing a claim; (c) an order striking out any application, answer, notice of motion, motion to change, response to motion to change, financial statement, affidavit, or any other document filed by a party;

userQuestion: We got an offer to settle, or want to make one — how long does it stay open?
whatsHappening: An offer is an offer to settle one or more claims in a case, motion, appeal or enforcement. A counter-offer is an offer too. The rule on offers applies to an offer made at any time, even before the case is started. An offer can set a time for it to be accepted. If it is not accepted in that time, it is treated as withdrawn.
whatToDoNext: A party may serve an offer on any other party. An offer must be signed personally by the party making it. A party may act in person, without a representative. If the party making the offer has a licensed representative, the representative must sign it too. A licensed representative is a lawyer or family legal services provider. The party who made an offer may withdraw it at any time before it is accepted, by serving a notice of withdrawal. The only valid way to accept an offer is to serve an acceptance on the party who made it. This must be done before the offer is withdrawn, and before the court begins to give a decision on a claim the offer deals with. You may accept an offer even if you rejected it before or made a counter-offer. The terms of an offer must not be mentioned in any document filed in the continuing record. They also must not be mentioned to the judge hearing the claim until the judge has dealt with all the issues except costs. A special party or a child party may make, withdraw or accept an offer. But an acceptance of their offer, or their acceptance of an offer, does not bind them until the court approves.
yourDeadline: To accept an offer, serve an acceptance on the party who made it. Do it before the offer is withdrawn or ends, and before the court starts to give a decision on the claim it covers. An offer not accepted within the time it sets is treated as withdrawn. The party who made it can withdraw it at any time before it is accepted, by serving a notice of withdrawal. It can still be accepted after it was rejected, or after a counter-offer. The party making it must sign it personally. Their licensed representative, if they have one, must sign it too. Making, withdrawing, accepting or rejecting an offer can affect costs. The costs rule in r. 24 (12) has conditions. An offer about a motion must be made at least 1 day before the motion date. An offer about a trial or other hearing must be made at least 7 days before it. The offer must not end or be withdrawn before the hearing starts. It must not be accepted. The party who made it must get an order as good as or better than the offer.
whatHappensAfter: Making, withdrawing, accepting and rejecting offers can have costs results under rule 24. If an accepted offer does not deal with costs, either party can ask the court for costs. If a party does not carry out the terms of an accepted offer, the other party has two choices. They may make a motion to turn the parts of the offer within the court's power into an order. Or they may go on with the case as if the offer had never been accepted.

citations.quote: “offer” means an offer to settle one or more claims in a case, motion, appeal or enforcement, and includes a counter-offer.

A party may serve an offer on any other party.
An offer must be signed personally by the party making it and by their licensed representative.
A party may, (a) act in person; (b) be represented by a lawyer;
“licensed representative” means a lawyer or family legal services provider;

A party may accept an offer in accordance with subrule (9) even if the party has previously rejected the offer or made a counter-offer.

The terms of an offer, (a) shall not be mentioned in any document filed in the continuing record; and (b) shall not be mentioned to the judge hearing the claim dealt with in the offer, until the judge has dealt with all the issues in dispute except costs.

An offer may be made, withdrawn or accepted by a special party or a child party, but neither a party’s acceptance of a special party’s or child party’s offer nor the special party’s or child party’s acceptance of another party’s offer are binding on the special party or child party until the court approves.
The making, withdrawal, acceptance and rejection of offers are subject to the costs consequences provided for under rule 24.
If an accepted offer does not deal with costs, either party is entitled to ask the court for costs.

If a party to an accepted offer does not carry out the terms of the offer, the other party may, (a) make a motion to turn the parts of the offer within the court’s jurisdiction into an order; or (b) continue the case as if the offer had never been accepted.

userQuestion: The applicant changed their application after I answered — do I have to answer again?
whatsHappening: After an answer is filed, an applicant can amend without the court's permission in one way. They serve and file the amended application and also file the consent of all parties. whatToDoNext: You may amend your answer without the court's permission. To do so, serve and file an amended answer within 14 days after you were served with the amended application. userQuestion: The other side is appealing an Ontario Court of Justice order to the Superior Court — what do I have to do?
whatsHappening: The other party is appealing an order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice. They started the appeal by serving a notice of appeal (Form 38) on you. In the appeal, they are the appellant and you are the respondent. The notice of appeal must state the order the appellant wants and the legal grounds for the appeal. At the hearing, no other grounds may be argued unless the court gives permission.
whatToDoNext: The appellant must decide, after talking with you, whether the appeal needs a transcript of the evidence. If you both agree on what evidence to transcribe, the appellant must order that evidence transcribed. If you cannot agree, the appellant must order a transcript of all the oral evidence from the hearing, unless the court orders otherwise. Within 60 days after the appellant serves its appeal record and factum, you must serve your respondent's factum on the appellant and anyone else entitled to be heard, and file it. In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, that time is 30 days instead. That shorter time does not apply to an appeal of an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. Some material from the first court may be needed for the appeal but missing from the appellant's appeal record. If so, you must also serve and file, in the same time, a respondent's appeal record with a copy of that material. Your factum can be no more than 30 pages long, and it must be signed by your lawyer or, if you have none, by you. Its parts include your position on each issue the appellant raised and the exact order you ask the appeal court to make. You may also want to appeal the same order yourself. If you do, the same rule applies to your appeal, and the two appeals are heard together. Your notice of appeal must be served on every other party affected by the appeal or entitled to appeal, and on the clerk of the court where the order was made. Some appeals are under section 121 of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. In those, also serve every other person entitled to notice under subsection 79 (3) of that Act who appeared at the hearing. It must be served within 30 days after the date of a final order, or seven days after the date of a temporary order. In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, it is 30 days for a temporary order too. Again, that does not apply to an appeal of an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. You must then file it within 10 days after serving it. If a transcript is needed, the appellant must file proof it was ordered within 30 days after filing the notice of appeal. Sometimes the appellant does not do that, or does not serve and file its appeal record and factum in time. If so, you may file a motion form (Form 14B) to have the appeal dismissed for delay.
yourDeadline:
Serve your respondent's factum on the appellant and anyone else entitled to be heard, and file it. Do the same with a respondent's appeal record if one is needed. You have 60 days after the day the appellant's appeal record and factum were served. The appellant decides whether a transcript is needed after talking with you. You may also want to appeal the same order. If so, the same rule applies, and the two appeals are heard together. Your own notice of appeal must be served within 30 days after the date of the order. For a temporary order, it is 7 days. Count from the order, not from when you were served. Serving a notice of appeal does not stop a support order from being enforced. It does hold back other payment orders until the appeal is decided. The appellant may miss a step. It may not file proof that a needed transcript was ordered within 30 days after filing the notice. Or it may not serve and file the appeal record and factum on time. You can then file a motion form (Form 14B) to have the appeal dismissed for delay. Other times apply in a child protection case. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: When the appellant's record and factum are filed, and yours are filed or your time to file has run out, the clerk must schedule the appeal for hearing. Serving a notice of appeal does not put a support order on hold, or an order that enforces one. It does put any other payment order in the order under appeal on hold until the appeal is decided. The appellant may withdraw the appeal by serving a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) on every other party and filing it.

userQuestion: FRO says my driver's licence may be suspended for unpaid support — what can I do, and how long do I have?
whatsHappening: A support order filed in the Director's office is in default, and the Director has served you with a first notice. It says your driver's licence may be suspended unless you act within 30 days after the day it was served. If you do not act in that time, the Director may direct the Registrar of Motor Vehicles to suspend your licence. An order to refrain is a court order that the Director not direct the suspension of your licence.
whatToDoNext: Within the 30 days, you can do one of three things. You can make an arrangement the Director accepts for paying the support and the arrears. You can pay all the arrears. Or you can get an order to refrain and file it in the Director's office. If you bring a motion to change the support order, you may also bring a motion for an order to refrain, on notice to the Director. You may bring the motion to refrain first if you or your lawyer undertakes to get a court date for the motion to change within 20 days after the order to refrain. If no court date is obtained within those 20 days, the order to refrain ends automatically. You do not need a motion to change if you have started an appeal of the support order and it has not been decided. Submitting a support variation application to the designated authority in Ontario under the Interjurisdictional Support Orders Act, 2002 counts as a motion to change. So does submitting one to the Central Authority in Ontario under the International Recovery of Child Support and Family Maintenance Convention Act, 2023. The motion for an order to refrain must be made in the court that can change the support order. With the notice of motion, you must serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1, or Form 4 under Ontario Regulation 167/97) and the proof of income set out in section 15 of that regulation. You may not be able to serve and file the proof of income before the motion is heard. If so, the court may still make the order if you or your lawyer undertakes to serve and file it within 20 days. This motion does not have to wait until a conference on the main issues in the case is over.
yourDeadline: To stop the suspension, do one of three things. Make an arrangement the Director accepts for paying the support and the arrears. Or get a court order to refrain and file it in the Director's office. Or pay all the arrears. You have 30 days after the day the first notice was served. For a court order to refrain, these 30 days cannot be extended. A court cannot make an order to refrain after the 30 days. It can make only one for each first notice. If the 30th day is a day court offices are closed, the time for the order does NOT move to the next open day. The order to refrain must be made by the last day court offices are open BEFORE the 30th day. To ask for an order to refrain, bring a motion to change the support order. Also bring a motion for the order to refrain, on notice to the Director. Bring both in the court that can change the support order. You can ask for the order to refrain before you bring the motion to change. To do that, you or your lawyer must give an undertaking (a formal promise) to get a court date for the motion to change. That date must be got within 20 days after the order. You do not need a motion to change if you have appealed the support order and the appeal is not decided. Serve and file a financial statement and proof of income with the notice of motion. If you cannot file proof of income before the motion is heard, the court can still make the order. You or your lawyer must then undertake to serve and file it within 20 days. This motion does not have to wait for a case conference. A motion must normally be served at least 6 days before it is heard, not counting weekends. The order must be made within the 30 days. So start right away.
whatHappensAfter: A court may make an order to refrain only within the 30 days in the first notice, which cannot be extended, and only one for each first notice. If the 30th day is a day court offices are closed, the order must be made by the last day they are open before then. The court must file a copy in the Director's office promptly after it is signed, and it takes effect only when filed there. It ends on the earliest of several days, which include six months after it is made and the day the motion to change or the appeal is decided. You may bring a motion, with notice to the Director, to extend it once for three months, or six months in some cases. The court must make the extending order before the order to refrain ends. If it ends on a day court offices are closed, the last day is the last day they are open before it ends. Payment terms in an order to refrain do not stop arrears from adding up or stop other ways of enforcing the support order.

userQuestion: I was served with a notice of garnishment for family support — can I dispute it?
whatsHappening: A payment order can be enforced in several ways, and garnishment is one of them. The notice of garnishment must be served on the payor and on the garnishee. The payor must also be served with the papers the recipient filed to get it. The notice covers money the garnishee owes the payor when it is served. It also covers money that becomes payable by the garnishee to the payor after that. If the garnishee is a financial institution served as rule 29 requires, the notice reaches only accounts that were open when it was served. The notice stays in effect until it is withdrawn or stopped under rule 29, or until the court orders otherwise. The notice can also cover a debt owed to the payor and another person jointly. Then the garnishee must pay half of that debt, or a larger or smaller amount the court orders. The garnishee must also right away send the other person a notice to co-owner of debt (Form 29C).
whatToDoNext: If you are the payor or the garnishee, you may dispute the garnishment. To do so, serve a dispute on the other parties and file it within 10 days after you were served. Those 10 days run from service of the notice of garnishment or of a statutory declaration of indexed support. Form 29E is the dispute for a payor. Form 29F is the dispute for a garnishee. Filing a dispute does not by itself stop the money being paid out. The Director or clerk must pay out money received right away, even if a dispute has been filed. There are two exceptions. The court may order that this does not apply, at a garnishment hearing or on a motion to change the garnishment. And once served with the notice to co-owner of debt, the sheriff, clerk or Director must hold the money for 30 days. If you are the co-owner, it may be paid out when the 30 days end, unless you serve and file a dispute within the 30 days. The dispute for a co-owner of the debt is Form 29G.
yourDeadline:
If you are the payor or the garnishee, you can dispute a notice of garnishment or a statutory declaration of indexed support. To do so, serve a dispute (Form 29E, 29F or 29G) on the other parties and file it. You have 10 days after the day you were served with the notice of garnishment or the statutory declaration of indexed support. Except for a joint debt, money taken under the garnishment is paid out even if a dispute is filed. The court can order otherwise. After a dispute is served and filed, the clerk issues a notice of garnishment hearing if asked. The payor's situation may later change in a way that affects their ability to pay. The payor can then bring a motion to change the garnishment. While the garnishment is in place, the payor may go back to work for the garnishee or start getting money from a new source. If so, the payor sends a notice to the clerk and to the recipient or the Director within 10 days. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you co-own a debt that was garnished and got a notice to co-owner of debt (Form 29C), you can dispute it. To stop the money being paid out, serve and file a dispute within the 30-day holding period. The sheriff, clerk or Director holds the money for 30 days. They may pay it out when the 30 days end, unless you serve and file a dispute within them. The rule does not say exactly when the 30 days start. So act as soon as you get the notice.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: Within 10 days after a dispute is served and filed, the clerk must issue a notice of garnishment hearing (Form 29H) on request. The clerk must serve and file that notice no later than 10 days before the hearing. At the hearing, the court may make temporary or final orders. These include an order dismissing the dispute or changing how much is garnished. They also include an order suspending the garnishment or setting aside the notice. If the payor's situation changes in a way that affects their ability to pay, the court may, on a motion, make the same kinds of orders. If you are the payor and you go back to work for or get money again from the garnishee, you must send a notice within 10 days. You must also do so within 10 days after you start work with or get money from a new income source. Send it to the clerk, and to the recipient or the Director, by mail or email.

userQuestion: The court sent a notice that our case or motion may be stayed or dismissed as frivolous or an abuse — what happens now?
whatsHappening: The court may stay or dismiss a case that appears on its face to be frivolous or vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the court process. It may do this on its own, or when a party asks for it in Form 1.4. The court may do the same with a motion. When the court decides such an order may be appropriate, it has the clerk give the parties a notice in Form 1.4A. If the notice is about a case, the case is automatically stayed once the clerk gives notice to any party. It stays that way until the court makes an order staying or dismissing it, or an order declining to. Until then, no party may take any step in the case other than the steps in rule 1.4, unless the court orders otherwise. This automatic stay does not apply when the notice is about a motion.
whatToDoNext: These steps apply unless the court orders otherwise. If you brought the case, you may file a written submission responding to the notice, no later than 15 days after receiving it. If the notice is about a motion, this is the party who made the motion. The submission may be no more than 10 pages long. If no submission is filed in time, the court may make the order without any further notice to the parties. If a submission is filed, the court may have the clerk give a copy of it to any other party. If you are another party and you receive a copy, you may file a responding submission of no more than 10 pages, no later than 10 days after receiving it. If you do, you must give a copy to the party who brought the case and to any other party who asks for one. If a party has a lawyer in the case, the copy goes to the lawyer instead of to the party. The notice and any copy of a submission are given by regular service, and rule 6 decides when they count as received. For example, service by mail is effective on the fifth day after it was mailed.
yourDeadline:
If you brought the case or motion the notice is about, file a written submission of no more than 10 pages responding to the notice. You have 15 days after the day you received the notice (Form 1.4A). If no submission is filed in time, the court may make the order without further notice. The notice is given by regular service. Rule 6 decides when it is received. For example, a notice sent by mail is received on the fifth day after mailing. These times apply unless the court orders otherwise.

If you are another party and the clerk gives you a copy of that submission, you may file a reply submission of no more than 10 pages. You have 10 days after the day you received the copy of the submission. Give a copy of your reply to the party who brought the case or motion. Also give one to any other party who asks. These times apply unless the court orders otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: The court may decide in a summary manner, subject to the steps in rule 1.4. For a case, it either makes an order staying or dismissing it, or an order declining to. If the court stays or dismisses a motion, it may also order that the party who made it may not make other motions in the case without the court's permission.

userQuestion: I was served with a request to admit facts or documents — what happens if I ignore it?
whatsHappening: Another party has served you with a request to admit (Form 22). It asks you to admit, for this case only, that a fact is true or that a document is genuine. A copy of each document named in it must be attached, unless you already have a copy or it is not practical to attach one.
whatToDoNext: If you do not serve a response (Form 22A) within 20 days, you are treated as admitting, for this case only, that the facts are true and the documents are genuine. In your response, you can deny that a particular fact is true or that a particular document is genuine. Or you can refuse to admit a particular fact or document, but you must give your reasons for each refusal. Your response must name each fact or document you deny or refuse to admit. Any fact or document your response does not deny, or refuse to admit with reasons, is treated as admitted for this case. Admitting that a document is genuine has a set meaning, which depends on what the document is said to be. For an original, it means the document was written, signed or sealed as it appears to have been. For a copy, it means the copy is complete and accurate. For a copy of something usually sent from one person to another, like a letter, fax or electronic message, it also means it was sent as it appears and was received by the person it is addressed to.
yourDeadline:
Serve a response (Form 22A) for each fact or document in the request that you do not accept. Deny it, or refuse to admit it and give your reasons. You have 20 days after the day you were served with the request to admit. If you do not respond in time, you are treated as admitting them for this case. You can withdraw an admission only if the other party agrees or the court allows it. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: An admission can be taken back only if the other party consents or the court gives permission. This includes an admission that comes from not responding in time.

That means papers about decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact, support or education. Serve them as if the Children's Lawyer were a party in the case. Within 90 days after serving the notice, the Children's Lawyer must serve a report on the parties and file it. The person who prepares the report must sign an affidavit that backs up the facts in it. userQuestion: I was served with a request for a financial statement because a payment order is in default — what do I have to do?
whatsHappening: You have been served with a request for a financial statement. A recipient may serve this request if a payment order is in default. A recipient may ask for a financial statement only once in six months, unless the court gives permission to ask more often.
whatToDoNext: Within 15 days after you were served with the request, you must send a completed financial statement (Form 13) to the recipient. You send it by mail, fax or email. Some parts of rule 13 also apply to your statement, with necessary changes. They are the rules on full disclosure, income tax documents, insufficient financial information, updating a financial statement, correcting and updating, and an order to file a statement. Under the rule on insufficient information, if the recipient believes your statement does not give enough information to fully understand your finances, they must ask you in writing for what is needed. userQuestion: We agreed to a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing — what do we file, and when?
whatsHappening: The purpose of this hearing is to let a judge, in a single hearing, help the parties settle issues and decide issues that are not settled. It is only available in the Superior Court of Justice, including its Family Court, in a municipality shown on the Ontario Courts website as chosen by the Chief Justice. It does not apply to cases under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, interjurisdictional support cases (rule 37) or international child abduction cases (rule 37.2). The parties may ask for it if each party is satisfied of three things. First, the case has no major credibility issues that need cross-examination. Second, no witness who is not a party needs to give oral evidence. Third, it is reasonable to expect the issues can be settled or decided in a summary way. If those conditions are not met, the court must not order the hearing, unless it decides the hearing is right in the circumstances.
whatToDoNext: To ask for the hearing, each party must serve and file a request and consent form (Form 43 or 43A) and a motion form (Form 14B). Form 43A is the version for the Office of the Children’s Lawyer. If you are serving and filing papers for a conference or other hearing, you may file the request and consent form with those papers instead of with a motion form. For the hearing, each party must serve and file a set of papers by the times below, unless the court orders otherwise. They include an affidavit (Form 43B or 14A) of no more than 12 pages, not counting exhibits. The exhibits can total no more than 10 pages, not counting the other listed papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They also include a draft order setting out what you are asking for. They also include any relevant agreements, minutes of settlement or court orders. Add any offer to settle that has not been withdrawn. Other papers depend on the claims and issues in your case. One example is an updated financial statement for a support claim. They are all listed under your deadline. The applicant, or the party who made a motion to change, must serve and file them no later than 20 days before the hearing. The respondent, or the party responding to a motion to change, must serve and file them no later than 10 days before the hearing. No later than five days before the hearing, the applicant or the party who made the motion may serve and file a reply affidavit (Form 14A) of no more than four pages. The reply may only deal with new matters raised in the other party's affidavit. The parts of an affidavit you fill in must be typed or written clearly, double spaced, in at least 12 point size. Each party must give a copy of a confirmation (Form 43C) to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other method. Then, no later than 2 p.m. three days before the hearing, you must give the confirmation to the clerk. You can deliver it to the court office, email it to the court office, or submit it through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. In the confirmation, you must say if you are satisfied that the other party's disclosure is enough for the issues to be settled or decided at the hearing. If you are not satisfied, you must explain why it would be unfair to go ahead without it.
yourDeadline:
If you are the applicant, or the party who made a motion to change, serve and file your hearing papers, as listed below. Do this at least 20 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. Your papers are these. An affidavit (Form 43B or 14A) of no more than 12 pages, with no more than 10 pages of exhibits. A draft order. Any relevant agreements, minutes of settlement or court orders. Any offer to settle that has not been withdrawn. For a support claim, an updated financial statement and certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). For a property claim, updated Forms 13.1, 13B and 13C, with Form 13A. For a parenting claim, an updated Form 35.1, and Form 35.1A if it applies. If the amount or length of support is an issue, your calculations. If support arrears are an issue, a statement of money owed. If special expenses are an issue, proof of the amount. For property issues, any supporting papers and expert or professional reports. For parenting issues, any expert or professional reports. Once the court has ordered the hearing, you cannot withdraw your consent. The exception is with every other party's written consent or the court's permission. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the respondent, or the party responding to a motion to change, serve and file the same hearing papers, as listed above. Do this at least 10 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the applicant or the party who made the motion, you may serve and file a reply affidavit of no more than four pages about new matters in the other party's affidavit. Do this at least 5 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation (Form 43C) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. The parties cannot change this time by agreement.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: The whole hearing is held under oath or affirmation. It starts with settlement talks, with the judge helping the parties settle issues by agreement. If the judge decides more talks are not expected to settle any more issues, the judge may decide any issue left. That decision may be temporary or final. If a party does not take part, the judge may hold the hearing based only on the evidence filed for or received at the hearing. The judge may end the hearing if the judge decides it is no longer appropriate in the circumstances. If that happens, the hearing counts as a conference in the case. The judge may also give any directions the judge thinks necessary on how the case goes on.

citations.quote: permit a judge to, in a single hearing, (i) assist parties in resolving issues on a final basis on consent, and (ii) finally determine, in a summary manner, any issues that are not resolved.

Subject to subrule (5), this rule applies in cases in the Superior Court of Justice, including cases in the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice, in any municipality that is indicated on the Ontario Courts website as having been designated by the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Justice for the purposes of this rule.

This rule does not apply with respect to cases, (a) under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017; (b) to which rule 37 (interjurisdictional support orders) applies; or (c) to which rule 37.2 (international child abduction) applies.

The parties to a case may request a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing in accordance with this rule if each party is satisfied that, (a) the case does not involve significant credibility issues that require cross-examination; (b) the oral evidence of a witness who is not a party is not required; and (c) it is reasonable to expect that the issues can be resolved or determined in a summary manner.

In order to request a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing, each party shall serve and file, (a) a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing request and consent in Form 43 or 43A; and (b) a motion form (Form 14B).

Despite clause (7) (b), if a party is serving and filing documents for the purposes of a conference or other hearing, the party may file the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing request and consent form together with the documents the party is filing for the conference or other hearing, instead of filing it together with a motion form.

The court shall not order a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing if the conditions listed in subrule (6) are not met, unless the court determines that a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing is appropriate in the circumstances.

Each party shall, within the time specified in subrule (15), serve and file the following documents, unless the court orders otherwise: 1. An affidavit (Form 43B or 14A) that meets the following requirements: i. The affidavit, excluding exhibits, is not longer than 12 pages.

ii. Any exhibits to the affidavit, not including any document referred to in paragraphs 2 to 12, do not total more than 10 pages in length, unless the court orders otherwise. 2. A draft order setting out the relief the party is seeking.
3. Any relevant agreements, minutes of settlement or court orders. 4. Any offer to settle that has not been withdrawn.

5. If the case involves a claim for support but not a property claim or a claim for exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents, an updated financial statement (Form 13), together with an updated certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A).

The documents shall be served and filed not later than, (a) 20 days before the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing, for documents filed by the applicant or, in the case of a motion to change a final order or agreement under rule 15, the party making the motion; (b) 10 days before the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing, for documents filed by the respondent or, in the case of a motion to change a final order or agreement under rule 15, the party responding to the motion.

The applicant or party making the motion may, not later than five days before the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing, serve and file an affidavit (Form 14A) that is not longer than four pages replying to any new matters raised by the respondent or party responding to the motion in their affidavit.

userQuestion: Can I question the other side under oath, or do I have to answer their questions?
whatsHappening: Questioning means asking a person questions out loud, under oath or affirmation. The right to question a person includes the right to cross-examine. In a case that is not a child protection case, a party can get information from another party about any issue in two ways. One is with that party's consent, and the other is by a court order. Outside a child protection case, if you do not consent to be questioned, the party who wants to question you needs a court order. In a child protection case, a party has a right to get information from another party about any issue. No consent or court order is needed. To question the other party, the party must serve them with a summons to witness (Form 23) by special service. The party can instead get it by affidavit or another way. To do that, the party must serve them with a request for information (Form 20). There is one exception to this. It is an application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. That regulation is made under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. For that application, the consent-or-order rule applies instead.
whatToDoNext: The court may, on motion, order a person to be questioned by a party, or to give information by affidavit or another way. The person can be a party or someone who is not a party. The court may make this order if three conditions are met. First, it would be unfair to make the party who wants it carry on with the case without it. Second, the information is not easily available any other way. Third, it will not cause unacceptable delay or undue expense. An order can affect someone who is not a party only if they were served by special service. They must have been served with the notice of motion, a summons to witness (Form 23) and the witness fee. If you want to question someone, you must first have served and filed any answer, financial statement or net family property statement the rules require. You must also promise in writing not to serve or file more papers for the next step in the case, except in reply to the answers or information you get. A party can be questioned on their financial statement only after a written request for more information has been made under rule 13 (11) (a). The questioning takes place in the municipality where the person to be questioned lives. But that person and the party asking can agree to hold it in another one. They may not agree on the date and time, who records the questioning, how it is recorded, or paying a non-party's expenses. If so, the court must decide the matter on a motion. All parties must be served with notice at least three days before the questioning. The notice gives the name of the person to be questioned and the address, date and time.
yourDeadline:
If you are arranging the questioning, serve every party with notice of who will be questioned, and the address, date and time. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the questioning. Before you can question anyone, you must have served and filed any answer, financial statement or net family property statement the rules require. You must also promise in writing not to serve or file more papers for the next step, except in reply. The questioning takes place in the city or town where the person lives, unless they and you agree on another. To question someone on their financial statement, you must first have asked in writing for the missing information under r. 13 (11) (a). The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If a person being questioned refuses to answer a question, the court may, on motion, decide whether the question is proper. It may also give directions for the person to return, and make a contempt order. Sometimes the person who refused is a party, or is questioned for a party. Then that party cannot use the refused information as evidence unless the court gives permission. You may find that an answer you gave was wrong or incomplete, or is no longer right or complete. If so, you must give the correct and complete information in writing to all parties right away. What a party gets this way may be used only for this case. There are some exceptions, such as when the person who gave it consents.

citations.quote: Questioning under this rule shall take place orally under oath or affirmation.
The right to question a person includes the right to cross- examine.

In a child protection case, a party is entitled to obtain information from another party about any issue in the case, (a) by questioning the other party, in which case the party shall serve the other party with a summons to witness (Form 23) by special service in accordance with subrule 6 (4); or (b) by affidavit or by another method, in which case the party shall serve the other party with a request for information (Form 20).

In a case other than a child protection case, a party is entitled to obtain information from another party about any issue in the case, (a) with the other party’s consent; or (b) by an order under subrule (5).

Despite subrules (3) and (4), subrule (4) applies with respect to an application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18 (General Matters Under the Authority of the Lieutenant Governor in Council) made under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017.

The court may, on motion, order that a person (whether a party or not) be questioned by a party or disclose information by affidavit or by another method about any issue in the case, if the following conditions are met: 1. It would be unfair to the party who wants the questioning or disclosure to carry on with the case without it. 2. The information is not easily available by any other method. 3. The questioning or disclosure will not cause unacceptable delay or undue expense.

The court may make an order under this rule affecting a non- party only if the non-party has been served with the notice of motion, a summons to witness (Form 23) and the witness fee required by subrule 23 (4), all by special service (subrules 6 (3) and (4)).

A party who wants to question a person or obtain information by affidavit or by another method may do so only if the party, (a) has served and filed any answer, financial statement or net family property statement that these rules require; and (b) promises in writing not to serve or file any further material for the next step in the case, except in reply to the answers or information obtained.
A party may be questioned under rule 20 on a financial statement provided under this rule, but only after a request for information has been made under clause (11) (a).

The questioning shall take place in the municipality in which the person to be questioned lives, unless that person and the party who wants to do the questioning agree to hold it in another municipality.

If the person to be questioned and the party who wants to do the questioning do not agree on one or more of the following matters, the court shall, on motion, make an order to decide the matter: 1. The date and time for the questioning. 2. The person responsible for recording the questioning. 3. The method for recording the questioning. 4. Payment of the expenses of the person to be questioned, if a non-party.
The parties shall, not later than three days before the questioning, be served with notice of the name of the person to be questioned and the address, date and time of the questioning.

If a person being questioned refuses to answer a question, (a) the court may, on motion, (i) decide whether the question is proper, (ii) give directions for the person’s return to the questioning, and (iii) make a contempt order against the person; and (b) if the person is a party or is questioned on behalf or in place of a party, the party shall not use the information that was refused as evidence in the case, unless the court gives permission under subrule (20).

A person who has been questioned or who has provided information in writing by affidavit or by another method and who finds that an answer or information given was incorrect or incomplete, or is no longer correct or complete, shall immediately provide the correct and complete information in writing to all parties.

userQuestion: I want to drop my case or part of it — how do I withdraw, and does it cost me anything?
whatsHappening: A party who does not want to go on with all or part of a case may withdraw all or part of their application, answer or reply. A party who made a motion may also withdraw it, in the same way.
whatToDoNext: To withdraw, serve a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) on every other party and file it. A motion is withdrawn the same way as an application or answer. There is an exception for a special party or a child party. Their application, answer or reply, in whole or in part, can be withdrawn only with the court's permission. The notice of motion for permission must be served on every other party. It must also be served on the Public Guardian and Trustee for a special party, or on the Children's Lawyer for a child party.
whatHappensAfter: If you withdraw all or part of an application, answer or reply, you must pay every other party's costs. This covers their costs for the part you withdrew, up to the date you withdraw. This applies unless the court orders otherwise or the parties agree otherwise. If the party withdrawing is a government agency, costs are up to the court instead.

userQuestion: I need to change my application after I filed it — can I?
whatsHappening: You started a family case and now want to change your application. The rules let an applicant amend the application. How you do it depends on whether an answer has been filed.
whatToDoNext: If no answer has been filed, you may amend without the court's permission. To do so, serve and file an amended application the same way you start a case under rule 8. If an answer has been filed, you may still amend without the court's permission. To do so, serve and file the amended application the same way. Also file the consent of all parties to the change. You can also ask the court for permission to amend on a motion. The court must give it, unless the change would harm another party in a way that costs or a delay could not make up for. In your amended application, underline all changes. Also note in the margin of each changed page the rule or order that allows the change and the date of the change. Your change may add a new claim about a child that was not in your first application. If it does, it must come with the documents that rule 35.1 requires. A claim about a child here means one about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact. These include an affidavit in Form 35.1. A child protection case has its own rule. It applies if a significant change about the child happens after the first document is filed. Then the applicant may serve and file an amended application, an amended plan of care, or both. An application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18 is an exception to that rule.
whatHappensAfter: Under rule 8, an application must be served right away on every other party. Special service must be used, unless the party is one of those listed in rule 8 (6). Once served, the respondent may amend their answer without the court's permission. To do so, they serve and file an amended answer within 14 days after being served. In the child protection case described above, the respondent may serve and file an amended answer and plan of care. They have 30 days after being served if served in Canada or the United States, or 60 days if served outside them.

citations.quote: An applicant may amend the application without the court’s permission as follows: 1. If no answer has been filed, by serving and filing an amended application in the manner set out in rule 8 (starting a case). 2. If an answer has been filed, by serving and filing an amended application in the manner set out in rule 8 and also filing the consent of all parties to the amendment.

On motion, the court shall give permission to a party to amend an application, answer or reply, unless the amendment would disadvantage another party in a way for which costs or an adjournment could not compensate.
An amendment shall be clearly shown by underlining all changes, and the rule or order permitting the amendment and the date of the amendment shall be noted in the margin of each amended page.

If an application or answer is amended to include a claim respecting decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with respect to a child that was not in the original application or answer, the amended application or amended answer shall be accompanied by the applicable documents referred to in rule 35.1.

If an application, answer or motion to change a final order contains a claim respecting decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with respect to a child, the party making the claim shall serve and file with the document that contains the claim, (a) an affidavit in Form 35.1 and, if the child or any party to the case has been involved in a child protection case or has received services from a child protection agency, an affidavit in Form 35.1A; and (b) any other documents required by this rule.

In a child protection case, if a significant change relating to the child happens after the original document is filed, (a) the applicant may serve and file an amended application, an amended plan of care or both; and (b) the respondent may serve and file an amended answer and plan of care, but no later than, (i) 30 days after being served under clause (a), if service was within Canada or the United States of America, or (ii) 60 days after being served under clause (a), if service was outside Canada or the United States of America.

Subrule (2.1) does not apply with respect to an application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18 (General Matters Under the Authority of the Lieutenant Governor in Council) made under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017.
The application shall be served immediately on every other party, and special service shall be used unless the party is listed in subrule (6).

userQuestion: I was served with an appointment for a financial examination about unpaid support — what do I have to do?
whatsHappening: The recipient can serve an appointment for a financial examination (Form 27C) when a payment order is in default. You have been served with one. It is served by special service. At the examination, you may be asked about many things. They include why you have not paid, your income and property, and the debts owed to and by you. You may also be asked about your ability to pay under the order, and whether you intend to obey it.
whatToDoNext: The appointment requires you to come to the financial examination. You must bring any document or thing named in the appointment that meets three tests. You control it or can get it on request. It relates to enforcing the order. And it is not protected by legal privilege. You must also serve a financial statement (Form 13) on the recipient. Do this no later than seven days before the date of the examination. Some parts of rule 13 apply to this statement, such as full disclosure and income tax documents. You must be given at least 10 days' notice of the time and place. The examination is held in one of three places. It can be a place the parties and you agree on. If you live in Ontario, it can be the city or town where you live. Or it can be a place the court chooses. It is held under oath or affirmation. It is held before a person you and the recipient agree on, or as set out in rule 20 (12). The way it is recorded is chosen in the same way.
yourDeadline:
Serve a financial statement (Form 13) on the recipient. Do this at least 7 days before the date of the examination. You must also come to the examination. Bring any document or thing named in the appointment that you control or can get, that relates to enforcing the order, and that is not protected by legal privilege. The examination is held where the parties and you agree. If not, it is in the city or town in Ontario where you live, or where the court chooses. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: Rule 27 (19) applies if you miss the examination or fail to serve the financial statement. It also applies if you come but fail to bring a named document or thing. And it applies if you refuse to take an oath or affirm, or to answer a question. Then the court may, on motion, order another examination and give directions. It may also require you to post a bond (Form 32). If you then fail, without sufficient excuse, to obey that order or direction, the court may act on a motion with special service. It may order you jailed for up to 40 days, all at once or in parts.

citations.quote: If a payment order is in default, the recipient may serve on the payor, by special service (subrule 6 (3)), an appointment for a financial examination (Form 27C), requiring the payor to, (a) come to a financial examination; (b) bring to the examination any document or thing named in the appointment that is in the payor’s control or available to the payor on request, relevant to the enforcement of the order, and not protected by a legal privilege; and (c) serve a financial statement (Form 13) on the recipient, not later than seven days before the date of the examination.

On a financial examination, the payor or other person may be questioned about, (a) the reason for the payor’s default; (b) the payor’s income and property; (c) the debts owed to and by the payor; (d) the disposal of any property by the payor either before or after the making of the order that is in default; (e) the payor’s past, present and future ability to pay under the order; (f) whether the payor intends to obey the order, and any reason for not doing so; and (g) any other matter relevant to the enforcement of the order.

If a party is required under this rule to give a financial statement, the following subrules apply with necessary changes: 13 (6) (full disclosure) 13 (7) or (7.1) (income tax documents) 13 (11) (insufficient financial information) 13 (12) (updating financial statement) 13 (15) (correcting and updating) 13 (16) (order to file statement).
A payor who is served with an appointment or a person who is served with a summons for a financial examination shall have at least 10 days’ notice of the time and place of the examination.

A financial examination shall be held, (a) in a place where the parties and the person to be examined agree; (b) where the person to be examined lives in Ontario, in the municipality where the person lives; or (c) in a place chosen by the court.

A financial examination shall be held under oath or affirmation, before a person chosen by agreement of the payor and recipient or in accordance with subrule 20 (12) (other arrangements for questioning), and shall be recorded by a method chosen in the same way.

Subrule (19) applies if a payor who is served with an appointment or a person who is served with a summons for a financial examination, (a) does not come to the examination as required by the appointment or summons; (b) does not serve on the recipient a financial statement as required by the appointment; (c) comes to the examination, but does not bring a document or thing named in the appointment or summons; or (d) comes to the examination, but refuses to take an oath or affirm or to answer a question.
The court may, on motion, make an order and give directions for another financial examination of the payor or other person and may in addition require the payor or person to post a bond (Form 32).

If a payor or other person, without sufficient excuse, fails to obey an order or direction made under subrule (19), the court may, on motion with special service (subrule 6 (3)), order that the payor or person be imprisoned continuously or intermittently for not more than 40 days.
